<!-- result-1: body_md -->
\label{informal-integ}
Let $A : V_n \to \mathcal{U}(\mathcal{H}_n)$ be a non-abelian $1$-cocycle. There exists a $U \in \mathcal{U}(\mathcal{H}_n)$, unique up to a $U(1)$ phase, such that $A = A_U$.
<!-- end result-1 -->
<!-- result-2: body_md -->
\label{informal-abstract}
Let \(Z_{\tau}^{1}(V_n,\mathcal{U}(\mathcal{H}_n))\) denote the set of non-abelian \(1\)-cocycles for the action of \(V_n\) on \(\mathcal{U}(\mathcal{H}_n)\) by conjugation, \(\tau_a(T)=w(a)Tw(a)^*\), and let \(Z_{\tau}^{1,k}(V_n)\) denote the subset of such $1$-non-abelian cocycles taking values in \(\mathcal{C}^{(k-1)}\). We have
\begin{equation}
\mathcal{C}^{(k)}/U(1)\cong Z_{\tau}^{1,k}(V_n),
\end{equation}
where \(\mathcal{C}^{(k)}/U(1)\) is the \(k\)-th level of the Clifford hierarchy modulo multiplication by $U(1)$ phases.
<!-- end result-2 -->
<!-- result-3: body_md -->
\label{informal-third-cohom}
Let $p$ be an odd prime. Gates in \(\mathcal{C}^{(3)}/U(1)\) are in bijection with triples \((S,q,\alpha)\) defining three maps
\begin{equation}
S:V_n\longrightarrow \operatorname{Sp}(V_n), \qquad
q:V_n\longrightarrow V_n,
\qquad
\alpha:V_n\longrightarrow U(1),
\end{equation}
where \(S\) is a group homomorphism, \(q\) is a \(1\)-cocycle, and \(\alpha\) is a phase function.  
\begin{enumerate}
    \item For fixed \(S\), the possible choices of \(q\), modulo translation, are parametrized by \(H^1(V_n,V_{n,S})\), where $V_{n,S}$ is the group $V_n$ with the group action of $V_n$ defined by \(a\cdot v:=S(a)v\). 
    \item For a fixed pair \((q,S)\), a compatible phase function \(\alpha\) exists if and only if the associated \(U(1)\)-valued \(2\)-cocycle \(R_{q,S}\), defined in \cref{rqs}, is cohomologically trivial in \(H^2(V_n,U(1))\).
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end result-3 -->
<!-- result-4: body_md -->
\label{informal-third-moduli}
Let \(p\) be an odd prime and fix a homomorphism \(S:V_n\to\operatorname{Sp}(V_n)\). The obstruction class \([R_{q,S}]\in H^2(V_n,U(1))\) depends only on the cohomology class \([q]\in H^1(V_n,V_{n,S})\), giving a well-defined map
\begin{align}
\operatorname{ob}_S:H^1(V_n,V_{n,S})&\longrightarrow H^2(V_n,U(1)),\\
[q]&\longmapsto[R_{q,S}].
\end{align}
defined in terms of the symplectic form and the cup product. Consequently, modulo left and right multiplication by Weyl operators, third-level gates with fixed \(S\) are classified by the cohomology classes \([q]\in H^1(V_n,V_{n,S})\) satisfying \(\operatorname{ob}_S([q])=0\).
<!-- end result-4 -->
<!-- result-5: body_md -->
\label{informal-semi-clifford}
Let $p$ be an odd prime and \(U\in\mathcal{C}^{(3)}\). \(U\) is semi-Clifford if and only if \(K_U:=\ker S_U\) contains a Lagrangian subspace of \(V_n\). Equivalently,
    \begin{equation}\label{witt-informal}
    \dim K_U+\dim (K_U\cap K_U^\perp )\geq 2n.
    \end{equation}
    or $K_U^\perp \subseteq K_U$. Every two and three-qudit gate in \(\mathcal{C}^{(3)}\) is semi-Clifford.
<!-- end result-5 -->
<!-- defn-1: body_md -->
\label{weyl-def}
The \(n\)-qudit Weyl group is the subgroup of \(\mathcal U(\mathcal H_n)\) generated by the operators \(X^s\), \(Z^t\), and the scalar phases in \(\Gamma_p\). Equivalently,
\begin{equation}
\mathcal W_n=\{\lambda Z^tX^s:\lambda\in\Gamma_p,\ s,t\in\mathbb F_p^n\}\subseteq\mathcal U(\mathcal H_n).
\end{equation}
<!-- end defn-1 -->
<!-- defn-2: body_md -->
\label{modify-ops}
For \(a=(s,t)\in V_n\), define the normalized Weyl operator
\begin{equation}
w(a)=w(s,t):=
\begin{cases}
\omega^{-2^{-1}s\cdot t}Z^tX^s, & p \text{ odd},\\
i^{-s\cdot t}Z^tX^s, & p=2.
\end{cases}
\end{equation}
<!-- end defn-2 -->
<!-- lem-1: body_md -->
\label{weyl-mul-law}
Let \(p\) be an odd prime. The map
\begin{align}
w : V_n & \longrightarrow \mathcal{U}(\mathcal{H}_n) \\
a & \longmapsto w(a)
\end{align}
is a projective representation of the additive group \(V_n\). More explicitly, \(w(a)w(b)=\omega^{\frac12[a,b]}w(a+b)\) for all \(a,b\in V_n\). Consequently,
\begin{equation}\label{comm-relation-odd prime}
w(a)w(b)=\omega^{[a,b]}w(b)w(a)
\end{equation}
for all \(a,b\in V_n\).
<!-- end lem-1 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
Let \(a=(s,t)\) and \(b=(s',t')\) be elements of \(V_n\). By definition, \(w(a)=\omega^{-2^{-1}s\cdot t}Z^tX^s\) and \(w(b)=\omega^{-2^{-1}s'\cdot t'}Z^{t'}X^{s'}\). Using \(X^sZ^{t'}=\omega^{-s\cdot t'}Z^{t'}X^s\), we obtain
\begin{align}
w(a)w(b)=\omega^{-2^{-1}s\cdot t}\omega^{-2^{-1}s'\cdot t'}Z^tX^sZ^{t'}X^{s'} = \omega^{-2^{-1}s\cdot t-2^{-1}s'\cdot t'-s\cdot t'} Z^{t+t'}X^{s+s'}.
\end{align}
On the other hand, \(w(a+b)=\omega^{-2^{-1}(s+s')\cdot(t+t')}Z^{t+t'}X^{s+s'}\). Therefore,
\begin{align}
w(a)w(b) &= \omega^{-2^{-1}s\cdot t-2^{-1}s'\cdot t'-s\cdot t' +2^{-1}(s+s')\cdot(t+t')} w(a+b) \\ &= \omega^{2^{-1}(t\cdot s'-s\cdot t')} w(a+b) = \omega^{\frac12[a,b]}w(a+b).
\end{align}
\cref{comm-relation-odd prime} follows by comparing \(w(a)w(b)\) and \(w(b)w(a)\) and using \([b,a]=-[a,b]\). This completes the proof.
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- remark-1: body_md -->
\label{qubit-mult-comm}
Let \(p=2\). For \(a=(s,t)\in V_n\), define $\vartheta(a):=s\cdot t,$ where the dot product is evaluated in \(\mathbb Z\) using the representatives \(0,1\). If \(a=(s,t)\) and \(b=(s',t')\), then
\begin{equation}\label{p=2}
w(a)w(b)=i^{\mu(a,b)}w(a+b),
\end{equation}
where
$\mu(a,b):=\vartheta(a+b)-\vartheta(a)-\vartheta(b)+2s\cdot t'
\pmod 4.$
It can be checked that the analog of \cref{comm-relation-odd prime} is
\begin{equation}\label{comm-weyl-qubit}
w(a)w(b)=(-1)^{[a,b]}w(b)w(a),
\end{equation}
where $[a,b]=t\cdot s'+s\cdot t'\in\mathbb F_2.$
Thus, although the commutation relation has the same symplectic form as in the odd prime case, the multiplication multiplier is different.  In what follows, we prove statements for odd \(p\) and indicate the modifications required when \(p=2\).
<!-- end remark-1 -->
<!-- remark-2: body_md -->
\label{symplectic-invariance-weyl-multiplier}
For \(p=2\), the commutator determined by the symplectic form remains
invariant under \(\operatorname{Sp}(V_n)\), but the fourth-root multiplier
\(i^{\mu(a,b)}\) from \cref{p=2} need not be symplectically invariant.
This failure occurs already for one qubit. 
Consider the linear map
\begin{align}
S\colon \mathbb F_2^2 &\longrightarrow \mathbb F_2^2,\\
(s,t) &\longmapsto (s,t+s).
\end{align}
It can be checked that $S \in \operatorname{Sp}(\mathbb F^2_2)$. Let $a=(1,0)$ and $b=(0,1)$.  Then
$\mu(a,b)=3\pmod 4$, $Sa=(1,1)$, $Sb=(0,1)$ and $\mu(Sa,Sb)=1\pmod 4$. Therefore,
$i^{\mu(Sa,Sb)} = i \neq -i = i^{\mu(a,b)}.$
Thus, the multiplier in \cref{p=2} is not invariant under the symplectic group. This distinction will be relevant in \cref{formal-framework}.
<!-- end remark-2 -->
<!-- defn-3: body_md -->
\label{clifford-def}
Let \(\mathcal C^{(0)}:=U(1)I\). The Clifford hierarchy is the family \(\{\mathcal C^{(k)}\}_{k\geq 0}\) of subsets of \(\mathcal U(\mathcal H_n)\) defined recursively as follows. The first level is the Weyl group (up to phase):
\begin{equation}
\mathcal C^{(1)}:=\{\lambda w(a):\lambda\in U(1),\ a\in V_n\}.
\end{equation}
For \(k\geq2\),
\begin{equation}
\mathcal C^{(k)}
:=
\{U\in\mathcal U(\mathcal H_n):U\mathcal C^{(1)}U^*\subseteq\mathcal C^{(k-1)}\}.
\end{equation}
<!-- end defn-3 -->
<!-- fact-1: body_md -->
\label{clifford-props-no-proof}
The Clifford hierarchy satisfies the following properties:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item For each \(k\geq0\), \(\mathcal C^{(k)}\subseteq\mathcal C^{(k+1)}\).
    \item For \(k\geq3\), \(\mathcal C^{(k)}\) is generally not a group.
    \item For each \(k\geq1\), if \(U\in\mathcal C^{(k)}\) then \(w(a)Uw(b)\in\mathcal C^{(k)}\) for all \(a,b\in V_n\).
    \item For each \(k\geq1\), if \(U\in\mathcal C^{(k)}\) then \(CUC^*\in\mathcal C^{(k)}\) for all \(C\in\mathcal C^{(2)}\).
    \item For each \(k\geq2\), if \(U\in\mathcal C^{(k)}\) then $C_1UC_2\in\mathcal C^{(k)}$ for all \(C_1,C_2\in\mathcal C^{(2)}\). 
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end fact-1 -->
<!-- remark-3: body_md -->
The second statement of \cref{clifford-props-no-proof} follows from Anderson's example~\cite{anderson2024groups}: the single-qubit gate \(HT\) lies in \(\mathcal C^{(3)}\), whereas \((HT)^2\) does not belong to \(\mathcal C^{(k)}\) for any \(k\geq1\).
<!-- end remark-3 -->
<!-- defn-4: body_md -->
\label{def:semi-clifford}
An \(n\)-qudit unitary operator \(U\) is called semi-Clifford if there exist \(C_1,C_2\in\mathcal C^{(2)}\) and an \(n\)-qudit diagonal unitary \(D\) such that \(U=C_1DC_2\).
<!-- end defn-4 -->
<!-- lem-2: body_md -->
\label{lem:semi-clifford-diagonal-equivalence}
An \(n\)-qudit unitary operator \(U\) is semi-Clifford if and only if there exist maximal abelian subgroups \(A,A'\subseteq \mathcal C^{(1)}\) such that \(UAU^*=A'\).
<!-- end lem-2 -->
<!-- defn-5: body_md -->
\label{left-action}
Define the action
\begin{align}
\tau:V_n\times \operatorname{End}(\mathcal H_n)
&\longrightarrow \operatorname{End}(\mathcal H_n),
\label{eqn:tau-def}\\
(a,T)&\longmapsto w(a)T w(a)^* .
\end{align}
We refer to \(\tau\) as the conjugation action of \(V_n\) on \(\operatorname{End}(\mathcal H_n)\) and write \(\tau_a(T):=w(a)T w(a)^*\).
<!-- end defn-5 -->
<!-- defn-6: body_md -->
\label{def:derivative}
Let \(U\in\mathcal U(\mathcal H_n)\) and \(a\in V_n\). The quantum derivative of \(U\) in the direction \(a\) is
$\partial_a U:=\tau_a(U)U^*=w(a)Uw(a)^*U^*.$
<!-- end defn-6 -->
<!-- fact-2: body_md -->
\label{derivative-characterization}
For every \(k\geq 1\) and every unitary \(U\in\mathcal U(\mathcal H_n)\), we have \(U\in\mathcal C^{(k)}\) if and only if \(\partial_aU\in\mathcal C^{(k-1)}\) for every \(a\in V_n\).
<!-- end fact-2 -->
<!-- defn-7: body_md -->
\label{def:derivative-field}
For \(U\in \mathcal U(\mathcal H_n)\), define its \emph{Weyl derivative field} to be the map
\begin{align}
A_U : V_n &\longrightarrow \mathcal U(\mathcal H_n), \label{eqn:derivative-field-def}\\
a &\longmapsto \partial_a U.
\end{align}
Equivalently, \(A_U\) records the first order quantum derivative of \(U\) in every direction \(a\in V_n\).
<!-- end defn-7 -->
<!-- lem-3: body_md -->
\label{lem:derivative-field-cocycle-identity}
For every \(U\in \mathcal U(\mathcal H_n)\), the derivative field \(A_U\)
satisfies
\begin{equation}\label{eqn:derivative-field-cocycle-identity}
\tau_b(A_U(a))A_U(b)=A_U(a+b)=\tau_a(A_U(b))A_U(a)
\end{equation}
for all \(a,b\in V_n\). That is,  $A_U$ is a $1$-cocycle.
<!-- end lem-3 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
We have
$A_U(a+b)=\tau_{a+b}(U)U^*=\tau_a(\tau_b(U))U^*.$
Inserting the identity operator in the form $\tau_a(U^*)\tau_a(U) = I$ between the two factors, we get
\begin{align}
A_U(a+b)
&=\tau_a(\tau_b(U))\tau_a(U^*)\tau_a(U)U^*  \\
&=\tau_a(\tau_b(U)U^*)\tau_a(U)U^*=\tau_a(A_U(b))A_U(a).
\end{align}
Since \(V_n\) is abelian, we may interchange \(a\) and \(b\) in the preceding
identity. Hence, $A_U(a+b)=A_U(b+a)=\tau_b(A_U(a))A_U(b)$. This completes the proof.
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- defn-8: body_md -->
\label{def:flat-field}
Let \(A:V_n\to\mathcal U(\mathcal H_n)\) be a map, called a \emph{derivative field}. \(A\) is \emph{flat} if
\begin{equation}
A(a+b)=(A(a)\cdot b)A(b)
\end{equation}
for all \(a,b\in V_n\), where \(T\cdot b:=\tau_b(T)\). We denote the set of \emph{flat derivative fields} by $Z^1_\tau(V_n,\mathcal U(\mathcal H_n))$.
<!-- end defn-8 -->
<!-- example-1: body_md -->
For every \(U\in\mathcal U(\mathcal H_n)\), \cref{lem:derivative-field-cocycle-identity} implies that \(A_U\) is a flat derivative field.
<!-- end example-1 -->
<!-- defn-9: body_md -->
\label{def:gauge-equivalence}
Let \(A,B\in Z^1_\tau(V_n,\mathcal U(\mathcal H_n))\). We say that \(A\) and \(B\) are gauge equivalent, and write \(A\sim B\), if there exists \(G\in \mathcal U(\mathcal H_n)\) such that $B(a)=\tau_a(G)A(a)G^*$ for all \(a\in V_n\).
<!-- end defn-9 -->
<!-- example-2: body_md -->
\label{ex:weyl-field-gauge}
Let \(U,G\in \mathcal U(\mathcal H_n)\). Then the Weyl derivative fields
\(A_U\) and \(A_{GU}\) are gauge equivalent. Indeed, for every \(a\in V_n\) we have
\begin{align}
A_{GU}(a)
&=\tau_a(GU)(GU)^*\\
&=\tau_a(G)\tau_a(U)U^*G^*\\
&=\tau_a(G)A_U(a)G^* .
\end{align}
Thus \(A_{GU}\sim A_U\). In particular, gauge equivalence of Weyl derivative
fields records the effect of left multiplication of the underlying unitary.
<!-- end example-2 -->
<!-- lem-4: body_md -->
\label{lem:gauge-equivalence-preserves-flatness}
Let \(A:V_n\to\mathcal U(\mathcal H_n)\) be a flat derivative field, and let \(G\in\mathcal U(\mathcal H_n)\). Define \(B:V_n\to\mathcal U(\mathcal H_n)\) by $B(a):=\tau_a(G)A(a)G^*$.  Then \(B\) is also a flat derivative field.
<!-- end lem-4 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
Note that $B(0)=\tau_0(G)A(0)G^*=GG^*=I$. Using the flatness of \(A\), we have
\begin{align}
B(a+b)
&=\tau_{a+b}(G)A(a+b)G^* \\
&=\tau_b(\tau_a(G))\tau_b(A(a))A(b)G^* \\
&=\tau_b(\tau_a(G)A(a)G^*)\tau_b(G)A(b)G^*=\tau_b(B(a))B(b)=(B(a)\cdot b)B(b).
\end{align}
for \(a,b\in V_n\). Hence, \(B\in Z^1_\tau(V_n,\mathcal U(\mathcal H_n))\).
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- defn-10: body_md -->
\label{def:non-abelian-H1}
The first non-abelian cohomology set of \(V_n\) with coefficients in \(\mathcal U(\mathcal H_n)\) for the right conjugation action \(T\cdot a:=\tau_a(T)\) is $H^1_\tau(V_n,\mathcal U(\mathcal H_n)):= Z^1_\tau(V_n,\mathcal U(\mathcal H_n))/\sim$, where \(\sim\) is the relation in \cref{def:gauge-equivalence}.
<!-- end defn-10 -->
<!-- fact-3: body_md -->
\label{fact:finite-stone-von-neumann}
Let $p$ be an odd prime and \((V,\beta)\) be a finite-dimensional symplectic vector space over \(\mathbb F_p\). Let \(H(V)\) be a finite group fitting into an extension
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:finite-heisenberg-extension-full}
1 \longrightarrow \mathbb F_p \overset{\iota}{\longrightarrow}
H(V) \overset{\pi}{\longrightarrow} V \longrightarrow 1
\end{equation}
such that \(\iota(\mathbb F_p)=Z(H(V))\).  Assume that the commutator pairing of \(H(V)\) recovers the symplectic form \(\beta\). Namely, for every \(v,w\in V\), and for any lifts \(\widetilde v,\widetilde w\in H(V)\) satisfying $\pi(\widetilde v)=v$ and  $\pi(\widetilde w)=w$ one has $\widetilde v\widetilde w\widetilde v^{-1}\widetilde w^{-1} = \iota(\beta(v,w))$. Fix a non-trivial character \(\chi:\mathbb F_p\to \mathbb C^\times\) given by \(\chi(z)=\omega^z\). There exists, up to unitary equivalence, a unique irreducible unitary representation \(\rho_\chi:H(V)\to \mathcal U(\mathcal H_\chi)\) such that $\rho_\chi(\iota(z))=\chi(z)I_{\mathcal H_\chi}$ for every $z\in\mathbb F_p$.
<!-- end fact-3 -->
<!-- thm-1: body_md -->
\label{thm:integrability}
Let \(p\) be an odd prime. If \(A \in Z_\tau^1(V_n,\mathcal U(\mathcal H_n))\), there exists a unitary \(U \in \mathcal U(\mathcal H_n)\), unique up to global phase, such that \(A = A_U\). Equivalently, every flat derivative field is the Weyl derivative field of a unitary, and the unitary is unique modulo a \(U(1)\)-phase.
<!-- end thm-1 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
Let $H(V_n):=\mathbb F_p \times V_n \cong \mathbb F_p \times \mathbb F^{2n}_p \cong \mathbb F^{2n+1}_p$ with multiplication law
\begin{equation}\label{eqn:explicit-heisenberg-product}
(z,a)(z',b) := \left(z+z'+\frac12[a,b], a+b\right).
\end{equation}
We first verify that \(H(V_n)\) is a central extension of \(V_n\) by \(\mathbb{F}_p\), with central subgroup \(\mathbb{F}_p\times\{0\}\), and that its commutator pairing recovers the symplectic form \([\,\cdot,\cdot\,]\) on \(V_n\). Let \(\pi:H(V_n)\to V_n\) denote the canonical projection. Then \(\pi\) is a group homomorphism with \(\ker\pi=\mathbb{F}_p\times\{0\}\). The inclusion \(\iota:\mathbb{F}_p\to H(V_n)\), defined by \(\iota(z)=(z,0)\), identifies \(\mathbb{F}_p\) with \(\ker\pi\). Moreover, this subgroup is central since
\begin{equation}
(z,0)(z',a)=(z+z',a)=(z',a)(z,0)
\end{equation}
for all \(z,z'\in\mathbb{F}_p\) and \(a\in V_n\).  In fact, this central subgroup is the full center of \(H(V_n)\). Indeed, suppose \((z,a)\in Z(H(V_n))\). Then \((z,a)\) commutes with every \((0,b)\in H(V_n)\). We have
\begin{align}
(z,a)(0,b)(z,a)^{-1}(0,b)^{-1}
&=(z,a)(0,b)(-z,-a)(0,-b)\\
&=\left(z+\frac{1}{2}[a,b],a+b\right)(-z,-a)(0,-b)\\&=\left([a,b],b\right)(0,-b)=\left([a,b],0\right).
\end{align}
Therefore, \([a,b]=0\) for every \(b\in V_n\). Since the symplectic form  on \(V_n\) is non-degenerate, this implies \(a=0\). Hence, every central  element of \(H(V_n)\) lies in \(\mathbb F_p\times\{0\}\). Therefore, $Z(H(V_n))=\mathbb F_p\times\{0\}$. We have that \(H(V_n)\) fits into the central extension of groups
\begin{equation}
1\longrightarrow \mathbb{F}_p
\overset{\iota}{\longrightarrow}
H(V_n)
\overset{\pi}{\longrightarrow}
V_n
\longrightarrow 1.
\end{equation}
It remains to compute the commutator pairing. Let $a,b \in V_n$ and let \((z,a),(z',b)\in H(V_n)\) be arbitrary lifts of \(a\) and \(b\), respectively. Since $(z,a)^{-1}=(-z,-a)$, we compute
\begin{align}
(z,a)(z',b)(z,a)^{-1}(z',b)^{-1}
&=(z,a)(z',b)(-z,-a)(-z',-b) \\
&=\left(z+z'+\frac12[a,b],a+b\right)(-z,-a)(-z',-b) \\
&=\left(z'+\frac12[a,b]+\frac12[a+b,-a],b\right)(-z',-b) \\
&=\left(z'+[a,b],b\right)(-z',-b)=\left([a,b]+\frac12[b,-b],0\right)=([a,b],0).
\end{align}
Hence, the commutator is independent of the lifts and recovers the symplectic form. That is,
\begin{equation}\label{eqn:heisenberg-commutator-recovers-symplectic-form}
[(z,a),(z',b)]_{H(V_n)}=([a,b],0)=\iota([a,b]).
\end{equation}
By \cref{weyl-mul-law}, the map \(a \mapsto w(a)\) defines a projective representation of \(V_n\) with multiplier \(\alpha(a,b)=\omega^{\frac{1}{2}[a,b]}\). Define the map
\begin{align}
B_A : V_n & \longrightarrow \mathcal{U}(\mathcal{H}_n) \\
a & \longmapsto A(a)^*w(a).
\end{align}
Since \(A\) is a flat derivative field, it satisfies \(A(a+b)=\tau_a(A(b))A(a)\). Taking adjoints gives \(A(a+b)^*=A(a)^*\tau_a(A(b)^*)\). Thus, for \(a,b\in V_n\), we have
\begin{align}
B_A(a)B_A(b) &=A(a)^*w(a)A(b)^*w(b) \\ &=A(a)^*\tau_a(A(b)^*)w(a)w(b)\\&=\omega^{\frac12[a,b]}A(a)^*\tau_a(A(b)^*)w(a+b)\\&=\omega^{\frac12[a,b]}A(a+b)^*w(a+b)=\omega^{\frac12[a,b]}B_A(a+b).
\end{align}
Hence, \(B_A\) is also a projective representation of \(V_n\) with the same multiplier \(\alpha\).  We now lift these projective representations to irreducible unitary representations of \(H(V_n)\). Define
\begin{align}
\rho_w:H(V_n)&\longrightarrow \mathcal{U}(\mathcal{H}_n), \label{eqn:rho-w-def}\\
(z,a)&\longmapsto \omega^z w(a).
\end{align}
For every \((z,a)\in H(V_n)\) the operator \(w(a)\) is unitary and \(\omega^z\in U(1)\), so \(\rho_w(z,a)\in \mathcal U(\mathcal H_n)\). Moreover, we have
\begin{align}
\rho_w(z,a)\rho_w(z',b)&=\omega^{z+z'}w(a)w(b) \\
&=\omega^{z+z'+\frac12[a,b]}w(a+b) \\
&=\rho_w\left(z+z'+\frac12[a,b],a+b\right)=\rho_w((z,a)(z',b)).
\end{align}
Hence, $\rho_w$ is a unitary representation of $H(V_n)$. 
\(\rho_w\) is irreducible. Indeed, if \(T\in\operatorname{End}(\mathcal H_n)\) commutes with \(\rho_w(z,a)\) for all \((z,a)\in H(V_n)\), then \(T\) commutes with \(w(a)\) for every \(a\in V_n\). Equivalently, \(\tau_a(T)=T\) for every \(a\in V_n\). 
By \cref{cor:tau-invariants-are-scalars}, we have \(T=\lambda I\) for $\lambda \in U(1)$. Hence, \(\rho_w\) is irreducible. Similarly, define
\begin{align}
\rho_A:H(V_n)&\longrightarrow \mathcal{U}(\mathcal{H}_n), \label{eqn:rho-A-def}\\
(z,a)&\longmapsto \omega^z B_A(a).
\end{align}
As above, \(\rho_A\) is a unitary representation of \(H(V_n)\). We now show that \(\rho_A\) is irreducible. Since \(H(V_n)\) is finite, Maschke's theorem~\cite{serre1977linear,etingof2011introduction} implies that \(\rho_A\) decomposes as a direct sum of irreducible unitary representations. Let \(\mathcal K\subseteq \mathcal H_n\) be any irreducible summand. We have 
$\rho_A(z,0)=\omega^z I$ for \(z\in\mathbb F_p\). Hence, it acts on \(\mathcal K\) by the same scalar character \(z\mapsto \omega^z\). Therefore \(\mathcal K\) is an irreducible representation of \(H(V_n)\) with the central character \(\chi(z)=\omega^z\). By \cref{fact:finite-stone-von-neumann}, we must have \(\dim \mathcal K=p^n\). But \(\dim \mathcal H_n=p^n\). Thus \(\mathcal K=\mathcal H_n\), and so \(\rho_A\) is irreducible. Putting everything together, \(\rho_w\) and \(\rho_A\) are irreducible unitary representations of \(H(V_n)\) with the same central character \(\chi(z)=\omega^z\). By \cref{fact:finite-stone-von-neumann}, \(\rho_w\) and \(\rho_A\) are unitarily equivalent. Hence, there exists \(U\in \mathcal U(\mathcal H_n)\) such that $\rho_A(z,a)=U\rho_w(z,a)U^*$ for all $(z,a)\in H(V_n)$. Setting \(z=0\), we obtain
\begin{equation}
A(a)^*w(a)=B_A(a)=Uw(a)U^* \quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad w(a)Uw(a)^*=A(a)U
\end{equation}
for all $a\in V_n$. Therefore, $\tau_a(U)=A(a)U$. Multiplying on the right by \(U^*\), we obtain
\begin{equation}\label{eqn:integrability-proof-11}
A(a)=\tau_a(U)U^*=\partial_a(U)=A_U(a).
\end{equation}
This proves existence. We now prove uniqueness. Suppose \(U_1,U_2\in \mathcal U(\mathcal H_n)\) both satisfy  $A(a)=\tau_a(U_j)U_j^*$ for all $a\in V_n$ and $j=1,2$. Then $\tau_a(U_2^*U_1)=U_2^*U_1$ for all $a\in V_n$. By \cref{cor:tau-invariants-are-scalars}, we have \(U_2^*U_1=\lambda I\) for $\lambda \in U(1)$. Hence, \(U_1\) and \(U_2\) differ by a $U(1)$ phase. This completes the proof.
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- remark-4: body_md -->
\label{rem:integrability-qubit-case}
When \(p=2\), the normalized Weyl operators satisfy \cref{p=2}. The corresponding Heisenberg group is \(H_2(V_n):=\mathbb Z_4\times V_n\) with multiplication
\begin{equation}
(r,a)(s,b):=(r+s+\mu(a,b),a+b),
\end{equation}
where \(\mu(a,b)\) is the multiplier from \cref{p=2}. Its center is \(\mathbb Z_4\times\{0\}\), and the central character is \(z\mapsto i^z\). Thus, for \(p=2\), the \(\mathbb F_p\)-central Heisenberg group used above is replaced by this \(\mathbb Z_4\)-central extension. The $p=2$ version of the finite Stone--von Neumann theorem~\cite{gurevich-hadani-char2} states that there is, up to unitary equivalence, a unique irreducible unitary representation of $H_2(V_n)$ with this central character. Applying this result to $a\mapsto A(a)^*w(a)$ gives the same conclusion as \cref{thm:integrability}.
<!-- end remark-4 -->
<!-- cor-1: body_md -->
\label{cor:trivial-H1}
Every flat derivative field is gauge equivalent to the trivial field. Equivalently, \(H^1_\tau(V_n,\mathcal U(\mathcal H_n))=\{[A_I]\}\), where \(A_I:V_n\to \mathcal U(\mathcal H_n)\) is defined by $A_I(a)=I$ for all \(a\in V_n\).
<!-- end cor-1 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
By \cref{thm:integrability} and \cref{rem:integrability-qubit-case}, every flat derivative field \(A\) has the form $A(a)=\tau_a(U)U^*$ for some \(U\in \mathcal U(\mathcal H_n)\). Since \(A_I(a)=I\), this can be
rewritten as $A(a)=\tau_a(U)A_I(a)U^*$ for all \(a\in V_n\). By \cref{ex:weyl-field-gauge}, \(A \sim A_I\). Hence, $H^1_\tau(V_n,\mathcal U(\mathcal H_n))=\{[A_I]\}$.
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- defn-11: body_md -->
\label{def:constrained-cocycle-space}
For $k\ge 1$, define
\begin{equation}\label{eqn:Z1k-def}
Z^{1,k}_\tau(V_n) :=
\{A\in Z^1_\tau(V_n,\mathcal U(\mathcal H_n)): A(a)\in \mathcal C^{(k-1)}\ \text{for every } a\in V_n \}.
\end{equation}
<!-- end defn-11 -->
<!-- thm-2: body_md -->
\label{thm:abstract-classification}
For every \(k\ge 1\), the map 
\begin{align}
\Phi_k:\mathcal{C}^{(k)}&\longrightarrow Z^{1,k}_\tau(V_n), \label{eqn:abstract-classification-map}\\
U&\longmapsto A_U.
\end{align}
induces a bijection $\overline{\mathcal C}^{(k)}\cong Z^{1,k}_\tau(V_n)$.
<!-- end thm-2 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
We first check that $\Phi_k$ is well-defined. Let \(U\in \mathcal C^{(k)}\). By \cref{derivative-characterization}, we have \(A_U(a)=\partial_aU\in \mathcal C^{(k-1)}\) for every \(a\in V_n\). By \cref{lem:derivative-field-cocycle-identity}, \(A_U\) is flat. Therefore, $A_U\in Z^{1,k}_\tau(V_n)$. Moreover, if \(U'=\lambda U\) for some \(\lambda\in U(1)\), then $A_{U'}(a)=\tau_a(\lambda U)(\lambda U)^*=A_U(a)$. Thus \(\Phi_k\) is constant modulo global phases and descends to a map
\begin{align}
\overline{\Phi}_k:\overline{\mathcal C}^{(k)}&\longrightarrow Z^{1,k}_\tau(V_n) \\
[U] &\longmapsto A_U
\end{align}
We first prove injectivity. Suppose \(\overline{\Phi}_k([U])=\overline{\Phi}_k([V])\). Then \(A_U=A_V\).  By uniqueness in \cref{thm:integrability} and \cref{rem:integrability-qubit-case}, \(U\) and \(V\) differ by a global phase. Hence \([U]=[V]\) in \(\overline{\mathcal C}^{(k)}\). We now prove surjectivity. Let \(A\in Z^{1,k}_\tau(V_n)\). By \cref{thm:integrability} and \cref{rem:integrability-qubit-case}, there exists a unitary \(U\in \mathcal U(\mathcal H_n)\), unique up to global phase, such that
$A(a)=\tau_a(U)U^*=A_U(a)$
for every \(a\in V_n\). Since \(A\in Z^{1,k}_\tau(V_n)\), we have \(A(a)\in \mathcal C^{(k-1)}\) for every \(a\in V_n\). Therefore, \(A_U(a)=\partial_aU\in \mathcal C^{(k-1)}\) for every \(a\in V_n\). By \cref{derivative-characterization}, \(U\in \mathcal C^{(k)}\). Hence, \(A=\Phi_k(U)\).
<!-- end proof-6 -->
<!-- cor-2: body_md -->
\label{cor:equiv-abstract}
Assume that \(p\) is an odd prime number. For every \(k\geq 2\), the assignment 
\begin{align} \overline \Theta_k:\overline{\mathcal C}^{(k)} &\longrightarrow Y^{k}_\omega(V_n), \\ [U]&\longmapsto B_U, \end{align}
where $B_U(a):=Uw(a)U^*$ induces a bijection $\overline{\mathcal C}^{(k)} \cong Y^{k}_\omega(V_n)$.  Equivalently, \(\overline{\mathcal C}^{(k)}\) is identified with the set of all \(\mathcal C^{(k-1)}\)-valued projective Weyl fields.
<!-- end cor-2 -->
<!-- proof-7: body_md -->
For \(A\in Z^{1,k}_{\tau}(V_n)\), we define \(B_A\) as above. Conversely, for \(B\in Y^{k}_\omega(V_n)\), define \(A_B:V_n\to\mathcal U(\mathcal H_n)\) by \(A_B(a)=w(a)B(a)^*\) for all \(a\in V_n\). We show that the maps
\begin{equation}
\begin{aligned}
f : Z^{1,k}_{\tau}(V_n) &\longrightarrow Y^{k}_\omega(V_n) \\
A &\longmapsto B_A
\end{aligned}
\qquad\qquad
\begin{aligned}
g : Y^{k}_\omega(V_n) &\longrightarrow Z^{1,k}_{\tau}(V_n) \\
B &\longmapsto A_B
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
are inverse to each other. We first show that $f$ is well-defined. Let $A \in Z^{1,k}_{\tau}(V_n)$. By \cref{thm:integrability}, $B_A$ is indeed a projective representation with multiplier $\omega^{\frac{1}{2}[a,b]}$. Putting $b=-a$ in the cocycle identity, we obtain $A(a)^*=\tau_a(A(-a))$ for all $a \in V_n$. Therefore, we have
\begin{align}
B_A(a)=A(a)^*w(a)=\tau_a(A(-a))w(a)&=w(a)A(-a).
\end{align}
Since $A(-a)\in \mathcal C^{(k-1)}$ and $\mathcal C^{(k-1)}$ is stable under left multiplication by Weyl operators by \cref{clifford-props-no-proof}, it follows that $B_A(a)\in \mathcal C^{(k-1)}$ for every $a\in V_n$. Hence, $f$ is well-defined. We now show that $g$ is well-defined.
Let $B \in Y^{k}_\omega(V_n)$. We have $B(0)=I$ and $B(a)B(-a)=I$ for all $a \in V_n$. Hence, $B(a)^*=B(-a)$ for all $a \in V_n$. Therefore, we have
\begin{align}
A_B(a)=w(a)B(a)^*=w(a)B(-a).
\end{align}
Since $B(-a)\in \mathcal C^{(k-1)}$ and $\mathcal C^{(k-1)}$ is stable under left multiplication by Weyl operators by \cref{clifford-props-no-proof}, it follows that $A_B(a)\in \mathcal C^{(k-1)}$ for every $a\in V_n$. We now check flatness. Taking adjoints in the defining relation for the projective representation, we obtain
\begin{equation}\label{eqn:B-projective-adjoint}
B(a+b)^*=\omega^{\frac12[a,b]}B(b)^*B(a)^*.
\end{equation}
for all $a,b \in V_n$. Therefore, we have
\begin{align}
A_B(a+b)
&=w(a+b)B(a+b)^* \\
&=\omega^{\frac12[a,b]}w(a+b)B(b)^*B(a)^* =w(a)w(b)B(b)^*B(a)^*=\tau_a(A_B(b))A_B(a).
\end{align}
Since $V_n$ is abelian, this is equivalent to the cocycle identity. Therefore, $A_B\in Z^{1,k}_{\tau}(V_n)$. Hence, $g$ is well-defined. Note that $g \circ f = \operatorname{Id}_{Z^{1,k}_{\tau}(V_n)}$. Indeed, for \(A\in Z^{1,k}_{\tau}(V_n)\) we have
\begin{align}
A_{B_A}(a)&=w(a)B_A(a)^*\\&=w(a)(A(a)^*w(a))^*=w(a)w(a)^*A(a)=A(a).
\end{align}
for all $a \in V_n$. Hence, $g \circ f = \operatorname{Id}_{Z^{1,k}_{\tau}(V_n)}$. A similar argument shows that $f \circ g = \operatorname{Id}_{Y^{k}_\omega(V_n)}$. Hence, we have $Z^{1,k}_{\tau}(V_n) \cong Y^{k}_\omega(V_n)$. By \cref{thm:abstract-classification}, we have $\mathcal{C}^{(k)}/U(1) \cong Y^{k}_\omega(V_n)$. Explicitly, the bijection is given by the map
\begin{align}
\overline \Theta_k:\overline{\mathcal C}^{(k)}&\longrightarrow Y^{k}_\omega(V_n), \\
[U]&\longmapsto B_{A_U}
\end{align}
such that
\begin{align}
B_{A_U}(a)
&=A_U(a)^*w(a) \\
&=(w(a)Uw(a)^*U^*)^*w(a) \\
&=Uw(a)U^*.
\end{align}
for all $a \in V_n$. This completes the proof.
<!-- end proof-7 -->
<!-- remark-5: body_md -->
\label{rem:equiv-abstract-qubit}
When \(p=2\), one replaces the multiplier \(\omega^{\frac12[a,b]}\) by the multiplier \(i^{\mu(a,b)}\) from \cref{qubit-mult-comm}. Moreover, for \(k\geq2\) define \(Y^{k}_2(V_n)\) to be the set of maps \(B:V_n\to\mathcal C^{(k-1)}\) satisfying $B(a)B(b)=i^{\mu(a,b)}B(a+b)$ for all \(a,b\in V_n\). The proof of \cref{cor:equiv-abstract} is otherwise unchanged.
<!-- end remark-5 -->
<!-- prop-1: body_md -->
\label{level-one-computation}
The map
\begin{align}
f :V_n&\longrightarrow Z^{1,1}_\tau(V_n), \label{eqn:level-one-theta-map}\\
v&\longmapsto A^{(v)}
\end{align}
where $A^{(v)}(a):=\omega^{[a,v]}I$ for all $a \in V_n$.
Consequently, we have $\overline{\mathcal C}^{(1)}\cong V_n$.
<!-- end prop-1 -->
<!-- proof-8: body_md -->
Let \(A\in Z^{1,1}_\tau(V_n)\). By definition, \(A(a)\in \mathcal C^{(0)}=U(1)I\) for every \(a\in V_n\). Hence, there exists a function \(\chi:V_n\to U(1)\) such that
$A(a)=\chi(a)I$. Since \(A\) is flat, we have $A(a+b)=\tau_a(A(b))A(a)$. 
Substituting \(A(a)=\chi(a)I\) gives 
$\chi(a+b)=\chi(a)\chi(b)$
for all $a,b\in V_n$. 
Thus, \(\chi\) is a character of the additive group \(V_n\). Since \(V_n\) is an \(\mathbb F_p\)-vector space, every such character is of the form $\chi(a)=\omega^{\ell(a)}$ for a unique linear functional \(\ell:V_n\to \mathbb F_p\). 
By non-degeneracy of the symplectic form, the map
\begin{align}
V_n &\longrightarrow V_n^*, \\
v &\longmapsto (a \longmapsto [a,v])
\end{align}
is an isomorphism. Therefore there exists a unique \(v\in V_n\) such that $\ell(a) = [a,v]$ for all $a\in V_n$. Therefore, \(A=A^{(v)}\) so \(f\) is surjective. Suppose \(A^{(v)}=A^{(v')}\). Then $\omega^{[a,v]}=\omega^{[a,v']}$ for all $a\in V_n$. Equivalently, $[a,v-v']=0$ for all $a\in V_n$. By non-degeneracy of the symplectic form, \(v-v'=0\). Hence, \(v=v'\) so \(f\) is injective. Thus,  \(Z^{1,1}_\tau(V_n)\cong V_n\). By \cref{thm:abstract-classification}, we have $\overline{\mathcal C}^{(1)}\cong V_n$.
<!-- end proof-8 -->
<!-- lem-5: body_md -->
\label{Pauli-cocycle-equations}
Let \(A:V_n\to \mathcal C^{(1)}\) be a map. Write $A(a)=\beta(a)w(\ell(a))$ for $\beta(a)\in U(1)$ and  $\ell(a)\in V_n$ for all $a \in V_n$. Then \(A\in Z^{1,2}_\tau(V_n)\) if and only if the following conditions hold:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item $\ell(a+b)=\ell(a)+\ell(b)$ for all $a,b\in V_n$. 
    \item If \(p\) is odd, then
    \begin{equation}\label{eqn:beta-cocycle-odd}
    \beta(a+b)=\beta(a)\beta(b)\omega^{[a,\ell(b)]+\frac12[\ell(b),\ell(a)]}
    \end{equation}
    for all $a,b\in V_n$. If \(p=2\), then
    \begin{equation}\label{eqn:beta-cocycle-qubit}
    \beta(a+b)=\beta(a)\beta(b)(-1)^{[a,\ell(b)]}i^{\mu(\ell(b),\ell(a))}
    \end{equation}
    for all $a,b\in V_n$. 
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end lem-5 -->
<!-- proof-9: body_md -->
If $p$ is odd, using \cref{tau-on-Weyl} and \cref{weyl-mul-law} we have
\begin{align}
\beta(a+b) w(\ell(a+b))
&=: A(a+b) \\
&= \tau_a(A(b)) A(a) \\
&= \beta(a)\beta(b)\omega^{[a,\ell(b)]} w(\ell(b))w(\ell(a))\\
&= \beta(a)\beta(b)
   \omega^{[a,\ell(b)] + \frac{1}{2}[\ell(b),\ell(a)]}
   w(\ell(b)+\ell(a)).
\end{align}
Similarly, if \(p=2\) then \cref{qubit-mult-comm} gives
\begin{align}
A(a+b)
&:= \beta(a+b)w(\ell(a+b)) \\
&= \tau_a(A(b))A(a) = \beta(a)\beta(b)(-1)^{[a,\ell(b)]}i^{\mu(\ell(b),\ell(a))}w(\ell(b)+\ell(a)).
\end{align}
Invoking \cref{lem:Weyl-label-phase-uniqueness} shows that $\ell$ is additive and proves \cref{eqn:beta-cocycle-odd} and \cref{eqn:beta-cocycle-qubit}. Conversely, suppose that \(\ell\) and \(\beta\) satisfy (1) and (2). We show that \(A\) is flat. If \(p\) is odd, we have
\begin{align}
\tau_a(A(b))A(a)
&= \beta(a)\beta(b)\,
   \omega^{[a,\ell(b)]+\frac{1}{2}[\ell(b),\ell(a)]}
   w(\ell(b)+\ell(a)) \\& 
   = \beta(a+b)w(\ell(a+b))= A(a+b).
\end{align}
Thus, \(A(a+b)=\tau_a(A(b))A(a)\) for all \(a,b\in V_n\).  A similar argument works for the case \(p=2\). Therefore, \(A\in Z^{1,2}_\tau(V_n)\). This completes the proof.
<!-- end proof-9 -->
<!-- lem-6: body_md -->
\label{lem:clifford-symplectic-consequence}
Let \(C\in \mathcal C^{(2)}\), and write $A_C(a)=\beta(a)w(\ell(a))$. 
Then \(\ell:V_n\to V_n\) is \(\mathbb F_p\)-linear. Moreover, let \(S_C:V_n\to V_n\) be the Weyl-label map determined by
\begin{equation}\label{eqn:UwaUstar-S}
Cw(a)C^*=\gamma(a)w(S_Ca).
\end{equation}
Then \(S_C\) is \(\mathbb F_p\)-linear and symplectic, and
$\ell=\operatorname{Id}_{V_n} - S_C$.
<!-- end lem-6 -->
<!-- proof-10: body_md -->
Since \(C\in \mathcal C^{(2)}\), \cref{derivative-characterization} implies that \(A_C(a)\in \mathcal C^{(1)}\) for every \(a\in V_n\). Therefore, \(A_C\in Z^{1,2}_\tau(V_n)\). By \cref{Pauli-cocycle-equations}, \(\ell\) is additive. Since \(V_n\) is a vector space over \(\mathbb F_p\), every additive map \(V_n\to V_n\) is \(\mathbb F_p\)-linear. Hence, \(\ell\) is \(\mathbb F_p\)-linear. 
Define \(S_C\) by
\begin{equation}\label{eqn:S-label-definition}
Cw(a)C^*=\gamma(a)w(S_Ca), \quad \gamma(a) \in U(1).
\end{equation}
Such an \(S_C\) exists because \(C\in \mathcal C^{(2)}\). Since $Cw(a)w(b)C^* = (Cw(a)C^*)(Cw(b)C^*)$, comparison of both sides gives $S_C(a+b)=S_Ca+S_Cb$. Thus, \(S_C\) is \(\mathbb F_p\)-linear. Next, we show that \(S_C\) preserves the symplectic form. Since $w(a)w(b)w(a)^*w(b)^*=\omega^{[a,b]}I$ for all $a,b \in V_n$, we have
\begin{equation}\label{eqn:S-symplectic-proof-1}
Cw(a)w(b)w(a)^*w(b)^*C^*=\omega^{[a,b]}I.
\end{equation}
Using \(Cw(a)C^*=\gamma(a)w(S_Ca)\) and \(Cw(b)C^*=\gamma(b)w(S_Cb)\) the left-hand side becomes the commutator of \(\gamma(a)w(S_Ca)\) and \(\gamma(b)w(S_Cb)\). The scalar phases cancel in the commutator, so
\begin{align}
Cw(a)w(b)w(a)^*w(b)^*C^*
&= w(S_Ca)w(S_Cb)w(S_Ca)^*w(S_Cb)^*= \omega^{[S_Ca,S_Cb]} I.
\end{align}
Hence, $\omega^{[S_Ca,S_Cb]}=\omega^{[a,b]}$ for all $a,b\in V_n$. Since \(\omega\) is a primitive \(p\)-th root of unity, it follows that $[S_Ca,S_Cb]=[a,b]$ for all \(a,b\in V_n\). Thus, $S_C\in \operatorname{Sp}(V_n)$. Finally, note that
\begin{align}
\label{eqn:ell-S-proof-1}
A_C(a)= w(a)Cw(a)^*C^* \propto w(a)w(-S_Ca)\propto w(a-S_Ca),
\end{align}
where the proportionality factor is a $U(1)$ phase depending on whether $p=2$ or $p$ is odd. Uniqueness of Weyl labels gives $\ell(a)=a-S_Ca$. Hence,  $\ell=\operatorname{Id}_{V_n}-S_C$.
<!-- end proof-10 -->
<!-- prop-2: body_md -->
\label{second-level-symplectic-quotient}
Let \(p\) be an odd prime. The following is a short exact sequence of groups
\begin{equation}\label{eqn:clifford-symplectic-exact-sequence}
1
\longrightarrow
\mathcal C^{(1)}
\longrightarrow
\mathcal C^{(2)}
\longrightarrow
\operatorname{Sp}(V_n)
\longrightarrow
1.
\end{equation}
Consequently, $\mathcal C^{(2)}/\mathcal C^{(1)} \cong \operatorname{Sp}(V_n).$
<!-- end prop-2 -->
<!-- proof-11: body_md -->
Define $\Psi:\mathcal C^{(2)} \rightarrow \operatorname{Sp}(V_n)$ by \(\Psi(C)=S_C\), where $Cw(a)C^*=\gamma_C(a)w(S_Ca).$ By \cref{lem:clifford-symplectic-consequence}, \(S_C\in\operatorname{Sp}(V_n)\). Let \(C,D\in\mathcal C^{(2)}\) and \(a\in V_n\). We have
\begin{align}
\gamma_{CD}(a)w(S_{CD}a)
&=(CD)w(a)(CD)^*\\
&=C(Dw(a)D^*)C^*\\
&=C(\gamma_D(a)w(S_Da))C^*\\
&=\gamma_D(a)\gamma_C(S_Da)w(S_C(S_Da)).
\end{align}
By uniqueness, we have $S_{CD}(a)=S_C(S_Da)$ for all \(a\in V_n\). Therefore, $S_{CD}=S_C\circ S_D,$ so \(\Psi\) is a group homomorphism. We now identify \(\ker\Psi\). Suppose \(C\in\ker\Psi\). Then \(S_C=\operatorname{Id}_{V_n}\). Hence, we have $Cw(a)C^*=\gamma_C(a)w(a)$ for every \(a\in V_n\). Therefore,
\begin{equation}\label{eqn:kernel-derivative-scalar}
\partial_aC = w(a)Cw(a)^*C^* \in U(1)I
\end{equation}
for every \(a\in V_n\). By \cref{derivative-characterization} with \(k=1\), we have \(C\in\mathcal C^{(1)}\). Conversely, suppose that \(C\in\mathcal C^{(1)}\). Then $C=\lambda w(v)$ for some \(\lambda\in U(1)\) and \(v\in V_n\). By \cref{weyl-mul-law}, conjugation by \(w(v)\) only multiplies each \(w(a)\) by a scalar phase. Hence, $S_C=\operatorname{Id}_{V_n}.$ Therefore, $\ker\Psi=\mathcal C^{(1)}.$ It remains to prove surjectivity. Let \(S\in\operatorname{Sp}(V_n)\) and define $w_S(a):=w(Sa).$ Since \(p\) is odd and \(S\) is symplectic, it follows from
\cref{weyl-mul-law} that
\begin{align}
w_S(a)w_S(b)
&=w(Sa)w(Sb)\\
&=\omega^{\frac12[Sa,Sb]}w(Sa+Sb)\\
&=\omega^{\frac12[a,b]}w(S(a+b))=\omega^{\frac12[a,b]}w_S(a+b).
\end{align}
Thus, \(a\mapsto w_S(a)\) is a projective representation of \(V_n\) with the same multiplier as \(a\mapsto w(a)\). Hence, it lifts to an ordinary representation of \(H(V_n)\) with the same central character as the standard Weyl representation. By \cref{fact:finite-stone-von-neumann}, there exists
\(C_S\in\mathcal U(\mathcal H_n)\) such that
$C_Sw(a)C_S^*=w(Sa)$
for every \(a\in V_n\). Hence, \(C_S\in\mathcal C^{(2)}\) and $\Psi(C_S)=S.$ Hence, \(\Psi\) is surjective.
<!-- end proof-11 -->
<!-- remark-6: body_md -->
When \(p=2\), \cref{eqn:clifford-symplectic-exact-sequence} continues to hold after adapting it to the qubit case.
<!-- end remark-6 -->
<!-- lem-7: body_md -->
\label{lem:kappa-cohomology-class}
Let \(p\) be an odd prime. The normalized \(2\)-cocycle
\begin{equation}
\kappa:\operatorname{Sp}(V_n)\times\operatorname{Sp}(V_n)\longrightarrow U(1)
\end{equation}
determines a cohomology class $[\kappa]\in H^2(\operatorname{Sp}(V_n),U(1))$ that is independent of the choice of representatives \(S\mapsto M_S\) 
for every \(S\in\operatorname{Sp}(V_n)\).
<!-- end lem-7 -->
<!-- proof-12: body_md -->
Let \(S\mapsto M_S\) and \(S\mapsto M'_S\) be two normalized choices such that \(M_{\operatorname{Id}_{V_n}}=M'_{\operatorname{Id}_{V_n}}=I\). For every \(S\in\operatorname{Sp}(V_n)\), we have
\begin{align}
M'_SM_S^*w(x)M_SM_S^{\prime *}
&=M'_Sw(S^{-1}x)M_S^{\prime *}=w(x)
\end{align}
for every \(x\in V_n\). Hence, \(M'_SM_S^*\) commutes with every Weyl operator. By \cref{cor:tau-invariants-are-scalars}, there exists \(\eta(S)\in U(1)\) such that $M'_S=\eta(S)M_S$.  Since both choices are normalized, \(\eta(\operatorname{Id}_{V_n})=1\). Let \(\kappa\) and \(\kappa'\) denote the corresponding normalized \(2\)-cocycles. We obtain
\begin{align}
\kappa'(S,T)\eta(ST)M_{ST}
&=\kappa'(S,T)M'_{ST}\\
&=M'_SM'_T\\
&=\eta(S)\eta(T)M_SM_T=\eta(S)\eta(T)\kappa(S,T)M_{ST}.
\end{align}
Therefore,
\begin{equation}\label{eqn:kappa-coboundary-change}
\kappa'(S,T)=\frac{\eta(S)\eta(T)}{\eta(ST)}\kappa(S,T).
\end{equation}
Thus, \(\kappa'=\kappa\cdot\delta\eta\), so \(\kappa\) and \(\kappa'\) determine the same class in \(H^2(\operatorname{Sp}(V_n),U(1))\).
<!-- end proof-12 -->
<!-- remark-7: body_md -->
\label{p2-clifford-remark}
When \(p=2\), the choice of representatives \(M_S\) requires a modification. The reason is that, for \(S\in\operatorname{Sp}(V_n)\), the projective representations \(a\mapsto w(a)\) and \(a\mapsto w(Sa)\) need not have the same multiplier. The details are discussed in \cref{appendix:characteristic-two-third-level}. As in the odd prime case, \cref{eqn:odd-pre-kappa-product} continues to hold when \(p=2\). However, in the odd prime case we showed that the representatives may be chosen so that \(c(S,T)=0\), whereas this need not hold a priori when \(p=2\). This is why the discussion above and the parametrization in \cref{third-clifford} are developed under the assumption that \(p\) is odd. The discussion of \(\kappa\) remains unchanged.
<!-- end remark-7 -->
<!-- lem-8: body_md -->
\label{clifford-normal-form}
Let $p$ be an odd prime. Every \(C\in\mathcal C^{(2)}\) determines a unique triple \((\alpha_C,q_C,S_C)\in U(1)\times V_n\times\operatorname{Sp}(V_n)\) such that
\begin{equation}
C=\alpha_Cw(q_C)M_{S_C},
\end{equation}
for the fixed choice \(S\mapsto M_S\) above.
<!-- end lem-8 -->
<!-- proof-13: body_md -->
Let \(\Psi:\mathcal C^{(2)}\to\operatorname{Sp}(V_n)\) be the map from \cref{second-level-symplectic-quotient}. For \(C\in\mathcal C^{(2)}\), define \(S_C:=\Psi(C)\). By the choice of \(M_{S_C}\), we have \(\Psi(M_{S_C})=S_C\). Since \(\Psi\) is a group
homomorphism and \(M_{S_C}^*=M_{S_C}^{-1}\), we have
\begin{equation}
\Psi(CM_{S_C}^*) = \Psi(C)\Psi(M_{S_C}^*) = S_CS_C^{-1} = \operatorname{Id}_{V_n}.
\end{equation}
Hence, \(CM_{S_C}^*\in\ker\Psi=\mathcal C^{(1)}\). Therefore, there exist \(\alpha_C\in U(1)\) and \(q_C\in V_n\) such that $CM_{S_C}^*=\alpha_Cw(q_C).$ Multiplying on the right by \(M_{S_C}\), we obtain $C=\alpha_Cw(q_C)M_{S_C}$. It remains to prove uniqueness. Suppose that \(C=\alpha w(q)M_S\) for some \(\alpha\in U(1)\), \(q\in V_n\), and \(S\in\operatorname{Sp}(V_n)\). Applying \(\Psi\) gives \(\Psi(C)=S\), since \(\alpha I\) and \(w(q)\) lie in \(\mathcal C^{(1)}=\ker\Psi\). Thus, \(S=S_C\). Therefore, we have $\alpha w(q)M_{S_C} = \alpha_Cw(q_C)M_{S_C},$ which implies that \(\alpha w(q)=\alpha_Cw(q_C)\). By \cref{lem:Weyl-label-phase-uniqueness}, we have \(q=q_C\) and \(\alpha=\alpha_C\).
<!-- end proof-13 -->
<!-- remark-8: body_md -->
\cref{clifford-normal-form} continues to hold for \(p=2\), with essentially the same argument. The only difference lies in the multiplication law for the chosen representatives \(M_S\).
<!-- end remark-8 -->
<!-- cor-3: body_md -->
\label{cor:projective-clifford-affine-symplectic}
Let \(p\) be an odd prime. The map
\begin{align}
\Xi:\operatorname{ASp}(V_n)&\longrightarrow\overline{\mathcal C}^{(2)},\label{eqn:projective-clifford-asp-map}\\
(q,S)&\longmapsto[w(q)M_S]
\end{align}
is a group isomorphism. In particular, there is a split short exact sequence
\begin{equation}\label{eqn:projective-clifford-asp-exact-sequence}
1\longrightarrow V_n\longrightarrow\overline{\mathcal C}^{(2)}\longrightarrow\operatorname{Sp}(V_n)\longrightarrow1.
\end{equation}
<!-- end cor-3 -->
<!-- proof-14: body_md -->
We first show that \(\Xi\) is a homomorphism. Let \((q,S),(r,T)\in\operatorname{ASp}(V_n)\). We obtain
\begin{align}
[w(q)M_S][w(r)M_T]
&=[w(q)M_Sw(r)M_T]\\
&=[w(q)w(Sr)M_SM_T]\\
&=[\kappa(S,T)\omega^{\frac12[q,Sr]}w(q+Sr)M_{ST}]\\
&=[w(q+Sr)M_{ST}]\\
&=\Xi(q+Sr,ST).
\end{align}
This is precisely $\Xi((q,S)(r,T))=\Xi(q,S)\Xi(r,T).$
Thus, \(\Xi\) is a group homomorphism. We next prove surjectivity. Let \([C]\in\overline{\mathcal C}^{(2)}\). By \cref{clifford-normal-form}, there exist unique \(\alpha_C\in U(1)\), \(q_C\in V_n\), and \(S_C\in\operatorname{Sp}(V_n)\) such that  
$C=\alpha_Cw(q_C)M_{S_C}.$
Passing to projective classes gives
\begin{equation}
[C]=[w(q_C)M_{S_C}]=\Xi(q_C,S_C),
\end{equation}
so \(\Xi\) is surjective. Finally, suppose that $\Xi(q,S)=\Xi(r,T).$ Then there exists \(\lambda\in U(1)\) such that
$w(q)M_S=\lambda w(r)M_T.$
By \cref{clifford-normal-form}, we have \(S=T\) and \(q=r\). Hence, \(\Xi\) is injective and therefore an isomorphism. Under this identification, the inclusion \(V_n\to\overline{\mathcal C}^{(2)}\) is given by $q\mapsto[w(q)],$ and the projection \(\overline{\mathcal C}^{(2)}\to\operatorname{Sp}(V_n)\) is given by $[w(q)M_S]\mapsto S.$ The map $S\mapsto[M_S]$ is a section of this projection because \([M_SM_T]=[M_{ST}]\). Hence, \cref{eqn:projective-clifford-asp-exact-sequence} is split.
<!-- end proof-14 -->
<!-- prop-3: body_md -->
\label{third-level-classification}
Let \(p\) be an odd prime.
For each \(a\in V_n\), write \(B(a)\) as
\begin{equation}\label{eqn:third-level-B-normal-form}
B(a)=\alpha_B(a)w(q_B(a))M_{S_B(a)},
\end{equation}
where $\alpha_B(a)\in U(1)$, $q_B(a)\in V_n$ and $S_B(a)\in \operatorname{Sp}(V_n)$. Then \(B\in Y^3_\omega(V_n)\) if and only if for all \(a,b\in V_n\) we have
\begin{align}
S_B(a+b)&=S_B(a)S_B(b), \label{eqn:third-level-S-equation}\\
q_B(a+b)&=q_B(a)+S_B(a)q_B(b), \label{eqn:third-level-q-equation}\\
\alpha_B(a+b)
&=\alpha_B(a)\alpha_B(b)\kappa(S_B(a),S_B(b))
\omega^{\frac12\left([q_B(a),S_B(a)q_B(b)]-[a,b]\right)}.
\label{eqn:third-level-alpha-equation}
\end{align}
<!-- end prop-3 -->
<!-- proof-15: body_md -->
Fix a lifting map $S \mapsto M_S$ appearing in \cref{clifford-normal-form}. Then every element of \(\mathcal C^{(2)}\) has a unique expression of the form $\alpha w(q)M_S$ for some $\alpha\in U(1),\ q\in V_n,\ S\in \operatorname{Sp}(V_n)$. Consequently, for every map \(B:V_n\to \mathcal C^{(2)}\), the functions
\begin{equation}
\alpha_B:V_n\longrightarrow U(1),\qquad
q_B:V_n\longrightarrow V_n,\qquad
S_B:V_n\longrightarrow \operatorname{Sp}(V_n)
\end{equation}
defined by $B(a)=\alpha_B(a)w(q_B(a))M_{S_B(a)}$ are uniquely determined by \(B\). Using \cref{weyl-mul-law} and
\cref{eqn:kappa-third-level-definition}, we have
\begin{align}
B(a)B(b)
&=\alpha_B(a)\alpha_B(b)w(q_B(a))M_{S_B(a)}w(q_B(b))M_{S_B(b)} \\
&=\alpha_B(a)\alpha_B(b)w(q_B(a))w(S_B(a)q_B(b))M_{S_B(a)}M_{S_B(b)} \\
&=\alpha_B(a)\alpha_B(b)\kappa(S_B(a),S_B(b))
\omega^{\frac12[q_B(a),S_B(a)q_B(b)]}
w(q_B(a)+S_B(a)q_B(b))M_{S_B(a)S_B(b)} \notag,
\end{align}
where \(\kappa\) is defined at the end of \cref{sec:low-order}.
On the other hand, we have
\begin{align}
B(a)B(b)
&=\omega^{\frac12[a,b]}B(a+b)=\omega^{\frac12[a,b]}\alpha_B(a+b)w(q_B(a+b))M_{S_B(a+b)}.
\end{align}
Using the uniqueness in \cref{clifford-normal-form}, we obtain
\begin{align}
S_B(a+b)&=S_B(a)S_B(b),\\
q_B(a+b)&=q_B(a)+S_B(a)q_B(b), \\
\alpha_B(a)\alpha_B(b)\kappa(S_B(a),S_B(b))
\omega^{\frac12[q_B(a),S_B(a)q_B(b)]}
&= \omega^{\frac12 [a,b]} \alpha_B(a+b).
\end{align}
This completes the proof.
<!-- end proof-15 -->
<!-- cor-4: body_md -->
\label{cor:third-level-affine-symplectic-homomorphism}
Let \(p\) be an odd prime.
Let \(S:V_n\to \operatorname{Sp}(V_n)\) and \(q:V_n\to V_n\) be maps. Then \cref{eqn:third-level-triple-S} and \cref{eqn:third-level-triple-q} hold if and only if the map
\begin{align}
\Phi_{q,S}: V_n &\longrightarrow \operatorname{ASp}(V_n), \\
a &\longmapsto  (q(a),S(a) )
\end{align}
is a group homomorphism.
<!-- end cor-4 -->
<!-- proof-16: body_md -->
Note that 
\begin{equation}
\Phi_{q,S}(a)\Phi_{q,S}(b)=(q(a)+S(a)q(b),S(a)S(b)).
\end{equation}
Therefore, \(\Phi_{q,S}(a+b)=\Phi_{q,S}(a)\Phi_{q,S}(b)\) is equivalent to $S(a+b)=S(a)S(b)$ and $q(a+b)=q(a)+S(a)q(b)$ for all $a,b \in V_n$.
<!-- end proof-16 -->
<!-- cor-5: body_md -->
\label{cor:third-level-central-extension-form}
Let \(p\) be an odd prime. Define $\widetilde{\operatorname{ASp}}(V_n):=U(1)\times V_n\times \operatorname{Sp}(V_n)$ with multiplication
\begin{equation}
\label{eqn:central-extension-asp-multiplication}
(\alpha,q,S)(\beta,r,T)= (\alpha\beta\,\kappa(S,T)\omega^{\frac12[q,Sr]},q+Sr,ST ).
\end{equation}
Then \(\widetilde{\operatorname{ASp}}(V_n)\) is a central extension
\begin{equation}
1\longrightarrow U(1)\longrightarrow \widetilde{\operatorname{ASp}}(V_n)\longrightarrow \operatorname{ASp}(V_n)\longrightarrow 1,
\end{equation}
where the inclusion \(U(1)\to \widetilde{\operatorname{ASp}}(V_n)\) is given by $\lambda \mapsto (\lambda,0,\operatorname{Id}_{V_n})$ and the projection \(\widetilde{\operatorname{ASp}}(V_n)\to \operatorname{ASp}(V_n)\) is given by $(\alpha,q,S) \mapsto (q,S)$. Moreover, let \(B:V_n\to \mathcal C^{(2)}\) be written in the normal form as in \cref{eqn:third-level-B-normal-form}. Then \(B\) belongs to \(Y^3_\omega(V_n)\) if and only if the associated map
\begin{align}
\widetilde{\Phi}_B:V_n&\longrightarrow \widetilde{\operatorname{ASp}}(V_n), \\
a&\longmapsto  (\alpha_B(a),q_B(a),S_B(a) )
\end{align}
satisfies $\widetilde{\Phi}_B(a)\widetilde{\Phi}_B(b)= (\omega^{\frac12[a,b]},0,\operatorname{Id}_{V_n} )\widetilde{\Phi}_B(a+b)$ for all \(a,b\in V_n\).
<!-- end cor-5 -->
<!-- proof-17: body_md -->
Observe that the multiplication law on \(\widetilde{\operatorname{ASp}}(V_n)\) is induced by the normal form gates in $\mathcal{C}^{(2)}$. Indeed, using the multiplication law and the relation $M_SM_T=\kappa(S,T)M_{ST}$, we have 
\begin{align}
(\alpha w(q)M_S) \cdot (\beta w(r)M_T) &=\alpha\beta w(q)M_Sw(r)M_T \\ &=\alpha\beta w(q)w(Sr)M_SM_T=\alpha\beta\kappa(S,T)\omega^{\frac12[q,Sr]}w(q+Sr)M_{ST}.
\end{align}
Thus,  the product in \cref{eqn:central-extension-asp-multiplication} is associative, because it is transported from operator multiplication. The projection $(\alpha,q,S)\mapsto (q,S)$ is a group homomorphism, since the multiplication law on \(\operatorname{ASp}(V_n)\) is $(q,S)(r,T)=(q+Sr,ST)$. Its kernel is $\{(\lambda,0,\operatorname{Id}):\lambda\in U(1)\}$,  which is naturally identified with \(U(1)\). This subgroup is central because
\begin{equation}
(\lambda,0,\operatorname{Id})(\alpha,q,S)=(\lambda\alpha,q,S)=(\alpha,q,S)(\lambda,0,\operatorname{Id}).
\end{equation}
This defines the claimed central extension. Note that we have
\begin{align}
\widetilde{\Phi}_B(a)\widetilde{\Phi}_B(b) &= ( \alpha_B(a)\alpha_B(b)\kappa(S_B(a),S_B(b))\omega^{\frac12[q_B(a),S_B(a)q_B(b)]}, \\
& q_B(a)+S_B(a)q_B(b), S_B(a)S_B(b) ).
\end{align}
The right-hand side corresponds to
\begin{align}
(\omega^{\frac12[a,b]},0,\operatorname{Id})\widetilde{\Phi}_B(a+b) &= ( \omega^{\frac12[a,b]}\alpha_B(a+b), q_B(a+b), S_B(a+b) ).
\end{align}
Therefore, $B(a)B(b)=\omega^{\frac12[a,b]}B(a+b)$ is equivalent to $\widetilde{\Phi}_B(a)\widetilde{\Phi}_B(b)= (\omega^{\frac12[a,b]},0,\operatorname{Id})\widetilde{\Phi}_B(a+b)$.
<!-- end proof-17 -->
<!-- prop-4: body_md -->
\label{affine-part-H1}
Let \(p\) be an odd prime and \(S:V_n\to \operatorname{Sp}(V_n)\) be a homomorphism. The map $V_n \to V_n$ in \cref{eqn:third-level-triple-q} is an element of \(Z^1(V_n,V_{n,S})\). Replacing \(q\) by \(q+q_v\), where \(q_v(a)=S(a)v-v\), corresponds to conjugating the affine homomorphism $\Phi : V_n \to \operatorname{ASp}(V_n)$ by the translation \((-v,\operatorname{Id}_{V_n})\in \operatorname{ASp}(V_n)\). Consequently, affine symplectic homomorphisms with fixed symplectic part \(S\), up to conjugation by translations, are parametrized by $H^1(V_n,V_{n,S})$.
<!-- end prop-4 -->
<!-- proof-18: body_md -->
The first statement is exactly \cref{eqn:third-level-triple-q}, which is a \(1\)-cocycle from $V_n$ to \(V_{n,S}\). For the second statement, let \(v\in V_n\). In \(\operatorname{ASp}(V_n)\), we have
\begin{align}
(-v,\operatorname{Id}_{V_n})(q(a),S(a))(v,\operatorname{Id}_{V_n})
&=(-v+q(a)+S(a)v,S(a))\\
&=(q(a)+S(a)v-v,S(a)).
\end{align}
Thus, conjugation by the translation \((-v,\operatorname{Id}_{V_n})\) replaces
\(q\) by \(q+q_v\). This proves the claim.
<!-- end proof-18 -->
<!-- lem-9: body_md -->
\label{second-char}
Let \(p\) be an odd prime and \(R_{q,S}:V_n\times V_n\to U(1)\) such that
\begin{equation}\label{rqs}
R_{q,S}(a,b):= \kappa(S(a),S(b)) \omega^{\frac12\left([q(a),S(a)q(b)]-[a,b]\right)}.
\end{equation}
\(R_{q,S}\) is a \(U(1)\)-valued \(2\)-cocycle on \(V_n\).
<!-- end lem-9 -->
<!-- proof-19: body_md -->
Define $T_{q,S}(a):=w(q(a))M_{S(a)}.$ Using the multiplication law for Weyl operators and the cocycle \(\kappa\), we obtain
\begin{align}
T_{q,S}(a)T_{q,S}(b) &=
w(q(a))M_{S(a)}w(q(b))M_{S(b)} \\ &= w(q(a))w(S(a)q(b))M_{S(a)}M_{S(b)} \\ &= \kappa(S(a),S(b)) \omega^{\frac12[q(a),S(a)q(b)]} w(q(a)+S(a)q(b))M_{S(a)S(b)} \\ & =  \kappa(S(a),S(b)) \omega^{\frac12[q(a),S(a)q(b)]} T_{q,S}(a+b).
\end{align}
Thus, \(T_{q,S}\) is a projective representation of \(V_n\) and its multiplier is
\begin{equation}\label{multiplier}
F_{q,S}(a,b)
:=
\kappa(S(a),S(b))
\omega^{\frac12[q(a),S(a)q(b)]}.
\end{equation}
Associativity implies that \(F_{q,S}\) is a \(2\)-cocycle. The multiplier $\omega^{\frac12[a,b]}$ is also a \(2\)-cocycle. Therefore, $R_{q,S}(a,b) = F_{q,S}(a,b)\omega^{-\frac12[a,b]}$ is a \(2\)-cocycle since a ratio of two \(2\)-cocycles is a \(2\)-cocycle.
<!-- end proof-19 -->
<!-- prop-5: body_md -->
\label{phase-cohomology}
Let \(p\) be an odd prime, Let \(q : V_n\to V_n\) and \(S : V_n\to \operatorname{Sp}(V_n)\) satisfy \cref{eqn:third-level-triple-S} and \cref{eqn:third-level-triple-q}, respectively. There exists a phase function \(\alpha:V_n\to U(1)\) such that
$B(a):=\alpha(a)w(q(a))M_{S(a)}$
is in \(Y^3_\omega(V_n)\) if and only if $[R_{q,S}]=0$ in $H^2(V_n,U(1))$, where \(H^2(V_n,U(1))\) denotes group cohomology of \(V_n\) with coefficients in \(U(1)\)  and \(V_n\) acts trivially on \(U(1)\).
<!-- end prop-5 -->
<!-- proof-20: body_md -->
By \cref{third-level-classification}, the map $B(a)=\alpha(a)w(q(a))M_{S(a)}$ belongs to \(Y^3_\omega(V_n)\) if and only if
\begin{equation}
\frac{\alpha(a+b)}{\alpha(a)\alpha(b)} = R_{q,S}(a,b)
\end{equation}
for all \(a,b\in V_n\). Recall that for a \(1\)-cochain \(\phi:V_n\to U(1)\), its \(2\)-coboundary is defined by
\begin{equation}
(\delta\phi)(a,b) = \frac{\phi(a)\phi(b)}{\phi(a+b)}.
\end{equation}
Thus, we have $R_{q,S}(a,b) = (\delta(\alpha^{-1}))(a,b)$. Hence, \(\alpha\) exists if and only if \(R_{q,S}\) is a \(2\)-coboundary. Equivalently, $[R_{q,S}]=0$ in \(H^2(V_n,U(1))\).
<!-- end proof-20 -->
<!-- cor-6: body_md -->
\label{no-choice-kappa}
Let \(p\) be an odd prime.
Let \(S\mapsto M_S\) and \(S\mapsto M'_S\) be two choices of Clifford lifts such that $M'_S=\eta(S)M_S$ for some function \(\eta:\operatorname{Sp}(V_n)\to U(1)\). Let \(\kappa\) and \(\kappa'\) denote the corresponding \(2\)-cocycles, and let \(R_{q,S}\) and \(R'_{q,S}\) denote the corresponding phase-obstruction cocycles. Then the associated cohomology classes agree. That is, $[R'_{q,S}]=[R_{q,S}]$ in $H^2(V_n,U(1))$.
<!-- end cor-6 -->
<!-- proof-21: body_md -->
By \cref{lem:kappa-cohomology-class}, we have $\kappa'(S,T)=\frac{\eta(S)\eta(T)}{\eta(ST)}\kappa(S,T)$. It follows that
\begin{align}
R'_{q,S}(a,b)
&=\kappa'(S(a),S(b))\omega^{\frac12\left([q(a),S(a)q(b)]-[a,b]\right)} \\
&=\frac{\eta(S(a))\eta(S(b))}{\eta(S(a)S(b))}R_{q,S}(a,b)=\frac{\eta(S(a))\eta(S(b))}{\eta(S(a+b))}R_{q,S}(a,b).
\end{align}
If we define $\eta_S(a):=\eta(S(a))$, then $R'_{q,S}=R_{q,S}\cdot\delta\eta_S$.  Thus, \(R'_{q,S}\) and \(R_{q,S}\) differ by a $2$-coboundary, and therefore determine the same cohomology class in \(H^2(V_n,U(1))\).
<!-- end proof-21 -->
<!-- cor-7: body_md -->
\label{cor:third-level-generator-equations}
Let \(p\) be an odd prime.
Let \(e_1,\ldots,e_{2n}\) be an \(\mathbb F_p\)-basis of \(V_n\). A pair of maps $S:V_n\to \operatorname{Sp}(V_n)$ and $q:V_n\to V_n$ satisfies \cref{eqn:third-level-triple-S} and \cref{eqn:third-level-triple-q} if and only if the data $S_i:=S(e_i)$ and $q_i:=q(e_i)$ satisfy
\begin{align}
S_iS_j&=S_jS_i, \label{eqn:third-level-generator-S-commute}\\ S_i^p&=\operatorname{Id}_{V_n}, \label{eqn:third-level-generator-S-order}\\ q_i+S_iq_j&=q_j+S_jq_i, \label{eqn:third-level-generator-q-commute}\\
q_i+S_iq_i+\cdots+S_i^{p-1}q_i&=0 \label{eqn:third-level-generator-q-order}
\end{align}
for all \(1\leq i,j\leq 2n\).
<!-- end cor-7 -->
<!-- proof-22: body_md -->
By \cref{cor:third-level-affine-symplectic-homomorphism}, specifying the pair \((q,S)\) is equivalent to specifying a group homomorphism \(\Phi:V_n\to \operatorname{ASp}(V_n)\) such that \(\Phi(a)=(q(a),S(a))\). The additive group \(V_n\) is generated by \(e_1,\ldots,e_{2n}\), subject to the relations $e_i+e_j=e_j+e_i$ and $pe_i=0$ for \(1\leq i,j\leq 2n\). Therefore, \(\Phi\) is a homomorphism if and only if the elements $\Phi(e_i)=(q_i,S_i)$ commute pairwise and have order dividing \(p\). Using the multiplication law in \(\operatorname{ASp}(V_n)\), the commutativity condition $(q_i,S_i)(q_j,S_j)=(q_j,S_j)(q_i,S_i)$ becomes equivalent to
\begin{align}
S_iS_j=S_jS_i, \qquad
q_i+S_iq_j=q_j+S_jq_i.
\end{align}
Similarly, since \((q_i,S_i)^p= (q_i+S_iq_i+\cdots+S_i^{p-1}q_i, S_i^p )\), the condition \((q_i,S_i)^p=(0,\operatorname{Id}_{V_n})\) holds if and only if $S_i^p=\operatorname{Id}_{V_n}$ and 
\begin{align}
q_i+S_iq_i+\cdots+S_i^{p-1}q_i=0.
\end{align}
This completes the proof.
<!-- end proof-22 -->
<!-- prop-6: body_md -->
\label{cor-cohom}
Let \(p\) be an odd prime.
Let \(q:V_n\to V_n\) and \(S:V_n\to \operatorname{Sp}(V_n)\) 
satisfy \cref{eqn:third-level-triple-S} and \cref{eqn:third-level-triple-q}, respectively. The obstruction class \([R_{q,S}]\in H^2(V_n,U(1))\) vanishes if and only if
\begin{equation}
\frac{R_{q,S}(a,b)}{R_{q,S}(b,a)}=1 
\iff 
\frac{\kappa(S(a),S(b))}{\kappa(S(b),S(a))}\,\omega^{\frac12\left([q(a),S(a)q(b)]-[q(b),S(b)q(a)]-2[a,b]\right)}=1
\end{equation}
In particular, if \(e_1,\ldots,e_{2n}\) is an \(\mathbb{F}_p\)-basis of \(V_n\), then it suffices to check that
\begin{equation}
\frac{\kappa(S(e_i),S(e_j))}{\kappa(S(e_j),S(e_i))}\,\omega^{\frac12\left([q(e_i),S(e_i)q(e_j)]-[q(e_j),S(e_j)q(e_i)]-2[e_i,e_j]\right)}=1
\end{equation}
for all \(1\leq i,j\leq 2n\).
<!-- end prop-6 -->
<!-- lem-10: body_md -->
\label{cor:third-level-phase-lifting}
Let $p$ be an odd prime. Let $S:V_n\to\operatorname{Sp}(V_n)$ be a homomorphism, let $q\in Z^1(V_n,V_{n,S})$, and let $\Phi_{q,S}$ be as in \cref{cor:third-level-affine-symplectic-homomorphism}. Then $[R_{q,S}]=\Phi_{q,S}^*[\sigma]\,h_W^{-1}$ in $H^2(V_n,U(1))$. Consequently, the following statements are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}
\item there exists a phase function $\alpha:V_n\to U(1)$ such that $B(a):=\alpha(a)w(q(a))M_{S(a)}$ is in $Y^3_\omega(V_n)$;
\item $\Phi_{q,S}^*[\sigma]=h_W$ in $H^2(V_n,U(1))$;
\item $[R_{q,S}]=0$ in $H^2(V_n,U(1))$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end lem-10 -->
<!-- proof-23: body_md -->
Pulling back the cocycle $\sigma$ in \cref{eqn:third-level-central-extension-cocycle} along $\Phi_{q,S}$ gives
\begin{equation}\label{eqn:third-level-pulled-back-extension-cocycle}
(\Phi_{q,S}^*\sigma)(a,b)=\kappa(S(a),S(b))\omega^{\frac12[q(a),S(a)q(b)]}.
\end{equation}
Dividing \cref{eqn:third-level-pulled-back-extension-cocycle} by the Weyl multiplier $m_W(a,b)=\omega^{\frac12[a,b]}$ gives
\begin{equation}
(\Phi_{q,S}^*\sigma)(a,b)m_W(a,b)^{-1}=\kappa(S(a),S(b))\omega^{\frac12\left([q(a),S(a)q(b)]-[a,b]\right)}=R_{q,S}(a,b).
\end{equation}
Thus, $R_{q,S}=(\Phi_{q,S}^*\sigma)m_W^{-1}.$ Passing to cohomology and using $h_W=[m_W]$ gives
\begin{equation}
[R_{q,S}]=\Phi_{q,S}^*[\sigma]\,h_W^{-1}.
\end{equation}
Therefore, $\Phi_{q,S}^*[\sigma]=h_W$ if and only if $[R_{q,S}]=0$. By \cref{phase-cohomology}, the latter condition is equivalent to the existence of a phase function $\alpha$ for which $B(a)=\alpha(a)w(q(a))M_{S(a)}$ belongs to $Y^3_\omega(V_n)$.
<!-- end proof-23 -->
<!-- lem-11: body_md -->
\label{prop:third-level-obstruction-H1-invariant}
Let $p$ be an odd prime. Let $S:V_n\to\operatorname{Sp}(V_n)$ be a homomorphism. Suppose that $q,q'\in Z^1(V_n,V_{n,S})$ satisfy
$q'=q+q_v,$
where $q_v(a)=S(a)v-v$ for some $v\in V_n$. Then
$[R_{q',S}]=[R_{q,S}]$
in $H^2(V_n,U(1))$.
<!-- end lem-11 -->
<!-- proof-24: body_md -->
Define $T_{q,S}$ and $T_{q',S}$ as in \cref{cor:third-level-phase-lifting}. Let $\widetilde{T}(a):=w(-v)T_{q,S}(a)w(v)$. We have
\begin{align}
\widetilde{T}(a)&=w(-v)T_{q,S}(a)w(v)\\
&=w(-v)w(q(a))M_{S(a)}w(v)=w(-v)w(q(a))w(S(a)v)M_{S(a)}=\lambda_v(a)T_{q',S}(a),
\end{align}
where
\begin{equation}\label{eqn:third-level-lambda-v}
\lambda_v(a):=\omega^{\frac12\left([-v,q(a)]+[q(a)-v,S(a)v]\right)}.
\end{equation}
Let \(F_{q,S}\) be the multiplier of \(T_{q,S}\), as in \cref{multiplier}. Since conjugation by the fixed unitary \(w(-v)\) does not change the multiplier $F_{q,s}$, we have
\begin{equation}
\widetilde{T}(a)\widetilde{T}(b)=F_{q,S}(a,b)\widetilde{T}(a+b).
\end{equation}
Hence, we have
\begin{align}
\lambda_v(a)\lambda_v(b)F_{q',S}(a,b)T_{q',S}(a+b)&=\widetilde{T}(a)\widetilde{T}(b)=F_{q,S}(a,b)\lambda_v(a+b)T_{q',S}(a+b).
\end{align}
This implies we have
\begin{equation}
F_{q',S}(a,b)=F_{q,S}(a,b)\frac{\lambda_v(a+b)}{\lambda_v(a)\lambda_v(b)}=F_{q,S}(a,b)\bigl(\delta(\lambda_v^{-1})\bigr)(a,b).
\end{equation}
Hence,
$F_{q',S}=F_{q,S}\cdot\delta(\lambda_v^{-1}).$
The multiplier \(m_W(a,b)=\omega^{\frac12[a,b]}\) depends only on \(a\) and \(b\), and is therefore unchanged when \(q\) is replaced by \(q'\). Since \(R_{q,S}=F_{q,S}m_W^{-1}\), it follows that
$R_{q',S}=R_{q,S}\cdot\delta(\lambda_v^{-1}).$
Thus, \(R_{q',S}\) and \(R_{q,S}\) differ by a \(2\)-coboundary and therefore determine the same cohomology class in \(H^2(V_n,U(1))\).
<!-- end proof-24 -->
<!-- lem-12: body_md -->
\label{lem:third-level-symplectic-cup-product}
Let $p$ be an odd prime.
Let $S:V_n\to\operatorname{Sp}(V_n)$ be a homomorphism and let $q,r\in Z^1(V_n,V_{n,S})$. Define
\begin{equation}\label{eqn:third-level-symplectic-cup-cochain}
(q\smile_S r)(a,b):=[q(a),S(a)r(b)].
\end{equation}
Then $q\smile_S r$ is an $\mathbb F_p$-valued $2$-cocycle on $V_n$. Its cohomology class depends only on $[q]$ and $[r]$, and therefore determines a bilinear pairing
\begin{equation}\label{eqn:third-level-symplectic-cup-pairing}
\smile_S:H^1(V_n,V_{n,S})\times H^1(V_n,V_{n,S})\longrightarrow H^2(V_n,\mathbb F_p).
\end{equation}
<!-- end lem-12 -->
<!-- proof-25: body_md -->
The symplectic form is an \(\mathbb F_p\)-bilinear map \(V_{n,S}\times V_{n,S}\to\mathbb F_p\). Hence, it induces an \(\mathbb F_p\)-linear map
\begin{align}
\beta:V_{n,S}\otimes_{\mathbb F_p}V_{n,S}&\longrightarrow\mathbb F_p,\\
x\otimes y&\longmapsto[x,y].
\end{align}
We equip \(V_{n,S}\otimes_{\mathbb F_p}V_{n,S}\) with the diagonal \(V_n\)-action. That is, \(a\cdot(x\otimes y)=S(a)x\otimes S(a)y\) for $a \in V_n$. Similarly, we equip \(\mathbb F_p\) with the trivial \(V_n\)-action. Since \(S(a)\in\operatorname{Sp}(V_n)\) for every \(a\in V_n\), we have
\begin{equation}
\beta\bigl(a\cdot(x\otimes y)\bigr)=\beta\bigl(S(a)x\otimes S(a)y\bigr)=[S(a)x,S(a)y]=[x,y]=a\cdot\beta(x\otimes y).
\end{equation}
Thus, \(\beta\) is \(V_n\)-equivariant and therefore induces a homomorphism
\begin{align}
\beta_*:H^2\left(V_n,V_{n,S}\otimes_{\mathbb F_p}V_{n,S}\right)&\longrightarrow H^2(V_n,\mathbb F_p),\\
[\eta]&\longmapsto[\beta\circ\eta].
\end{align}
For \(q,r\in Z^1(V_n,V_{n,S})\), their ordinary cup product is the \(2\)-cochain with values in \(V_{n,S}\otimes_{\mathbb F_p}V_{n,S}\) given by
\begin{equation}
(q\smile r)(a,b)=q(a)\otimes S(a)r(b).
\end{equation}
The cup product is compatible with the group-cohomology differential:
\begin{equation}
\delta(f\smile g)=(\delta f)\smile g+(-1)^{\deg f}f\smile(\delta g).
\end{equation}
Since \(q\) and \(r\) are \(1\)-cocycles, \(\delta q=\delta r=0\), and hence \(q\smile r\) is a \(2\)-cocycle. The same identity shows that replacing either \(q\) or \(r\) by a cohomologous \(1\)-cocycle changes \(q\smile r\) by a \(2\)-coboundary. Therefore, the cohomology class \([q\smile r]\) depends only on \([q]\) and \([r]\), and the ordinary cup product induces a bilinear map
\begin{align}
\smile:\;H^1(V_n,V_{n,S})\times H^1(V_n,V_{n,S})&\longrightarrow H^2\left(V_n,V_{n,S}\otimes_{\mathbb F_p}V_{n,S}\right),\\
([q],[r])&\longmapsto[q\smile r].
\end{align}
Composing the ordinary cup product with \(\beta_*\) gives a bilinear pairing
\begin{align}
H^1(V_n,V_{n,S})\times H^1(V_n,V_{n,S})&\xrightarrow{\ \smile\ }H^2\left(V_n,V_{n,S}\otimes_{\mathbb F_p}V_{n,S}\right)\xrightarrow{\ \beta_*\ }H^2(V_n,\mathbb F_p),\\
([q],[r])&\longmapsto[q\smile r]\longmapsto[\beta\circ(q\smile r)].
\end{align}
At the cochain level,
\begin{equation}
\bigl(\beta\circ(q\smile r)\bigr)(a,b)=\beta\bigl(q(a)\otimes S(a)r(b)\bigr)=[q(a),S(a)r(b)]=(q\smile_S r)(a,b).
\end{equation}
Therefore,
$[q]\smile_S[r]=\beta_*([q\smile r])\in H^2(V_n,\mathbb F_p),$ which is the pairing in \cref{eqn:third-level-symplectic-cup-pairing}.
<!-- end proof-25 -->
<!-- cor-8: body_md -->
\label{cor:third-level-cup-square-obstruction}
Let $p$ be an odd prime and let $S:V_n\to\operatorname{Sp}(V_n)$ be a homomorphism. For every $[q]\in H^1(V_n,V_{n,S})$, the obstruction map satisfies
\begin{equation}\label{eqn:third-level-cup-square-obstruction}
\operatorname{ob}_S([q])=S^*[\kappa]\cdot\chi_*\left(\frac12([q]\smile_S[q])\right)\cdot h_W^{-1}.
\end{equation}
Here $\chi:\mathbb F_p\to U(1)$
is the standard additive character and
\begin{equation}
\chi_*:H^2(V_n,\mathbb F_p)\longrightarrow H^2(V_n,U(1))
\end{equation}
is the induced map on cohomology.
<!-- end cor-8 -->
<!-- proof-26: body_md -->
By \cref{cor:third-level-phase-lifting}, the map \(\operatorname{ob}_S\) satisfies
\begin{equation}\label{eqn:third-level-obstruction-via-extension}
\operatorname{ob}_S([q])=[R_{q,S}]=\Phi_{q,S}^*[\sigma]\,h_W^{-1}.
\end{equation}
The cocycle \(\kappa(S(a),S(b))\) represents the pullback class \(S^*[\kappa]\). By \cref{eqn:third-level-symplectic-cup-cochain}, the term \(\omega^{\frac12[q(a),S(a)q(b)]}\) represents
\(\chi_*\left(\frac12([q]\smile_S[q])\right)\). Hence,
\begin{equation}\label{pullback-identify}
\Phi_{q,S}^*[\sigma]
=
S^*[\kappa]\cdot\chi_*\left(\frac12([q]\smile_S[q])\right).
\end{equation}
Substituting \cref{pullback-identify} into \cref{eqn:third-level-obstruction-via-extension} gives \cref{eqn:third-level-cup-square-obstruction}.
<!-- end proof-26 -->
<!-- lem-13: body_md -->
\label{lem:third-level-phase-Weyl-actions}
Let \(p\) be an odd prime. Let \(S:V_n\to\operatorname{Sp}(V_n)\) be a homomorphism, and let \(q\in Z^1(V_n,V_{n,S})\) satisfy \(\operatorname{ob}_S([q])=0\). Then the following statements hold.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textnormal{(\arabic*)}]
\item The set of phase functions \(\alpha:V_n\to U(1)\) for which $B(a)=\alpha(a)w(q(a))M_{S(a)}$ belongs to \(Y^3_\omega(V_n)\) is a torsor over
\begin{equation}\label{eqn:third-level-phase-H1}
H^1(V_n,U(1))=\operatorname{Hom}(V_n,U(1)) \cong V_n. 
\end{equation}

\item If \([U]\in\overline{\mathcal C}^{(3)}\) and  $B_U(a):=Uw(a)U^*=\alpha(a)w(q(a))M_{S(a)},$ then left multiplication by \(w(-v)\), for \(v\in V_n\), leaves \(S\) unchanged and replaces \(q\) by the cohomologous cocycle $q+q_v$, where $q_v(a):=S(a)v-v$. 

\item Under the same assumptions as in (2), right multiplication by \(w(v)\) leaves \(S\) and \(q\) unchanged and replaces \(\alpha\) by \(\chi_v\alpha\), where $\chi_v(a)=\omega^{[v,a]}$. 
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end lem-13 -->
<!-- proof-27: body_md -->
Let \(\alpha\) and \(\alpha'\) be two compatible phase functions for the same \(q\) and \(S\). By \cref{third-level-classification}, both satisfy
\begin{equation}\label{ratio}
\frac{\alpha(a+b)}{\alpha(a)\alpha(b)}=R_{q,S}(a,b)=\frac{\alpha'(a+b)}{\alpha'(a)\alpha'(b)}.
\end{equation}
Define \(\chi(a):=\alpha'(a)\alpha(a)^{-1}\). \cref{ratio} implies 
$\chi(a+b)=\chi(a)\chi(b),$
so \(\chi\in\operatorname{Hom}(V_n,U(1))\). Conversely, let \(\chi\in\operatorname{Hom}(V_n,U(1))\) and let \(\alpha\) be a compatible phase function. Since \(\chi(a+b)=\chi(a)\chi(b)\), we have
\begin{align}
\frac{(\chi\alpha)(a+b)}{(\chi\alpha)(a)(\chi\alpha)(b)}
&=\frac{\chi(a+b)\alpha(a+b)}{\chi(a)\chi(b)\alpha(a)\alpha(b)}=\frac{\alpha(a+b)}{\alpha(a)\alpha(b)}=R_{q,S}(a,b).
\end{align}
Thus, \(\chi\alpha\) is again a compatible phase function. Hence, \(\operatorname{Hom}(V_n,U(1))\) acts on the set of compatible phase functions by pointwise multiplication. The calculation above shows that the action is transitive, since any two compatible phase functions differ by a character, and it is free, since \(\chi\alpha=\alpha\) implies \(\chi=1\). Therefore, the set of compatible phase functions is a torsor over
\begin{equation}
H^1(V_n,U(1))=\operatorname{Hom}(V_n,U(1)).
\end{equation}
This proves (1). (2) follows from the calculation in \cref{prop:third-level-obstruction-H1-invariant}, since for \(U_L:=w(-v)U\) we have $B_{U_L}(a)=w(-v)B_U(a)w(v)$. Finally, let \(U_R:=Uw(v)\). We have
\begin{align}
B_{U_R}(a)&=Uw(v)w(a)w(v)^*U^*=\omega^{[v,a]}Uw(a)U^*=\chi_v(a)B_U(a).
\end{align}
Therefore, \(S\) and \(q\) are unchanged, while \(\alpha\) is replaced by \(\chi_v\alpha\). This proves (3).
<!-- end proof-27 -->
<!-- prop-7: body_md -->
\label{prop:third-level-cohomological-moduli}
Let \(p\) be an odd prime. For every homomorphism \(S:V_n\to\operatorname{Sp}(V_n)\), there is a bijection
\begin{equation}\label{eqn:third-level-fixed-S-moduli}
\overline{\mathcal C}^{(3)}_S/ \sim_W \cong \mathfrak M_S=\operatorname{ob}_S^{-1}(0).
\end{equation}
Consequently,
\begin{equation}\label{eqn:third-level-global-moduli}
\overline{\mathcal C}^{(3)}/\!\sim_W \cong \bigsqcup_{S\in\operatorname{Hom}(V_n,\operatorname{Sp}(V_n))}\operatorname{ob}_S^{-1}(0).
\end{equation}
Thus, modulo left and right Weyl multiplication, the third Clifford level is classified by the zero loci of the phase-obstruction maps on the groups \(H^1(V_n,V_{n,S})\).
<!-- end prop-7 -->
<!-- proof-28: body_md -->
Let \([U]\in\overline{\mathcal C}^{(3)}_S\) and \(B_U(a)=\alpha(a)w(q(a))M_{S(a)}\). By \cref{affine-part-H1}, the affine data \(q\) determine a class \([q]\in H^1(V_n,V_{n,S})\). By \cref{phase-cohomology}, the existence of the phase function \(\alpha\) implies \(\operatorname{ob}_S([q])=0\). Hence, there is a map \begin{align}
\overline{\mathcal C}^{(3)}_S &\longrightarrow \mathfrak M_S,\\
[U] &\longmapsto [q].
\end{align} By \cref{lem:third-level-phase-Weyl-actions}, left Weyl multiplication changes \(q\) by a \(1\)-coboundary, while right Weyl multiplication leaves \(q\) unchanged. Therefore, the map is constant on \(\sim_W\)-equivalence classes and descends to a map
\begin{align}
\Theta_S:\overline{\mathcal C}^{(3)}_S/\!\sim_W&\longrightarrow\mathfrak M_S, \\
[U]_{\sim_W}&\longmapsto[q].
\end{align}
We show that \(\Theta_S\) is both injective and surjective.
\begin{enumerate} 
\item (Surjectivity)
Let \([q]\in\mathfrak M_S\), and choose a cocycle representative \(q\). Since \(\operatorname{ob}_S([q])=0\), \cref{phase-cohomology} gives a phase function \(\alpha\) such that \(B(a)=\alpha(a)w(q(a))M_{S(a)}\) belongs to \(Y^3_\omega(V_n)\). By \cref{cor:equiv-abstract}, there exists \([U]\in\overline{\mathcal C}^{(3)}\) with \(B=B_U\). Its symplectic component is \(S\), so \([U]\in\overline{\mathcal C}^{(3)}_S\), and its \(\sim_W\)-equivalence class maps to \([q]\). Thus, \(\Theta_S\) is surjective.

\item (Injectivity)
Suppose that \([U],[U']\in\overline{\mathcal C}^{(3)}_S\) determine the same class in \(\mathfrak M_S\), and write their data as \((\alpha,q,S)\) and \((\alpha',q',S)\). Since \([q']=[q]\), there exists \(v\in V_n\) such that \(q'=q+q_v\). By \cref{lem:third-level-phase-Weyl-actions}, left multiplication of \(U\) by \(w(-v)\) replaces \(q\) by \(q'\). We may therefore replace \(U\) by a \(\sim_W\)-equivalent gate whose affine cocycle is exactly \(q'\). After this replacement, both gates have the same affine and symplectic data \((q',S)\). By \cref{lem:third-level-phase-Weyl-actions}, their phase functions differ by a character of \(V_n\), which is of the form \(\chi_u\) for some \(u\in V_n\). Again by \cref{lem:third-level-phase-Weyl-actions}, right multiplication by \(w(u)\) realizes multiplication of the phase function by \(\chi_u\). Thus, after a further \(\sim_W\)-equivalent replacement, the two projective Weyl fields agree. By \cref{cor:equiv-abstract}, the resulting projective gates agree. Hence, \([U]\sim_W[U']\), so \(\Theta_S\) is injective.
\end{enumerate}
Therefore, \(\Theta_S\) is a bijection, establishing \cref{eqn:third-level-fixed-S-moduli}. Since left and right Weyl multiplication preserve the symplectic component \(S\), the equivalence relation \(\sim_W\) does not mix the strata \(\overline{\mathcal C}^{(3)}_S\). Taking the disjoint union over all homomorphisms \(S:V_n\to\operatorname{Sp}(V_n)\) gives \cref{eqn:third-level-global-moduli}.
<!-- end proof-28 -->
<!-- lem-14: body_md -->
\label{lem:semi-clifford-lagrangian-reformulation}
Let \(p\) be a prime and \(U\in U(\mathcal H_n)\). \(U\) is semi-Clifford if and only if there exist Lagrangian subspaces \(L,L'\subseteq V_n\) such that $U W_L U^*=W_{L'}$.
<!-- end lem-14 -->
<!-- proof-29: body_md -->
This follows directly from \cref{lem:semi-clifford-diagonal-equivalence}.
<!-- end proof-29 -->
<!-- lem-15: body_md -->
\label{C3-in-C2-criterion}
Let \(p\) be an odd prime.
Let \(U\in\mathcal C^{(3)}\). Then \(U\in\mathcal C^{(2)}\) if and only if \(S_U(a)=\operatorname{Id}_{V_n}\) for every \(a\in V_n\).
<!-- end lem-15 -->
<!-- proof-30: body_md -->
If \(U\in\mathcal C^{(2)}\), then \(Uw(a)U^*\in\mathcal C^{(1)}\) for every \(a\in V_n\). By \cref{eqn:BU-third-data-semi}, we have
\begin{equation}
Uw(a)U^*=\alpha_U(a)w(q_U(a))M_{S_U(a)} \in \mathcal{C}^{(1)}
\end{equation}
for all $a \in V_n$. Let $\Psi$ be the map from \cref{second-level-symplectic-quotient}. Since $\ker \Psi = \mathcal C^{(1)}$, we have
\begin{align}
\operatorname{Id}_{V_n}
&= \Psi(\alpha_U(a)w(q_U(a))M_{S_U(a)}) \\
&= \Psi(\alpha_U(a)w(q_U(a)))\Psi(M_{S_U(a)})= \Psi(M_{S_U(a)})=S_U(a)
\end{align}
for all $a \in V_n$. Conversely, if \(S_U(a)=\operatorname{Id}_{V_n}\) for every \(a \in V_n\), then $Uw(a)U^*=\alpha_U(a)w(q_U(a))\in\mathcal C^{(1)}$ for every \(a\in V_n\). Hence, \(U\in\mathcal C^{(2)}\).
<!-- end proof-30 -->
<!-- lem-16: body_md -->
\label{lem:kernel-cocycle-consequences}
Let \(p\) be an odd prime. Let \(U\in\mathcal C^{(3)}\), and set \(K_U:=\ker S_U\) and \(E_U:=\operatorname{im}S_U\). Then \(q_U|_{K_U}\) is linear and injective. Moreover,
\(q_U|_{K_U}\) preserves the symplectic form. That is, 
\begin{equation}\label{eqn:kernel-cocycle-isometry}
[q_U(k),q_U(\ell)]=[k,\ell]
\end{equation}
for all \(k,\ell\in K_U\). Moreover, \(E_U\) fixes \(q_U(K_U)\) pointwise, and
\begin{equation}\label{eqn:kernel-cocycle-mixed-pairing}
[q_U(k),q_U(a)]=[k,a]
\end{equation}
for all \(k\in K_U\) and \(a\in V_n\).
<!-- end lem-16 -->
<!-- proof-31: body_md -->
If \(k,\ell\in K_U\), then \(S_U(k)=S_U(\ell)=\operatorname{Id}_{V_n}\), so \cref{eqn:third-level-triple-q} gives $q_U(k+\ell)=q_U(k)+q_U(\ell).$ Thus,  \(q_U|_{K_U}\) is linear. If \(q_U(k)=0\), then
\begin{equation}
Uw(k)U^*=B_U(k)=\alpha_U(k)w(q_U(k))=\alpha_U(k)I.
\end{equation}
Hence, \(w(k)\in U(1)I\), so \(k=0\) by \cref{lem:weyl-scalar-label}. Thus, \(q_U|_{K_U}\) is injective.
For \(k,\ell\in K_U\), conjugating the Weyl commutator by \(U\) gives
\begin{equation}\label{co-1}
B_U(k)B_U(\ell)B_U(k)^*B_U(\ell)^*=Uw(k)w(\ell)w(k)^*w(\ell)^*U^*=\omega^{[k,\ell]}I.
\end{equation}
Since \(k,\ell\in K_U\), we have \(B_U(k)=\alpha_U(k)w(q_U(k))\) and \(B_U(\ell)=\alpha_U(\ell)w(q_U(\ell))\). Therefore, we have
\begin{equation}\label{co-2}
B_U(k)B_U(\ell)B_U(k)^*B_U(\ell)^*=\omega^{[q_U(k),q_U(\ell)]}I.
\end{equation}
Comparing \cref{co-1} and \cref{co-2} gives \cref{eqn:kernel-cocycle-isometry}. Now let \(k\in K_U\) and \(a\in V_n\). Since \(V_n\) is abelian, \cref{eqn:third-level-triple-q} gives
\begin{equation}
q_U(k)+q_U(a)=q_U(k+a)=q_U(a+k)=q_U(a)+S_U(a)q_U(k).
\end{equation}
Hence \(S_U(a)q_U(k)=q_U(k)\). Thus, \(E_U\) fixes \(q_U(K_U)\) pointwise. We have
\begin{equation}\label{co-3}
B_U(k)B_U(a)B_U(k)^*B_U(a)^*=\omega^{[k,a]}I.
\end{equation}
Since \(E_U\) fixes \(q_U(K_U)\) pointwise, we have
\begin{equation}
M_{S_U(a)}w(q_U(k))M_{S_U(a)}^*=w(S_U(a)q_U(k))=w(q_U(k)),
\end{equation}
so \(M_{S_U(a)}\) commutes with \(w(q_U(k))\). Since \(k\in K_U\), we have $B_U(k)=\alpha_U(k)w(q_U(k))$. Since  $B_U(a)=\alpha_U(a)w(q_U(a))M_{S_U(a)}$ and the scalar phases cancel in the commutator, we have
\begin{align}
B_U(k)B_U(a)B_U(k)^*B_U(a)^*
&=w(q_U(k))w(q_U(a))M_{S_U(a)}w(q_U(k))^*M_{S_U(a)}^*w(q_U(a))^* \\
&=w(q_U(k))w(q_U(a))w(q_U(k))^*w(q_U(a))^*\\
&=\omega^{[q_U(k),q_U(a)]}I. \label{co-4}
\end{align}
Comparing \cref{co-3} and \cref{co-4} gives \cref{eqn:kernel-cocycle-mixed-pairing}.
<!-- end proof-31 -->
<!-- prop-8: body_md -->
\label{semi-clifford-kernel-criterion}
Let \(p\) be an odd prime.
Let \(U\in\mathcal C^{(3)}\) and $K_U := \ker S_U =\{a\in V_n:S_U(a)=\operatorname{Id}_{V_n}\}$. 
Then \(U\) is semi-Clifford if and only if \(K_U\) contains a Lagrangian subspace of \(V_n\).
<!-- end prop-8 -->
<!-- proof-32: body_md -->
If \(U\) is semi-Clifford, then there exist Lagrangian subspaces \(L,L'\subseteq V_n\) such that \(UW_LU^*=W_{L'}\). Hence, \(Uw(\ell)U^*\) is a Weyl operator for every \(\ell\in L\). An argument analogous to that used in \cref{C3-in-C2-criterion} then shows that \(S_U(\ell)=\operatorname{Id}_{V_n}\) for every \(\ell\in L\). Thus, \(L\subseteq K_U\). Conversely, suppose that \(L\subseteq K_U\) is a Lagrangian subspace. We have 
\begin{equation}
Uw(\ell)U^*=B_U(\ell)=\alpha_U(\ell)w(q_U(\ell))
\end{equation}
for every \(\ell\in L\). Since \(L\) is isotropic, the operators \(w(\ell)\) commute for all \(\ell\in L\). This implies that $B_U(\ell)$ and $B_U(\ell')$ commute, which implies that $w(q_U(\ell))w(q_U(\ell'))= w(q_U(\ell'))w(q_U(\ell))$ for all $\ell,\ell' \in L$. This implies that $[q_U(\ell),q_U(\ell')]=0$ for all $\ell,\ell' \in L$. Let
\begin{equation}
L' := \{ q_U(\ell) \mid \ell \in L\} = q_U(L)
\end{equation}
Note that $q_U|_L$ is a linear map. This follows from \cref{lem:kernel-cocycle-consequences}. The argument presented above shows that $L' $ is an isotropic subspace of $V_n$. 
Moreover, the map \(q_U|_L\) is injective. This also follows from \cref{lem:kernel-cocycle-consequences}. 
Thus, \(q_U|_L : L \to L'\) is a linear isomorphism. We have $\dim  L = n$ since \(L\) is a Lagrangian subspace. Thus, \(L' := q_U(L)\) is an \(n\)-dimensional isotropic subspace, so it is also a Lagrangian subspace. Clearly,  $UW_LU^*=W_{L'}$ so \(U\) is semi-Clifford.
<!-- end proof-32 -->
<!-- lem-17: body_md -->
\label{lem:witt-index-subspace}
Let \(p\) be a prime and let \(K\subseteq V_n\) be a subspace. Define
\begin{equation}
\operatorname{rad}(K):=\{k\in K:[k,k']=0\text{ for all }k'\in K\}=K\cap K^\perp.
\end{equation}
Then there exists an isotropic subspace $L$ of $V_n$ such that \(L\subseteq K\) and
\begin{equation}
\dim L= \frac{\dim K+\dim \operatorname{rad}(K)}{2} = \frac{\dim K+\dim (K\cap K^\perp)}{2}. 
\end{equation}
Moreover, no isotropic subspace of $V_n$  contained in \(K\) has larger dimension. Hence, the maximum dimension of a subspace of \(K\) that is isotropic in \(V_n\) is
\begin{equation}\label{eqn:witt-index-formula}
\frac{\dim K+\dim \operatorname{rad}(K)}{2}
=
\frac{\dim K+\dim (K\cap K^\perp)}{2}.
\end{equation}
<!-- end lem-17 -->
<!-- proof-33: body_md -->
The restriction of the symplectic form to \(K\) may be degenerate, and its degeneracy is measured precisely by \(\operatorname{rad}(K)\). Since \(\operatorname{rad}(K)\) is the kernel of the restricted alternating form on \(K\), the form descends to a non-degenerate alternating form on the quotient \(K/\operatorname{rad}(K)\). Hence, \(K/\operatorname{rad}(K)\) is a symplectic vector space, and therefore it has Lagrangian subspaces of dimension
\begin{equation}
\frac{1}{2}\dim (K/\operatorname{rad}(K))=
\frac{1}{2}(\dim K-\dim \operatorname{rad}(K)).
\end{equation}
Let \(\overline L\subseteq K/\operatorname{rad}(K)\) be such a Lagrangian subspace, and let \(L\subseteq K\) be its inverse image under the quotient map \(K\to K/\operatorname{rad}(K)\). Since \(\overline L\) is isotropic, the subspace \(L\) is isotropic in \(V_n\). We have
\begin{equation}
\dim L = \dim \operatorname{rad}(K)+\dim \overline L = \frac{\dim K+\dim \operatorname{rad}(K)}{2}.
\end{equation}
This proves the attainability of the dimension in \cref{eqn:witt-index-formula}. Conversely, let \(M\subseteq K\) be any subspace that is isotropic in \(V_n\). Then \(M+\operatorname{rad}(K)\subseteq K\) is also isotropic, because \(M\) is isotropic and \(\operatorname{rad}(K)\) pairs trivially with all of \(K\). The image of \(M+\operatorname{rad}(K)\) in \(K/\operatorname{rad}(K)\) is therefore isotropic in the non-degenerate symplectic vector space \(K/\operatorname{rad}(K)\). Hence, we have
\begin{equation}
\dim  ((M+\operatorname{rad}(K))/\operatorname{rad}(K) )
\leq
