\frac{1}{2}\dim (K/\operatorname{rad}(K)).
\end{equation}
Therefore, we have
\begin{align}
\dim M&\leq \dim (M+\operatorname{rad}(K))\\ &= \dim \operatorname{rad}(K) + \dim  ((M+\operatorname{rad}(K))/\operatorname{rad}(K) )\\ &\leq \dim \operatorname{rad}(K) + \frac{1}{2}\dim (K/\operatorname{rad}(K))= \frac{\dim K+\dim \operatorname{rad}(K)}{2}.
\end{align}
Thus, no isotropic subspace of $V_n$ that is contained in \(K\) has dimension larger than the number in \cref{eqn:witt-index-formula}. This completes the proof.
<!-- end proof-33 -->
<!-- cor-9: body_md -->
\label{witt-index-consequences}
Let \(p\) be an odd prime. Let \(U \in \mathcal C^{(3)}\), and set \(K_U := \ker S_U\). Let \(w(K_U)\) denote the maximum dimension of a subspace of \(K_U\) that is isotropic in \(V_n\). Then the following statements hold:
\begin{enumerate}
\item \(U\) is semi-Clifford if and only if
\begin{equation}\label{eqn:witt-index-semi-clifford}
\dim K_U + \dim(K_U \cap K_U^\perp) \geq 2n.
\end{equation}
\item \(U\) is semi-Clifford if and only if \(K_U^\perp \subseteq K_U\). That is, $K_U$ is a coisotropic subspace of $V_n$. 
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end cor-9 -->
<!-- proof-34: body_md -->
By \cref{semi-clifford-kernel-criterion}, \(U\) is semi-Clifford if and only if \(K_U\) contains a Lagrangian subspace of \(V_n\). Since a Lagrangian subspace has dimension \(n\), \cref{lem:witt-index-subspace} implies this is the condition
\begin{equation}
w(K_U)\geq n \iff  \dim K_U+\dim(K_U\cap K_U^\perp) \geq 2n.
\end{equation}
This proves (1). For (2), if \(K_U^\perp\subseteq K_U\), then $K_U\cap K_U^\perp=K_U^\perp$. Hence,
\begin{equation}
\dim K_U+\dim(K_U\cap K_U^\perp)=\dim K_U+\dim K_U^\perp=2n.
\end{equation}
Thus, \(U\) is semi-Clifford by (1). Conversely, suppose that \(U\) is semi-Clifford. Then \cref{eqn:witt-index-semi-clifford} holds. Since $\dim K_U+\dim K_U^\perp=2n$, we have $\dim(K_U\cap K_U^\perp)\geq \dim K_U^\perp.$ On the other hand, \(K_U\cap K_U^\perp\) is a subspace of \(K_U^\perp\), so $\dim(K_U\cap K_U^\perp)\leq \dim K_U^\perp.$ Hence, $\dim(K_U\cap K_U^\perp)=\dim K_U^\perp$ and therefore
$K_U\cap K_U^\perp=K_U^\perp.$
Thus, \(K_U^\perp\subseteq K_U\).
<!-- end proof-34 -->
<!-- prop-9: body_md -->
\label{codim2-gen}
Let \(p\) be an odd prime. Let \(U \in \mathcal C^{(3)}\), and set \(K_U := \ker S_U\).  If \(\operatorname{codim} K_U \leq 2\), then \(U\) is semi-Clifford.
<!-- end prop-9 -->
<!-- proof-35: body_md -->
The \(\operatorname{codim} K_U=0\) case is immediate, since then \(K_U=V_n\). If \(\operatorname{codim} K_U=1\), then \(K_U\) is a hyperplane and \(\dim K_U^\perp=1\). Moreover, $K_U^\perp \subseteq K_U$. Indeed, let \(0\neq v\in K_U^\perp\). If \(v\notin K_U\), then $V_n=K_U\oplus \langle v\rangle$ since \(K_U\) is a hyperplane. Since $[v,v]=0$ and $[v,k]=0$ for each $k \in K_U$, the decomposition $V_n=K_U\oplus \langle v\rangle$ implies that $[v,x]=0$ for each $x \in V_n$. This contradicts the non-degeneracy of the symplectic form. Hence, $K_U^\perp \subseteq K_U$. Thus, \(U\) is semi-Clifford by \cref{witt-index-consequences}. Let $\operatorname{codim}K_U=2$. 
\begin{enumerate}
    \item[(i)] Suppose first that \(K_U\cap K_U^\perp\neq 0\). Note that \(K_U\cap K_U^\perp\) is the kernel of the map
\begin{align}
\varphi_K \colon K_U &\longrightarrow K_U^* \label{eq-1}, \\
x &\longmapsto \varphi_K(x), \qquad \varphi_K(x)(y) := [x,y].
\end{align}
By rank-nullity, $\dim K_U = \operatorname{rank}\varphi_K+\dim(K_U\cap K_U^\perp)$. 
Hence, 
\begin{equation}
\operatorname{rank}\varphi_K
=
\dim K_U-\dim(K_U\cap K_U^\perp). \label{eq-2}
\end{equation}
The map \(\varphi_K\) is represented, after choosing a basis of \(K_U\), by a skew-symmetric matrix. Every skew-symmetric matrix has even rank. Therefore, $\dim K_U - \dim(K_U\cap K_U^\perp)$ is even. Since \(\dim K_U=2n-2\) is even, it follows that $\dim(K_U\cap K_U^\perp)$ is also even. Since \(K_U\cap K_U^\perp\neq 0\), we conclude that $\dim(K_U\cap K_U^\perp)\geq 2$. Therefore, we have 
\begin{equation}
\dim K_U+\dim(K_U\cap K_U^\perp)\geq (2n-2)+2=2n.
\end{equation}
Thus, \(U\) is semi-Clifford by \cref{witt-index-consequences}. 

\item[(ii)] Suppose now that \(K_U\cap K_U^\perp = 0\). That is, the symplectic form restricts to a non-degenerate alternating form on \(K_U\). We show that this case cannot occur. Assume, for contradiction, that the symplectic form restricts to a non-degenerate alternating form on \(K_U\). By \cref{lem:kernel-cocycle-consequences}, the restriction \(q_U|_{K_U}\) is a linear injective map. Since $q_U|_{K_U}$ is linear and bijective onto 
$W:=q_U(K_U)$, we have  $\dim q_U(K_U)=\dim K_U=2n-2$.  By \cref{lem:kernel-cocycle-consequences}, we also have
\begin{equation}\label{restrict-nondeg}
[q_U(a),q_U(b)]=[a,b]
\end{equation}
for all \(a,b\in K_U\). Since \(K_U\cap K_U^\perp = 0\), \cref{restrict-nondeg} implies that the symplectic form restricts to a non-degenerate alternating form on \(W\). Since \(W\) is non-degenerate, we have a symplectic direct sum $V_n=W\oplus W^\perp$ such that $\dim W^\perp = 2$\footnote{Indeed, \(W\cap W^\perp=\operatorname{rad}(W)=0\), and non-degeneracy of the ambient symplectic form gives \(\dim W+\dim W^\perp=\dim V_n\). Hence \(V_n=W\oplus W^\perp\). Since \(\dim W=2n-2\), we get \(\dim W^\perp=2\).}.
Set $E_U := \operatorname{im}S_U$. By \cref{lem:kernel-cocycle-consequences}, we have that every element of \(E_U \) fixes \(W\) pointwise. Hence, each \(T\in \operatorname{im}S_U\) preserves \(W^\perp\). Indeed, if \(x\in W^\perp\) and \(w\in W\) then \(Tw=w\) and
\begin{equation}
[Tx,w]=[Tx,Tw]=[x,w]=0.
\end{equation}
Thus, \(Tx\in W^\perp\). Hence, restriction to \(W^\perp\) defines a group homomorphism
\begin{align}
\rho \colon E_U  &\longrightarrow \operatorname{Sp}(W^\perp), \\
T &\longmapsto T|_{W^\perp}.
\end{align}
$\rho$ is injective. Indeed, if \(\rho(T)=\operatorname{Id}_{W^\perp}\), then \(T\) is the identity on \(W^\perp\). Since \(T\) also fixes \(W\) pointwise and \(V_n=W\oplus W^\perp\), it follows that $T=\operatorname{Id}_{V_n}$. Therefore, \(E_U \) embeds into \(\operatorname{Sp}(W^\perp) \cong \operatorname{Sp}(\mathbb F^2_{p})\). Since
\begin{equation}
|\operatorname{Sp}(\mathbb F^2_p)|=p(p^2-1),
\end{equation}
every \(p\)-subgroup of \(\operatorname{Sp}(\mathbb F_p^2)\) has order at most \(p\). However, \(E_U\cong V_n/K_U\), and hence
$|E_U|=p^2.$
This contradiction shows that the case \(K_U\cap K_U^\perp=0\) cannot occur.
\end{enumerate}
This completes the proof.
<!-- end proof-35 -->
<!-- fact-4: body_md -->
\label{wong}
Let $p$ be an odd prime and let \(V\) be a \(2m\)-dimensional symplectic vector space over $\mathbb F_p$. Let
\begin{equation}
0=W_0\subset W_1\subset \cdots \subset W_m
\end{equation}
be a complete isotropic flag, so that \(\dim W_i=i\), each \(W_i\) is isotropic, and \(W_m\) is Lagrangian. Let \(P=P(W_0,W_1,\ldots,W_m)\) be the Sylow \(p\)-subgroup of \(\operatorname{Sp}(V)\) consisting of elements fixing each quotient \(W_i/W_{i-1}\) for $i=1,\cdots,m$. For a subspace \(X\subseteq V\), write \(A(X)\) for the subgroup of \(\operatorname{Sp}(V)\) fixing \(X\) pointwise. Then \(A(W_m)\) is the unique abelian subgroup of largest order in \(P\).
<!-- end fact-4 -->
<!-- thm-3: body_md -->
\label{two-qudit-c3-semi-clifford}
Let \(p\) be an odd prime. Every two-qudit gate in \(\mathcal C^{(3)}\) is semi-Clifford.
<!-- end thm-3 -->
<!-- prop-10: body_md -->
\label{codim4-two-qubit-rule}
Let \(p\) be an odd prime, and let \(U\in\mathcal{C}^{(3)}\) be a two-qudit gate. Set \(K_U:=\ker S_U\) and \(E_U:=\operatorname{im} S_U\). Then
$\operatorname{codim} K_U\neq 4.$
<!-- end prop-10 -->
<!-- proof-36: body_md -->
We first rule out the \(\operatorname{codim}K_U=4\) case. Assume, for the sake of contradiction, that \(\operatorname{codim}K_U=4\). We have $E_U\cong \mathbb F^4_p/K_U \cong \mathbb F^4_p$. Thus, \(\operatorname{im}S_U\) would be an abelian $p$-subgroup of \(\operatorname{Sp}(\mathbb F^4_p)\) of order \(p^4\). The standard order formula gives
\begin{equation}
|\operatorname{Sp}(\mathbb F^4_p)|=p^4(p^2-1)(p^4-1).
\end{equation}
Thus, an abelian $p$-subgroup of order \(p^4\) would be a Sylow \(p\)-subgroup. However, Sylow \(p\)-subgroups of \(\operatorname{Sp}(\mathbb F^4_p)\) are non-abelian. We can verify this claim explicitly. Let
\begin{equation}
A_t:=
\begin{pmatrix}
1&t\\
0&1
\end{pmatrix},
\quad t \in \mathbb F_p.
\end{equation}
Consider the set
\begin{equation}\label{sylow-sp4}
P:=\left\{\begin{pmatrix}A_t & A_t C\\0 & (A_t^{-1})^T\end{pmatrix}:t\in\mathbb F_p,\ C=C^T\in M_2(\mathbb F_p)\right\}
\end{equation}
Let
\begin{equation}\label{M-elem}
M=
\begin{pmatrix}
A_t&A_t C\\
0&(A_t^{-1})^T
\end{pmatrix},
\qquad C=C^T \in M_2(\mathbb F_p).
\end{equation}
With respect to the standard symplectic matrix
\begin{equation}\label{standard-sym-matrix}
J=\begin{pmatrix}0&I\\-I&0\end{pmatrix},
\end{equation}
we compute
\begin{align}
M^TJM
&=
\begin{pmatrix}
A_t^T&0\\
C^TA_t^T&A_t^{-1}
\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}
0&I\\
-I&0
\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}
A_t&A_t C\\
0&(A_t^{-1})^T
\end{pmatrix} \label{sym-1} \\
&=
\begin{pmatrix}
A_t^T&0\\
C^TA_t^T&A_t^{-1}
\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}
0&(A_t^{-1})^T\\
-A_t&-A_tC
\end{pmatrix}=
\begin{pmatrix}
0&I\\
-I&C^T-C
\end{pmatrix}
=
\begin{pmatrix}
0&I\\
-I&0
\end{pmatrix}
=J. \label{sym-2}
\end{align}
Hence, $P \subseteq \operatorname{Sp}(\mathbb F^4_p)$. It is straightforward to verify that $P$ is a subgroup. Moreover, $P$ is of order $p^4$. Indeed, \(t\) has \(p\) possible values and a symmetric \(2 \times 2\) matrix in $M_2(\mathbb F_p)$ has \(p^{3}\) possible values. Consequently, $|P|=p\cdot p^{3}=p^{4}$.  Hence, $P$ is a Sylow \(p\)-subgroup. $P$ is non-abelian. Indeed, let $A=A_1$ and $C=\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$.
Define
\begin{equation}
D:=\begin{pmatrix}
A&0\\
0& (A^{-1})^T
\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
U_C:=\begin{pmatrix}I&C\\ 0&I\end{pmatrix}.
\end{equation}
Both \(D\) and \(U_C\) belong to \(P\). Note that we have
\begin{align}
DU_CD^{-1}
&=
\begin{pmatrix}
A&0\\
0&(A^{-1})^T
\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}
I&C\\
0&I
\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}
A^{-1}&0\\
0&A^T
\end{pmatrix}=
\begin{pmatrix}
I&ACA^T\\
0&I
\end{pmatrix}.
\end{align}
Since
\begin{equation}
ACA^T
=
\begin{pmatrix}
1&1\\
1&1
\end{pmatrix}
\neq
\begin{pmatrix}
0&0\\
0&1
\end{pmatrix}
=
C,
\end{equation}
we have $DU_CD^{-1}\neq U_C$. Hence, \(P\) is non-abelian. Since all Sylow \(p\)-subgroups are conjugate, no Sylow \(p\)-subgroup of \(\operatorname{Sp}(\mathbb F^4_p)\) is abelian. Therefore, \(\operatorname{Sp}(\mathbb F^4_p)\) cannot contain an abelian subgroup of order \(p^4\). This contradicts \(E_U\cong \mathbb F^4_p\). Hence, $\operatorname{codim}K_U\neq 4$.
<!-- end proof-36 -->
<!-- prop-11: body_md -->
\label{codim3-two-qubit-rule}
Let \(p\) be an odd prime, and let \(U\in\mathcal{C}^{(3)}\) be a two-qudit gate. Set \(K_U:=\ker S_U\) and \(E_U:=\operatorname{im} S_U\). Then
$\operatorname{codim} K_U\neq 3.$
<!-- end prop-11 -->
<!-- proof-37: body_md -->
We divide the proof into several steps to make the otherwise lengthy argument easier to follow.
 
\begin{enumerate}
\item  First, we reduce by Clifford conjugation so that \(E_U\) lies in the fixed Sylow \(p\)-subgroup \(P\) in \cref{sylow-sp4}. 
\(E_U\cong \mathbb F^4_p/K_U\) is an abelian \(p\)-subgroup of \(\operatorname{Sp}(\mathbb F_p^4)\) of order \(p^3\). Since \(E_U\) is a \(p\)-subgroup, \(E_U\) is contained in a Sylow \(p\)-subgroup of \(\operatorname{Sp}(\mathbb F_p^4)\). Since all Sylow \(p\)-subgroups of \(\operatorname{Sp}(\mathbb F_p^4)\) are conjugate and \(P\) from \cref{sylow-sp4} is a Sylow \(p\)-subgroup, there exists \(R\in\operatorname{Sp}(\mathbb F_p^4)\) such that $RE_UR^{-1}\subseteq P$. Choose a Clifford lift \(C_R\) of \(R\). Let \(U':=C_RU\). Since \(C_R\in \mathcal C^{(2)}\), the gate \(U\) is semi-Clifford if and only if \(U'\) is semi-Clifford. Moreover,
\begin{align}
B_{U'}(a)
&=U'w(a)U'^* \\
&=C_RB_U(a)C_R^* \\
&=C_R (\alpha_U(a)w(q_U(a))M_{S_U(a)} )C_R^*=\alpha_{U'}(a)w(Rq_U(a))M_{RS_U(a)R^{-1}}\label{last-eq}.
\end{align}
for every \(a\in \mathbb F^4_p\). \cref{last-eq} follows because conjugating \(M_{S_U(a)}\) by \(C_R\) produces a gate in \(\mathcal C^{(2)}\) with symplectic part \(RS_U(a)R^{-1}\) up to a global phase. Hence, $S_{U'}(a)=RS_U(a)R^{-1}$ for every \(a\in \mathbb F^4_p\). It follows that $a\in K_{U'}$ if and only if $a\in K_U$. Thus, $K_{U'}=K_U$. Consequently, after replacing \(U\) by \(U'\), we may assume that \(E_U\subseteq P\).

\item Next, we use \cref{wong} to identify the 
unique abelian subgroup of largest order in \(P\), and then identify \(E_U\) with this subgroup.
Consider $\mathbb F_p^4$ with the symplectic basis $e_1,e_2,f_1,f_2$. Define $L:=\operatorname{span}\{e_1,e_2\}$ and  $L^*:=\operatorname{span}\{f_1,f_2\}$. Thus, $\mathbb F_p^4=L\oplus L^*$. Consider the complete isotropic flag
\begin{equation}\label{flag}
0\subseteq \langle e_1\rangle \subseteq \langle e_1, e_2 \rangle = L.
\end{equation}
We verify that \(P\) in \cref{sylow-sp4} is the Sylow \(p\)-subgroup attached to this flag as required in  \cref{wong}. Let $M$ be as in \cref{M-elem}. Since the lower-left block of \(M\) is zero, \(M\) preserves \(L\). Its induced action on \(L\) is given by \(A_t\). Since
\begin{equation}
A_te_1=e_1,
\qquad
A_te_2=e_2+te_1,
\end{equation}
the line \(W_1=\langle e_1\rangle\) is fixed pointwise, and the induced action on \(W_2/W_1\) is trivial. Hence, $P$ satisfies the assumption in \cref{wong}. Hence, \cref{wong} implies that $A(L)$ is the unique abelian subgroup of largest order in \(P\). We identify $A(L)$ explicitly. Consider the set
\begin{equation}
Q:=\left\{\begin{pmatrix}I&C\\0&I\end{pmatrix}:C=C^T\in M_2(\mathbb F_p)\right\}\subseteq P.
\end{equation}
Clearly, $Q$ is an abelian subgroup of $P$ and $Q$ fixes $L$. Hence, $Q \subseteq A(L)$. Conversely, if $M$ as in \cref{M-elem} fixes \(L\) pointwise then
\begin{equation}
M(x,0)=(A_tx,0)=(x,0)
\end{equation}
for every \(x\in \mathbb F_p^2\). Hence \(A_t=I\), so \(t=0\), and therefore \(M \in Q\). Hence, we have $A(L)=Q$. Since a symmetric \(2\times 2\) matrix has three independent entries, we have $|A(L)|=p^3.$ On the other hand, \(E_U\) is also an abelian subgroup of $P$ of  order $p^3$. Hence, we have $E_U=A(L)$ by \cref{wong}. That is, we have
\begin{equation}\label{ul-group}
E_U=\left\{\begin{pmatrix}I&C\\0&I\end{pmatrix}:C=C^T\in M_2(\mathbb F_p)\right\}:= A(L)
\end{equation}

\item We now express the symplectic data \(S_U\) as a linear map into \(\operatorname{Sym}_2(\mathbb F_p)\). For every \(a\in \mathbb F^4_p\) there is a unique symmetric matrix \(C(a)\in M_2(\mathbb F_p)\) such that
\begin{equation}\label{su-codim-3}
S_U(a)=\begin{pmatrix}I&C(a)\\0&I\end{pmatrix}.
\end{equation}
Since \(S_U:\mathbb F_p^4\to A(L)\) is a group homomorphism and multiplication in \(A(L)\) corresponds to addition in \(\operatorname{Sym}_2(\mathbb F_p)\), the map
\begin{align}
C:\mathbb F_p^4&\longrightarrow \operatorname{Sym}_2(\mathbb F_p),\\
a&\longmapsto C(a)
\end{align}
is \(\mathbb F_p\)-linear. Moreover, \(\ker C=\ker S_U=K_U\). Since \(\operatorname{codim}K_U=3\), we have
\begin{equation}
\operatorname{rank}C=\dim \mathbb F_p^4-\dim K_U=4-1=3.
\end{equation}
Since \(\dim \operatorname{Sym}_2(\mathbb F_p)=3\), it follows that \(C\) is surjective.



\item  We now use the cocycle equation for \(q_U\). Write $q_U(a)=(\alpha(a),\beta(a))\in L\oplus L^*$. Using \cref{su-codim-3}, we have
\begin{equation}
S_U(a)q_U(b)
=
\begin{pmatrix}
I&C(a)\\
0&I
\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}
\alpha(b)\\
\beta(b)
\end{pmatrix}
=
\begin{pmatrix}
\alpha(b)+C(a)\beta(b)\\
\beta(b)
\end{pmatrix}.
\end{equation}
Substituting this into the affine cocycle equation gives
\begin{equation}
\begin{pmatrix}
\alpha(a+b)\\
\beta(a+b)
\end{pmatrix}
=q_U(a+b)=q_U(a)+S_U(a)q_U(b)=\begin{pmatrix}
\alpha(a)+\alpha(b)+C(a)\beta(b)\\
\beta(a)+\beta(b)
\end{pmatrix}.
\end{equation}
Hence, we have
\begin{align}
\alpha(a+b)&=\alpha(a)+\alpha(b)+C(a)\beta(b),\\
\beta(a+b)&=\beta(a)+\beta(b).
\end{align}
Since \(\mathbb F^4_p\) is abelian, the same comparison as in \cref{lem:kernel-cocycle-consequences} applied to \(q_U(a+b)=q_U(b+a)\) gives \(C(a)\beta(b)=C(b)\beta(a)\) for all \(a,b\in\mathbb F_p^4\).

\item We show that the surjectivity of \(C\) forces the \(\beta\) component of $q$ to vanish. Since \(C:\mathbb F_p^4\to \operatorname{Sym}_2(\mathbb F_p)\) is surjective, choose elements \(a_{11},a_{22},a_{12}\in \mathbb F_p^4\) such that
\begin{equation}
C(a_{11})=E_{11},\qquad C(a_{22})=E_{22},\qquad C(a_{12})=E_{12},
\end{equation}
where \(E_{11}\), \(E_{12}\), and \(E_{22}\) are the standard basis matrices of \(\operatorname{Sym}_2(\mathbb F_p)\). Write
\begin{equation}
\beta(a_{11})=(u_1,u_2),
\qquad
\beta(a_{22})=(v_1,v_2),
\qquad
\beta(a_{12})=(w_1,w_2).
\end{equation}
Applying \(C(a)\beta(b)=C(b)\beta(a)\) to the pairs \((a_{11},a_{22})\), \((a_{11},a_{12})\) and \((a_{22},a_{12})\) gives
\begin{align}
(v_1,0)=E_{11}\beta(a_{22})&=E_{22}\beta(a_{11})=(0,u_2),\\
(w_1,0)=E_{11}\beta(a_{12})&=E_{12}\beta(a_{11})=(u_2,u_1),\\
(0,w_2)=E_{22}\beta(a_{12})&=E_{12}\beta(a_{22})=(v_2,v_1).
\end{align}
Hence, \(u_{1,2}=v_{1,2}=w_{1,2}=0\). Therefore,
\begin{equation}
\beta(a_{11})=\beta(a_{22})=\beta(a_{12})=0.
\end{equation}
Now let \(a\in\mathbb F_p^4\) be arbitrary. Since \(E_{11},E_{22},E_{12}\) form a basis of \(\operatorname{Sym}_2(\mathbb F_p)\), there exist \(c_{11},c_{22},c_{12}\in\mathbb F_p\) such that
\begin{equation}
C(a)=c_{11}E_{11}+c_{22}E_{22}+c_{12}E_{12}.
\end{equation}
Set $a_0:=c_{11}a_{11}+c_{22}a_{22}+c_{12}a_{12}$. Then $C(a_0)=C(a)$, so \(a-a_0\in\ker C\). We next show that \(\beta\) vanishes on \(\ker C\). If \(k\in\ker C\), then \(C(k)=0\). Hence, we have
\begin{equation}
C(a)\beta(k)=C(k)\beta(a)=0
\end{equation}
for every \(a\in\mathbb F_p^4\). Since \(C\) is surjective, every symmetric matrix annihilates \(\beta(k)\). In particular, the identity matrix annihilates \(\beta(k)\), so $\beta(k)=0$. Thus \(\beta(a-a_0)=0\). Since \(\beta\) is linear, we get $\beta(a)=\beta(a_0)$. Since
\begin{equation}
\beta(a_0)=c_{11}\beta(a_{11})+c_{22}\beta(a_{22})+c_{12}\beta(a_{12})=0,
\end{equation}
we have \(\beta(a)=0\) for every \(a\in\mathbb F_p^4\). Hence, $\beta=0$. Consequently, $q_U(\mathbb F_p^4)\subseteq L$.


\item Finally, we show that the vanishing of \(\beta\) forces all \(B_U(a)\) to commute, contradicting the Weyl commutator relation. Since \(L\) is Lagrangian, the Weyl operators \(w(q_U(a))\) and \(w(q_U(b))\) commute for all \(a,b\in \mathbb F_p^4\). Since every element of \(E_U\) fixes \(L\) pointwise, we have \(S_U(a)q_U(b)=q_U(b)\) for all \(a,b \in \mathbb F_p^4\). Since \(M_{S_U(a)}\) is a lift of \(S_U(a)\), we have
\begin{equation}
M_{S_U(a)}w(q_U(b))M_{S_U(a)}^*=w(S_U(a)q_U(b))=w(q_U(b)).
\end{equation}
Thus,
\begin{equation}
M_{S_U(a)}w(q_U(b))=w(q_U(b))M_{S_U(a)}
\end{equation}
for all \(a,b\in \mathbb F_p^4\). By \cref{lem:upper-unipotent-commuting-lifts} applied with \(m=2\), the fixed Clifford representatives \(M_{S_U(a)}=M_{u_{C(a)}}\) commute pairwise. Putting everything together, we have
\begin{equation}\label{compare-1}
B_U(a)B_U(b)=B_U(b)B_U(a)
\end{equation}
for all \(a,b\in\mathbb F_p^4\). On the other hand, by definition \(B_U(a)=Uw(a)U^*\). Hence, we have
\begin{align}\label{compare-2}
B_U(a)B_U(b)=Uw(a)w(b)U^*=\omega^{[a,b]}Uw(b)w(a)U^*=\omega^{[a,b]}B_U(b)B_U(a).
\end{align}
Comparing \cref{compare-1} and \cref{compare-2} gives $\omega^{[a,b]}=1$ for all \(a,b\in\mathbb F_p^4\). Since \(\omega\) is a primitive \(p\)-th root of unity, this implies $[a,b]=0$ for all \(a,b\in\mathbb F_p^4\). This contradicts the non-degeneracy of the symplectic form. Therefore, \(\operatorname{codim}K_U\neq3\).
\end{enumerate}
This completes the proof.
<!-- end proof-37 -->
<!-- proof-38: body_md -->
This follows from \cref{codim2-gen}, \cref{codim4-two-qubit-rule}, \cref{codim3-two-qubit-rule}.
<!-- end proof-38 -->
<!-- thm-4: body_md -->
\label{three-qudit-c3-semi-clifford}
Let \(p\) be an odd prime. Every three-qudit gate in \(\mathcal C^{(3)}\) is semi-Clifford.
<!-- end thm-4 -->
<!-- lem-18: body_md -->
\label{lem:pointwise-lagrangian-coordinate-setup}
Let \(p\) be an odd prime. Let \(U\in\mathcal C^{(3)}\) be a three-qudit gate and suppose that \(E_U:=\operatorname{im}S_U\) fixes a Lagrangian subspace \(L\subseteq \mathbb F^6_p\) pointwise. Choose a complementary Lagrangian \(L^*\), so that $\mathbb F^6_p=L\oplus L^*.$ Then for every \(a\in\mathbb F^6_p\), there is a symmetric matrix \(C(a)\in\operatorname{Sym}_3(\mathbb F_p)\) such that
\begin{equation}\label{eqn:pointwise-lagrangian-upper-unipotent}
S_U(a)=u_{C(a)}:=\begin{pmatrix}I&C(a)\\0&I\end{pmatrix}.
\end{equation}
Moreover, the map $C:\mathbb F^6_p \to \operatorname{Sym}_3(\mathbb F_p)$
is linear. If $q_U(a)=(\alpha(a),\beta(a))\in L\oplus L^*,$
then \(\beta:\mathbb F^6_p\to L^*\) is linear and
$C(a)\beta(b)=C(b)\beta(a)$
for all \(a,b\in\mathbb F^6_p\).
<!-- end lem-18 -->
<!-- proof-39: body_md -->
Write \(S_U(a)\) in block form relative to the decomposition \(\mathbb F_p^6=L\oplus L^*\):
\begin{equation}
S_U(a)=\begin{pmatrix}A&B\\C&D\end{pmatrix}.
\end{equation}
Since $S_U(a)$ fixes $L$ for each $a \in \mathbb F_p^6$, we have 
\begin{equation}
(x,0)=S_U(a)(x,0)=(Ax,Cx).
\end{equation}
for each $x \in L$. Thus, \(A=I\) and \(C=0\). Since \(S_U(a)\) is symplectic, a computation analogous to \cref{sym-1}--\cref{sym-2} gives \(D=I\) and \(B=B^T\). Therefore
\begin{equation}
S_U(a)=\begin{pmatrix}I&C(a)\\0&I\end{pmatrix}
\end{equation}
with \(C(a)=C(a)^T\). Thus, \(C(a)\in\operatorname{Sym}_3(\mathbb F_p)\). Since \(S_U:\mathbb F^6_p\to\operatorname{Sp}(\mathbb F^6_p)\) is a homomorphism and \(u_Cu_D=u_{C+D}\), the map $C:\mathbb F^6_p \to  \operatorname{Sym}_3(\mathbb F_p)$ is linear.  Write
\begin{equation}
q_U(a)=(\alpha(a),\beta(a))\in L\oplus L^*.
\end{equation}
Applying the cocycle identity and comparing the \(L\) and \(L^*\) components, as in \cref{codim3-two-qubit-rule}, gives
\begin{align}
\alpha(a+b)&=\alpha(a)+\alpha(b)+C(a)\beta(b),\\
\beta(a+b)&=\beta(a)+\beta(b).
\end{align}
Hence, \(\beta:\mathbb F^6_p\to L^*\) is linear. Since \(\mathbb F^6_p\) is abelian, the same cocycle comparison as in \cref{lem:kernel-cocycle-consequences} applied to \(q_U(a+b)=q_U(b+a)\)  gives $C(a)\beta(b)=C(b)\beta(a)$ for all \(a,b\in\mathbb F^6_p\).
<!-- end proof-39 -->
<!-- prop-12: body_md -->
\label{lem:three-qudit-codim-three}
Let \(p\) be an odd prime and let \(U\in\mathcal C^{(3)}\) be a three-qudit gate. Set \(K_U:=\ker S_U\) and \(E_U:=\operatorname{im}S_U\). If \(\operatorname{codim}K_U=3\), then \(U\) is semi-Clifford.
<!-- end prop-12 -->
<!-- proof-40: body_md -->
Since \(\operatorname{codim}K_U=3\), we have \(\dim K_U=3\). Set \(r_K:=\dim(K_U\cap K_U^\perp)\). As in \cref{eq-1}--\cref{eq-2} of \cref{codim2-gen}, the number \(3-r_K\) is the rank of the alternating bilinear form obtained by restricting the symplectic form to \(K_U\). Since every alternating bilinear form is represented by a skew-symmetric matrix, \(3-r_K\) is even.  Hence, \(r_K=1\) or \(r_K=3\). If \(r_K=3\), then \(K_U\cap K_U^\perp=K_U\), so \(K_U\subseteq K_U^\perp\).
Since $\dim K_U = 3$ in $\mathbb F_p^6$, this implies $K_U$ is a Lagrangian subspace. Hence, \(U\) is semi-Clifford. 
We rule out the \(r_K=1\) case.  We divide the proof into several steps to make the
otherwise lengthy argument easier to follow. 

\begin{enumerate} 
\item First, we reduce from \(K_U\) to a non-degenerate symplectic plane \(H\), so that \(E_U\) can be embedded into a four-dimensional symplectic group. By \cref{lem:kernel-cocycle-consequences}, \(q_U|_{K_U}\) is linear, injective, and preserves the restricted symplectic form. Hence, $W:=q_U(K_U)$ has dimension \(3\) and the radical of the restricted form on \(W\) is $R:=q_U(K_U\cap K_U^\perp),$ which is one-dimensional. Choose any two-dimensional subspace \(H\) in \(W\) such that
$W=H\oplus R. $
The symplectic form is non-degenerate on $H$. Indeed, suppose that \(h\in H\) satisfies \([h,h']=0\) for every \(h'\in H\). Since \(R=\operatorname{rad}(W)\), we also have \([h,r]=0\) for every \(r\in R\). As \(W=H\oplus R\), it follows that \(h\in\operatorname{rad}(W)=R\). But \(h\in H\) and \(H\cap R=0\), so \(h=0\). By \cref{lem:kernel-cocycle-consequences}, \(E_U\) fixes \(W\) pointwise. Hence, \(E_U\) fixes both \(H\) and \(R\) pointwise. Since \(H\) is non-degenerate, the symplectic complement argument used in the codimension two case of \cref{codim2-gen} gives $\mathbb F^6_p=H\oplus H^\perp$ and that \(E_U\) preserves \(H^\perp\). Therefore, we have a homomorphism
\begin{align}
E_U &\longrightarrow \operatorname{Sp}(H^\perp),\\
T &\longmapsto T|_{H^\perp}.
\end{align}
As in \cref{lem:kernel-cocycle-consequences}, the map is injective. Thus, $E_U$ embeds into $\operatorname{Sp}(H^\perp) \cong \operatorname{Sp}(\mathbb F_p^4)$ as an abelian $p$-subgroup of order \(p^3\).



\item Next, as in the two-qudit codimension three proof, we use \cref{wong} to identify the restricted image on \(H^\perp\) with a subgroup fixing a Lagrangian plane \(L_0\) pointwise. Since \(E_U\) is a \(p\)-subgroup of \(\operatorname{Sp}(H^\perp)\), choose a Sylow \(p\)-subgroup \(P\) containing \(E_U\). Conjugating inside \(\operatorname{Sp}(H^\perp)\), and extending this conjugation to \(\mathbb F_p^6=H\oplus H^\perp\) by the identity on \(H\), we may assume that \(P\) is the standard Sylow \(p\)-subgroup used in \cref{codim4-two-qubit-rule}. After this change of coordinates, the complete isotropic flag
\begin{equation}
0\subseteq \langle e_1\rangle\subseteq \langle e_1,e_2\rangle=L_0
\end{equation}
is contained in \(H^\perp\). Choose the complementary Lagrangian \(L_0^*\) in these coordinates, so that \(H^\perp=L_0\oplus L_0^*\). By \cref{wong}, and exactly as in the proof of \cref{codim3-two-qubit-rule}, the unique abelian subgroup of largest order in \(P\) is \(A(L_0)\), the subgroup fixing \(L_0\) pointwise. In the coordinates given by the decomposition \(H^\perp=L_0\oplus L_0^*\), this subgroup is
\begin{equation}
A(L_0)
=
\left\{
\begin{pmatrix}
I&C\\
0&I
\end{pmatrix}
:
C=C^T\in M_2(\mathbb F_p)
\right\}.
\end{equation}
In particular, \(|A(L_0)|=p^3\). Since \(E_U\subseteq P\) is abelian and \(|E_U|=p^3\), we have $E_U=A(L_0)$. It is clear that 
\begin{equation}\label{L0-fix}
L_0 = \{v\in H^\perp : Tv=v \text{ for every } T\in E_U\}.
\end{equation}

\item We now enlarge the Lagrangian plane \(L_0\subseteq H^\perp\) to a full Lagrangian \(L\subseteq \mathbb F_p^6\). Since \(R\subseteq H^\perp\) and \(R\) is fixed pointwise by \(E_U\), we have \(R\subseteq L_0\). Choose a line \(\ell\subseteq H\) and set $L:=\ell\oplus L_0$.  
Then \(\dim L=1+2=3\). Moreover, \(L\) is isotropic. Indeed, if \(x=x_\ell+x_0\) and \(y=y_\ell+y_0\), with \(x_\ell,y_\ell\in \ell\) and \(x_0,y_0\in L_0\), then
\begin{equation}
[x,y]=[x_\ell,y_\ell]+[x_\ell,y_0]+[x_0,y_\ell]+[x_0,y_0].
\end{equation}
The first term is zero because \(\ell\) is isotropic in \(H\), the last term is zero because \(L_0\) is Lagrangian in \(H^\perp\), and the two middle terms are zero because \(H\perp H^\perp\). Hence, \([x,y]=0\) for all \(x,y\in L\). Since \(\dim L=3=\frac{1}{2}\dim \mathbb F^6_p\), \(L\) is Lagrangian. Choose a complementary Lagrangian \(L^*\) such that $\mathbb F^6_p=L\oplus L^*$. Note that \(E_U\) fixes \(\ell\) pointwise because it fixes \(H\) pointwise, and \(E_U\) fixes \(L_0\) pointwise because \(E_U=A(L_0)\). Hence, $E_U$ fixes $L$ pointwise. 

\item We now express the symplectic data \(S_U\) as a linear map into \(\operatorname{Sym}_3(\mathbb F_p)\). \cref{lem:pointwise-lagrangian-coordinate-setup} implies for every \(a\in\mathbb F^6_p\) we may write
\begin{equation}\label{eqn:three-qudit-c3-upper-unipotent-form}
S_U(a)=u_{C(a)}=\begin{pmatrix}I&C(a)\\0&I\end{pmatrix},
\qquad C(a)\in\operatorname{Sym}_3(\mathbb F_p),
\end{equation}
where \(C:\mathbb F^6_p\to\operatorname{Sym}_3(\mathbb F_p)\) is linear. Let $B:=C(\mathbb F^6_p).$ Since \(C(a)=0\) if and only if \(S_U(a)=I\), we have \(\ker C=K_U\). Hence, 
$\dim B =\dim \mathbb F_p^6-\dim K_U=6-3=3.$
Note that, unlike in the two-qudit case, \(C\) is not surjective.

\item   We compute \(B\) explicitly before using the cocycle identity to derive a contradiction. Using \cref{L0-fix} and the fact that \(E_U=A(L_0)\), the subspace of \(\mathbb F_p^6\) fixed by \(E_U\) is \(H\oplus L_0\), which has dimension \(4\). On the other hand, in the coordinates \(\mathbb F^6_p=L\oplus L^*\), the same fixed subspace is $L\oplus N(B),$ where
\begin{equation}\label{eqn:three-qudit-c3-NB}
N(B):=\bigcap_{a\in\mathbb F_p^6} \ker C(a) \subseteq L^*.
\end{equation}
Indeed, \(u_{C(a)}(x,y)=(x+C(a)y,y)\), so \((x,y)\) is fixed by every \(u_{C(a)}\) if and only if \(C(a)y=0\) for every \(a \in \mathbb F_p^6\). Therefore, \(\dim N(B)=1\). Choose \(0\neq r_0\in N(B)\). Since \(r_0\in N(B)\), we have
\begin{equation}
B\subseteq \{A\in\operatorname{Sym}_3(\mathbb F_p):Ar_0=0\}.
\end{equation}
We claim that the space on the right has dimension \(3\). Indeed, choose a basis of \(L^*\) whose third basis vector is \(r_0\). In this basis, the condition \(Ar_0=0\) says that the third column of \(A\) is zero. Since \(A\) is symmetric, the third row is also zero. Therefore every such \(A\) has the form
\begin{equation}
A=
\begin{pmatrix}
a_{11}&a_{12}&0\\
a_{12}&a_{22}&0\\
0&0&0
\end{pmatrix}.
\end{equation}
Thus, the space \(\{A\in\operatorname{Sym}_3(\mathbb F_p):Ar_0=0\}\) has the three free parameters \(a_{11},a_{12},a_{22}\), and hence has dimension \(3\). Since \(\dim B=3\), we have
\begin{equation}\label{eqn:three-qudit-c3-B-space}
B=\{A\in\operatorname{Sym}_3(\mathbb F_p):Ar_0=0\}.
\end{equation}

\item We now use the cocycle identity to constrain the \(L^*\) component of \(q_U\). In contrast with the two-qudit proof, this will force \(\beta\) into a line rather than forcing \(\beta=0\). Write
\begin{equation}\label{eqn:three-qudit-c3-q-alpha-beta}
q_U(a)=(\alpha(a),\beta(a))\in L\oplus L^*.
\end{equation}
By \cref{lem:pointwise-lagrangian-coordinate-setup}, the map \(\beta:\mathbb F^6_p\to L^*\) is linear and
\begin{equation}\label{eqn:three-qudit-c3-C-beta-symmetry}
C(a)\beta(b)=C(b)\beta(a)
\end{equation}
for all \(a,b\in\mathbb F^6_p\). If \(k\in K_U\), then \(C(k)=0\), so \(C(a)\beta(k)=0\) for every \(a\in\mathbb F_p^6\). Hence, \(\beta(k)\in N(B)\). Let \(\pi:L^*\to L^*/N(B)\) be the quotient map. It follows that $K_U=\ker C\subseteq\ker(\pi\circ\beta)$. Therefore, there is a unique linear map
\begin{align}
\widetilde T:\mathbb F_p^6/K_U &\longrightarrow L^*/N(B),\\
a+K_U &\longmapsto \beta(a)+N(B).
\end{align}
Since \(C:\mathbb F_p^6\to B\) is surjective with kernel \(K_U\), we have an isomorphism
\begin{align}
\overline C:\mathbb F_p^6/K_U &\xrightarrow{\sim} B,\\
 a+K_U & \longmapsto C(a).
\end{align}
Therefore, we can define
\begin{equation}
T:=\widetilde T\circ\overline C^{-1}:B\longrightarrow L^*/N(B).
\end{equation}
By construction, $T(C(a))=\beta(a)+N(B)$ for every \(a\in\mathbb F_p^6\). The entire factorization is summarized by the diagram in \cref{factoriztion}.

\begin{equation}\label{factoriztion}
\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=huge,row sep=large]
\mathbb F_p^6 \arrow[r,"\beta"] \arrow[d,two heads,"q"'] & L^* \arrow[r,"\pi"] & L^*/N(B) \\
\mathbb F_p^6/K_U \arrow[r,leftrightarrow,"\overline C"] \arrow[rru,"\widetilde T"',swap, dashed] & B \arrow[ur,"T"'] &
\end{tikzcd}
\end{equation}


\item We show that \(T\) is in fact the zero map. Choose coordinates on \(L^*\) with \(r_0=e_3\), together with the corresponding coordinates on \(L\). Then \cref{eqn:three-qudit-c3-B-space} identifies \(B\) with \(\operatorname{Sym}_2(\mathbb F_p)\), while \(L^*/N(B)\) is identified with \(\mathbb F_p^2\). Since \(N(B)\subseteq\ker A\) for every \(A\in B\), each linear map \(A:L^*\to L\) factors uniquely through the quotient \(L^*/N(B)\). Under the chosen coordinates, the resulting map is represented by the corresponding \(2\times2\) symmetric matrix \(A\). Thus, for \(x\in L^*\), its value on the coset \(x+N(B)\) is represented by \(Ax\).
Let \(A,D\in\operatorname{Sym}_2(\mathbb F_p)\), and choose \(a,b\in\mathbb F_p^6\) such that \(A=C(a)\) and \(D=C(b)\). By the definition of \(T\),
\begin{equation}
T(A)=\beta(a)+N(B),\qquad T(D)=\beta(b)+N(B).
\end{equation}
Therefore, \cref{eqn:three-qudit-c3-C-beta-symmetry} gives
\begin{equation}\label{eqn:three-qudit-c3-ATD-DTA}
AT(D)=DT(A)
\end{equation}
for all \(A,D\in\operatorname{Sym}_2(\mathbb F_p)\). Taking \(D=I\) gives \(AT(I)=T(A)\). Setting \(t:=T(I)\), we therefore have \(T(A)=At\) for every \(A\in\operatorname{Sym}_2(\mathbb F_p)\). Substituting this into \cref{eqn:three-qudit-c3-ATD-DTA} gives
\begin{equation}\label{eqn:three-qudit-c3-commutator-kills-t}
(AD-DA)t=0
\end{equation}
for all symmetric \(A,D\). Taking
\begin{equation}
A=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&0\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
D=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}
\end{equation}
gives
\begin{equation}
AD-DA=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{pmatrix},
\end{equation}
which is invertible over \(\mathbb F_p\). Thus \(t=0\), and hence \(T=0\). Since \(T(C(a))=\beta(a)+N(B)\), it follows that
\begin{equation}
\beta(\mathbb F_p^6)\subseteq N(B)=\mathbb F_pr_0.
\end{equation}
Write \(\beta(a)=\lambda(a)r_0\) for a linear functional \(\lambda:\mathbb F_p^6\to\mathbb F_p\), and define \(\nu(a):=r_0^T\alpha(a)\).

\item Finally, as in the two-qudit codimension three proof, we compare the commutator of \(B_U(a)\) and \(B_U(b)\) in two ways. Since \(C(a)r_0=0\) for every \(a\in\mathbb F^6_p\), each \(u_{C(a)}\) fixes \(q_U(b)\) for every \(b\in\mathbb F^6_p\). Therefore, \(M_{S_U(a)}\) commutes with \(w(q_U(b))\) for all \(a,b\). By \cref{lem:upper-unipotent-commuting-lifts}, applied with \(m=3\), the fixed Clifford representatives \(M_{S_U(a)}=M_{u_{C(a)}}\) commute pairwise. Therefore, we have
\begin{equation}\label{hi-1}
B_U(a)B_U(b)=\omega^{[q_U(a),q_U(b)]}B_U(b)B_U(a).
\end{equation} 
On the other hand, since \(B_U(a)=Uw(a)U^*\), we also have
\begin{equation}\label{hi-2}
B_U(a)B_U(b)=\omega^{[a,b]}B_U(b)B_U(a).
\end{equation}
Comparing \cref{hi-1} and \cref{hi-2} gives $[a,b]=[q_U(a),q_U(b)]$
for all \(a,b\in\mathbb F^6_p\). Since \(q_U(a)=(\alpha(a),\lambda(a)r_0)\), we obtain
\begin{equation}\label{eqn:three-qudit-c3-rank-two-form}
[a,b]=[q_U(a),q_U(b)]=\lambda(a)\nu(b)-\lambda(b)\nu(a).
\end{equation}
It remains to note that \(\nu\) is linear. By \cref{lem:pointwise-lagrangian-coordinate-setup}, we have
\begin{equation}
\alpha(a+b)=\alpha(a)+\alpha(b)+C(a)\beta(b).
\end{equation}
Since \(\beta(b)=\lambda(b)r_0\) and \(C(a)r_0=0\), this becomes $\alpha(a+b)=\alpha(a)+\alpha(b).$
Thus, \(\nu(a+b)=\nu(a)+\nu(b)\). Therefore, the right side of \cref{eqn:three-qudit-c3-rank-two-form} is an alternating form of rank at most \(2\), contradicting the fact that the symplectic form on \(\mathbb F^6_p\) has rank \(6\). Hence, the case \(r_K=1\) is impossible.
\end{enumerate}
This completes the proof.
<!-- end proof-40 -->
<!-- lem-19: body_md -->
\label{lem:three-qudit-large-image-obstruction}
Let \(p\) be an odd prime. Let \(U\in\mathcal C^{(3)}\) be a three-qudit gate, and set \(E_U:=\operatorname{im}S_U\). If \(\dim E_U\geq4\), then \(E_U\) does not fix any Lagrangian subspace of \(\mathbb F_p^6\) pointwise.
<!-- end lem-19 -->
<!-- proof-41: body_md -->
Set \(d:=\dim E_U\geq4\). Suppose, for contradiction, that \(E_U\) fixes a Lagrangian subspace \(L\subseteq\mathbb F_p^6\) pointwise. Choose a complementary Lagrangian \(L^*\). By \cref{lem:pointwise-lagrangian-coordinate-setup}, we may write
\begin{equation}\label{eqn:large-image-upper-unipotent-form}
S_U(a)=u_{C(a)}=\begin{pmatrix}I&C(a)\\0&I\end{pmatrix},
\end{equation}
where \(C:\mathbb F_p^6\to\operatorname{Sym}_3(\mathbb F_p)\) is linear. By \cref{lem:pointwise-lagrangian-coordinate-setup}, if \(q_U(a)=(\alpha(a),\beta(a))\in L\oplus L^*\) then \(\beta:\mathbb F_p^6\to L^*\) is linear and satisfies
\begin{equation}\label{eqn:large-image-C-beta-symmetry}
C(a)\beta(b)=C(b)\beta(a)
\end{equation}
for all \(a,b\in\mathbb F_p^6\). As in the proof of \cref{lem:three-qudit-codim-three}, let \(B:=C(\mathbb F_p^6)\). Since \(\ker C=K_U\), we have
\begin{equation}
\dim B=\operatorname{codim}K_U=\dim E_U=d.
\end{equation}
Define $N(B)$ as in \cref{eqn:three-qudit-c3-NB}. If \(N(B)\neq0\), choose \(0\neq r\in N(B)\). Then
\begin{equation}
B\subseteq\{A\in\operatorname{Sym}_3(\mathbb F_p):Ar=0\}.
\end{equation}
The dimension calculation in the proof of \cref{lem:three-qudit-codim-three} shows that the space on the right has dimension \(3\). This contradicts \(\dim B=d\geq4\). Hence,
$N(B)=0$. If \(k\in K_U\), then \(C(k)=0\), so \cref{eqn:large-image-C-beta-symmetry} gives \(C(a)\beta(k)=0\) for every \(a\in\mathbb F_p^6\). Hence \(\beta(k)\in N(B)\), and therefore \(\beta(k)=0\). Thus, \(K_U=\ker C\subseteq\ker\beta\). Since \(C:\mathbb F_p^6\to B\) is surjective with kernel \(K_U\), the same factorization argument used in \cref{lem:three-qudit-codim-three}, now with \(L^*/N(B)=L^*\), gives a unique linear map
\begin{equation}\label{eqn:large-image-T-map}
T:B\longrightarrow L^*
\end{equation}
such that
$T(C(a))=\beta(a)$
for every \(a\in\mathbb F_p^6\). Let \(A,D\in B\), and choose \(a,b\in\mathbb F_p^6\) such that \(A=C(a)\) and \(D=C(b)\). By \cref{eqn:large-image-C-beta-symmetry}, we have
\begin{equation}\label{eqn:large-image-ATD-DTA}
AT(D)=DT(A)
\end{equation}
for all \(A,D\in B\). Set
$s:=\dim\operatorname{im}T.$
If \(A\in\ker T\), then \cref{eqn:large-image-ATD-DTA} gives
$AT(D)=0$
for every \(D\in B\). Since \(T(B)=\operatorname{im}T\), the matrix \(A\) therefore annihilates \(\operatorname{im}T\). A symmetric \(3\times3\) matrix annihilating a fixed \(s\)-dimensional subspace is determined by a symmetric \((3-s)\times(3-s)\) block. Consequently,
\begin{equation}\label{eqn:large-image-dimension-inequality}
d-s\leq\frac{(3-s)(4-s)}{2}.
\end{equation}
Suppose first that \(d=5\) or \(d=6\). Then \cref{eqn:large-image-dimension-inequality} forces \(s=0\). Hence \(T=0\), so \(\beta=0\) and
$q_U(\mathbb F_p^6)\subseteq L.$
The same commutator argument used at the end of \cref{codim3-two-qubit-rule}, together with \cref{lem:upper-unipotent-commuting-lifts} applied with \(m=3\), implies that the operators \(B_U(a)\) commute pairwise. On the other hand,
\begin{equation}
B_U(a)B_U(b)=\omega^{[a,b]}B_U(b)B_U(a)
\end{equation}
for all \(a,b\in\mathbb F_p^6\). This contradicts the non-degeneracy of the symplectic form. Hence \(d\neq5,6\). It remains to consider \(d=4\). By \cref{eqn:large-image-dimension-inequality}, either \(s=0\) or \(s=1\). If \(s=0\), then \(T=0\), hence \(\beta=0\), and the same commuting-lift argument used above gives a contradiction. Therefore,  \(s=1\). Thus,
$T(A)=\lambda(A)r$
for some non-zero \(r\in L^*\) and non-zero linear functional \(\lambda:B\to\mathbb F_p\). Choose \(D_0\in B\) such that \(\lambda(D_0)=1\). Taking \(D=D_0\) in \cref{eqn:large-image-ATD-DTA} gives
\begin{equation}\label{eqn:large-image-Ar-lambda}
Ar=\lambda(A)D_0r
\end{equation}
for every \(A\in B\). Set \(v:=D_0r\) and \(\xi:=r^Tv\). Then
\begin{equation}\label{eqn:large-image-rAr}
r^TAr=\xi\lambda(A)
\end{equation}
for every \(A\in B\). For \(a\in\mathbb F_p^6\), write
\begin{equation}
A_a:=C(a),\qquad \lambda_a:=\lambda(A_a),\qquad \nu_a:=r^T\alpha(a).
\end{equation}
Then
$\beta(a)=T(A_a)=\lambda_ar.$
Using the commuting lifts from \cref{lem:upper-unipotent-commuting-lifts} and comparing the commutators of \(B_U(a)\) and \(B_U(b)\), we obtain
\begin{equation}\label{eqn:large-image-commutator-formula}
[a,b]=[q_U(a),q_U(b)]+\frac12\left(\beta(a)^TA_b\beta(a)-\beta(b)^TA_a\beta(b)\right).
\end{equation}
Substituting \(\beta(a)=\lambda_ar\) and using \cref{eqn:large-image-rAr} gives
\begin{equation}\label{eqn:large-image-pre-eta}
[a,b]=\lambda_a\nu_b-\lambda_b\nu_a+\frac{\xi}{2}\left(\lambda_a^2\lambda_b-\lambda_b^2\lambda_a\right).
\end{equation}
Define
$\eta_a:=\nu_a-\frac{\xi}{2}\lambda_a^2.$
By \cref{lem:pointwise-lagrangian-coordinate-setup}, we have
\begin{equation}
\alpha(a+b)=\alpha(a)+\alpha(b)+A_a\beta(b).
\end{equation}
Using \(\beta(b)=\lambda_br\) and \cref{eqn:large-image-Ar-lambda}, we obtain
\begin{equation}
\nu_{a+b}=\nu_a+\nu_b+\xi\lambda_a\lambda_b.
\end{equation}
Since \(\lambda_{a+b}=\lambda_a+\lambda_b\), it follows that
\begin{align}
\eta_{a+b}
&=\nu_{a+b}-\frac{\xi}{2}\lambda_{a+b}^2=\nu_a+\nu_b+\xi\lambda_a\lambda_b-\frac{\xi}{2}(\lambda_a+\lambda_b)^2=\eta_a+\eta_b.
\end{align}
Thus \(\eta:\mathbb F_p^6\to\mathbb F_p\) is linear. \cref{eqn:large-image-pre-eta} therefore becomes
\begin{equation}\label{eqn:large-image-rank-two-form}
[a,b]=\lambda_a\eta_b-\lambda_b\eta_a.
\end{equation}
As in the proof of \cref{lem:three-qudit-codim-three}, the alternating form on the right has rank at most \(2\), whereas the symplectic form on \(\mathbb F_p^6\) has rank \(6\). This contradiction rules out \(d=4\), and completes the proof.
<!-- end proof-41 -->
<!-- prop-13: body_md -->
\label{lem:three-qudit-codim-four-impossible}
Let \(p\) be an odd prime and let \(U\in\mathcal C^{(3)}\) be a three-qudit gate. Set \(K_U:=\ker S_U\) and \(E_U:=\operatorname{im}S_U\). Then \(\operatorname{codim}K_U\neq4\).
<!-- end prop-13 -->
<!-- proof-42: body_md -->
Suppose, for contradiction, that \(\operatorname{codim}K_U=4\). Then $\dim K_U=2$ and  $\dim E_U=4.$
Since an alternating form is skew-symmetric and has even rank, the restriction of the symplectic form to \(K_U\) is either non-degenerate or identically zero. Suppose first that \(K_U\) is non-degenerate. By \cref{lem:kernel-cocycle-consequences}, \(W:=q_U(K_U)\) is a non-degenerate symplectic plane fixed pointwise by \(E_U\). Hence, \(\mathbb F_p^6=W\oplus W^\perp\), \(E_U\) acts on \(W^\perp\) and we obtain an injective homomorphism
\begin{equation}
E_U\lhook\joinrel\longrightarrow\operatorname{Sp}(W^\perp)\cong\operatorname{Sp}(\mathbb F_p^4).
\end{equation}
Thus, \(\operatorname{Sp}(\mathbb F_p^4)\) would contain an abelian \(p\)-subgroup of order \(p^4\).
This is impossible by \cref{codim4-two-qubit-rule}. Therefore, the symplectic form on \(K_U\) is identically zero. That is, \(K_U\) is isotropic. We rule out this case to derive a contradiction. We divide the proof into several steps to make the otherwise lengthy argument easier to follow.

\begin{enumerate} 
\item We first construct a decomposition of \(\mathbb F_p^6\) adapted to the isotropic plane \(W:=q_U(K_U)\)\footnote{This differs from the non-degenerate case where \(W\cap W^\perp=0\), and from the one-dimensional-radical case in the proof of \cref{lem:three-qudit-codim-three}, where a non-degenerate symplectic plane \(H\subseteq W\) could be split off. Here \(W\) is totally isotropic, so \(W\subseteq W^\perp\) and \(W\) contains no non-degenerate symplectic plane. We obtain the required symplectic plane from \(W^\perp/W\) instead.}. By \cref{lem:kernel-cocycle-consequences}, \(W\) is an isotropic plane fixed pointwise by \(E_U\). Since \(\dim W=2\), we have \(\dim W^\perp=4\). The radical of the restricted symplectic form on \(W^\perp\) is
\begin{equation}
\operatorname{rad}(W^\perp)=W^\perp\cap(W^\perp)^\perp=W^\perp\cap W=W,
\end{equation}
where we have used that \(W\subseteq W^\perp\). Thus, the quotient \(W^\perp/W\) is a two-dimensional non-degenerate symplectic space. We first choose a symplectic plane representing this quotient. Choose a basis \(w_1,w_2\) of \(W\) and extend it to a basis \(w_1,w_2,h_1,h_2\) of \(W^\perp\). Setting \(H:=\operatorname{span}\{h_1,h_2\}\), we have
\begin{equation}
W^\perp=W\oplus H,\qquad W^\perp/W\cong H.
\end{equation}
The restricted symplectic form on \(H\) is non-degenerate. Indeed, if \(h\in H\) and \([h,h']=0\) for all \(h'\in H\), then since \(h\in W^\perp\) we also have \([h,w]=0\) for all \(w\in W\). As \(W^\perp=W\oplus H\), it follows that \(h\in\operatorname{rad}(W^\perp)=W\). Since \(H\cap W=0\), we obtain \(h=0\). Since \(H\) is non-degenerate, we have
$\mathbb F_p^6=H\oplus H^\perp.$
Moreover, \(W\subseteq H^\perp\) because \(H\subseteq W^\perp\), and \(\dim H^\perp=4\). Since \(W\) is isotropic and has dimension \(2\), it is therefore Lagrangian in the four-dimensional symplectic space \(H^\perp\). Hence, there exists a Lagrangian subspace \(W^*\subseteq H^\perp\) such that
$H^\perp=W\oplus W^*,$
and the symplectic pairing identifies \(W^*\) with the dual space of \(W\). Consequently,
\begin{equation}\label{eqn:three-qudit-c4-witt}
\mathbb F_p^6=W\oplus H\oplus W^*.
\end{equation}

\item We next choose a basis adapted to the decomposition in \cref{eqn:three-qudit-c4-witt} and use it to determine explicitly the form of every symplectic transformation fixing \(W\) pointwise. Since the pairing between \(W\) and \(W^*\) is non-degenerate, we may choose bases \(w_1,w_2\) of \(W\) and \(w_1^*,w_2^*\) of \(W^*\) such that
\begin{equation}
[w_i,w_j^*]=\delta_{ij},\qquad [w_i,w_j]=[w_i^*,w_j^*]=0.
\end{equation}
Since \(H\) is a two-dimensional non-degenerate symplectic space, we may also choose a symplectic basis \(h_1,h_2\) satisfying
\begin{equation}
[h_1,h_2]=1,\qquad [h_2,h_1]=-1,\qquad [h_1,h_1]=[h_2,h_2]=0.
\end{equation}
Thus, relative to the ordered basis $w_1,w_2,h_1,h_2,w_1^*,w_2^*$
the symplectic form is represented by
\begin{equation}\label{eqn:three-qudit-c4-symplectic-matrix}
\Omega:=\begin{pmatrix}0&0&I\\0&J&0\\-I&0&0\end{pmatrix}, \qquad J=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{pmatrix}.
\end{equation}
We now determine the form of a symplectic transformation fixing \(W\) pointwise. First, such a transformation preserves \(W^\perp=W\oplus H\). Indeed, if \(x\in W^\perp\) and \(w\in W\), then
\begin{equation}
[Tx,w]=[Tx,Tw]=[x,w]=0,
\end{equation}
so \(Tx\in W^\perp\). Moreover, \(T\) induces the identity on \(\mathbb F_p^6/W^\perp\). Indeed, for every \(x\in\mathbb F_p^6\) and \(w\in W\),
\begin{equation}
[Tx-x,w]=[Tx,Tw]-[x,w]=0,
\end{equation}
and hence \(Tx-x\in W^\perp\). Therefore, relative to the decomposition in \cref{eqn:three-qudit-c4-witt}, fixing \(W\) pointwise gives the first block column \((I,0,0)^T\), preservation of \(W^\perp=W\oplus H\) forces the lower-middle block to vanish, and triviality on the quotient forces the lower-right block to be \(I\). Thus, \(T\) has the block form
\begin{equation}
T=\begin{pmatrix}I&A&B\\0&g&C\\0&0&I\end{pmatrix}
\end{equation}
for some \(2\times2\) matrices \(A,B,C,g\). Imposing the symplectic condition
$T^T\Omega T=\Omega,$
we compute
\begin{align}
T^T\Omega T
&=
\begin{pmatrix}
I&0&0\\
A^T&g^T&0\\
B^T&C^T&I
\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}
0&0&I\\
0&J&0\\
-I&0&0
\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}
I&A&B\\
0&g&C\\
0&0&I
\end{pmatrix}\\
&=
\begin{pmatrix}
I&0&0\\
A^T&g^T&0\\
B^T&C^T&I
\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}
0&0&I\\
0&Jg&JC\\
-I&-A&-B
\end{pmatrix}=
\begin{pmatrix}
0&0&I\\
0&g^TJg&A^T+g^TJC\\
-I&C^TJg-A&B^T+C^TJC-B
\end{pmatrix}.
\end{align}
Comparing this with $\Omega$ gives
\begin{equation}
g^TJg=J,\qquad A^T+g^TJC=0,\qquad B-B^T=C^TJC.
\end{equation}
The first identity says that \(g\in\operatorname{Sp}(H)\cong\operatorname{Sp}(\mathbb F^2_p)\). Using \(g^TJg=J\), the second identity gives
$C=gJA^T.$
Substituting this into the third identity gives
$B-B^T=AJA^T.$
Since \(p\) is odd, this is equivalent to writing
$B=Z+\frac12AJA^T$
for a unique symmetric matrix \(Z=Z^T\). Consequently, every symplectic transformation fixing \(W\) pointwise has a unique expression
\begin{equation}\label{eqn:three-qudit-c4-stabilizer}
T(g,A,Z):=\begin{pmatrix}I&A&Z+\frac12AJA^T\\0&g&gJA^T\\0&0&I\end{pmatrix},
\end{equation}
where $g\in\operatorname{Sp}(H)\cong\operatorname{Sp}(\mathbb F^2_p)$, $A\in M_2(\mathbb F_p)$ and $ Z\in\operatorname{Sym}_2(\mathbb F_p).$ Finally, direct block multiplication gives
\begin{equation}\label{eqn:three-qudit-c4-product}
T(g_1,A_1,Z_1)T(g_2,A_2,Z_2)=T\left(g_1g_2,A_2+A_1g_2,Z_1+Z_2+\operatorname{sym}(A_1g_2JA_2^T)\right),
\end{equation}
where $\operatorname{sym}(X):=\frac12(X+X^T).$

\item We next isolate a linear component of \(q_U\) that will provide the contradiction in both remaining cases. Write
\begin{equation}\label{eqn:three-qudit-c4-q}
q_U(a)=(\alpha(a),\gamma(a),\beta(a))\in W\oplus H\oplus W^*.
\end{equation}
Since every matrix in \cref{eqn:three-qudit-c4-stabilizer} acts as the identity on the \(W^*\) component, taking \(W^*\) components in the cocycle identity gives $\beta(a+b)=\beta(a)+\beta(b)$. Thus, $\beta:\mathbb F_p^6\to W^*$ is linear. We claim that
$\operatorname{rank}\beta=2.$
Let \(k\in K_U\) and \(a\in\mathbb F_p^6\). By \cref{lem:kernel-cocycle-consequences}, we have
$[q_U(k),q_U(a)]=[k,a].$
Since \(q_U(k)\in W\), while \(W\) is orthogonal to both \(W\) and \(H\), only the \(W^*\) component of \(q_U(a)\) contributes to the left hand side. Hence, we have
\begin{equation}\label{eqn:three-qudit-c4-beta-pairing}
[q_U(k),\beta(a)]=[k,a].
\end{equation}
\(q_U|_{K_U}:K_U\to W\) is an isomorphism. Since \(\beta(a)\in W^*\), it defines the functional on \(W\) given by \(w\mapsto[w,\beta(a)]\), and pulling this functional back along \(q_U|_{K_U}\) gives \(k\mapsto[q_U(k),\beta(a)]\). Hence, through \cref{eqn:three-qudit-c4-beta-pairing}, each \(\beta(a)\in W^*\) represents the linear functional on \(K_U\)
$k\longmapsto[k,a].$
On the other hand, non-degeneracy of the ambient symplectic form implies that
\begin{align}
\mathbb{F}_p^6 &\longrightarrow K_U^*,\\
a &\longmapsto \left(k\longmapsto[k,a]\right).
\end{align}
is surjective. 
If \(f\in K_U^*\), then there exists \(a\in\mathbb F_p^6\) such that
$f(k)=[k,a]$
for every \(k\in K_U\). By \cref{eqn:three-qudit-c4-beta-pairing},
\begin{equation}
f(k)=[k,a]=[q_U(k),\beta(a)].
\end{equation}
Thus, under the identification \(W^*\cong K_U^*\), the vector \(\beta(a)\) corresponds exactly to \(f\). Hence, \(\beta:\mathbb F_p^6\to W^*\) is surjective. As \(\dim W^*=2\), this proves $\operatorname{rank}\beta=2.$

\item We now record the action of \(E_U\) on the symplectic plane \(H\), which reduces the remaining argument to two possible cases. Taking the middle diagonal block in \cref{eqn:three-qudit-c4-stabilizer} defines a homomorphism
\begin{align}
\rho:E_U&\longrightarrow\operatorname{Sp}(\mathbb F^2_p),\\
T(g,A,Z)&\longmapsto g.
\end{align}
That \(\rho\) is a homomorphism follows from \cref{eqn:three-qudit-c4-product}. Since
$|\operatorname{Sp}(\mathbb F^2_p)|=p(p^2-1),$
every \(p\)-subgroup of \(\operatorname{Sp}(\mathbb F^2_p)\) has order at most \(p\). Hence, 
$\dim \rho(E_U)\in\{0,1\}.$
We rule out the possibility that $\dim \rho(E_U)=0$. The $\dim \rho(E_U)=1$ case is proved in \cref{appendix:rank-one-codim4-three}.  Let \(\dim \rho(E_U)=0\). In this case, all $g$'s are equal to the identity. We determine the possible \(A\)'s in \cref{eqn:three-qudit-c4-stabilizer} and then use the cocycle to contradict $\operatorname{rank}(\beta)=2$.  We proceed in several steps.

\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]

\item  Define
\begin{equation}
\mathcal A:=\{A\in M_2(\mathbb F_p):T(I,A,Z)\in E_U\text{ for some }Z\}.
\end{equation}
                                                                                                     
If \(A_1,A_2\in\mathcal A\), then there exist \(Z_1,Z_2\) such that \(T(I,A_1,Z_1),T(I,A_2,Z_2)\in E_U\), and we have
\begin{equation}
T(I,A_1,Z_1)T(I,A_2,Z_2)=T\left(I,A_1+A_2,Z_1+Z_2+\operatorname{sym}(A_1JA_2^T)\right)\in E_U.
\end{equation}
by \cref{eqn:three-qudit-c4-product}. Thus, \(A_1+A_2\in\mathcal A\). Clearly, \(0\in\mathcal A\). If \(A\in\mathcal A\), then for some \(Z\) we have \(T(I,A,Z)\in E_U\). By \cref{eqn:three-qudit-c4-product}, we have
\begin{equation}
T(I,A,Z)T(I,-A,-Z)=T\left(I,0,\operatorname{sym}(-AJA^T)\right)=T(I,0,0),
\end{equation}
where the final equality follows because \(AJA^T\) is skew-symmetric. Hence
\begin{equation}
T(I,A,Z)^{-1}=T(I,-A,-Z)\in E_U,
\end{equation}
so \(-A\in\mathcal A\). Therefore, \(\mathcal A\) is a linear subspace of \(M_2(\mathbb F_p)\). Let \(T(I,A,Z),T(I,D,Y)\in E_U\). By \cref{eqn:three-qudit-c4-product},
\begin{align}
T(I,A,Z)T(I,D,Y)
&=
T\left(I,A+D,Z+Y+\operatorname{sym}(AJD^T)\right),\\
T(I,D,Y)T(I,A,Z)
&=
T\left(I,A+D,Z+Y+\operatorname{sym}(DJA^T)\right).
\end{align}
Since \(E_U\) is abelian, these products are equal and their last components agree. Therefore,
$\operatorname{sym}(AJD^T)=\operatorname{sym}(DJA^T).$
Since we have
\begin{align}
\operatorname{sym}(AJD^T) &= \frac12(AJD^T-DJA^T),\\
\operatorname{sym}(DJA^T) &= \frac12(DJA^T-AJD^T),
\end{align}
equating these two expressions gives $2(AJD^T-DJA^T)=0$ and hence 
\begin{equation}\label{eqn:three-qudit-c4-AJD}
AJD^T=DJA^T
\end{equation}
for all \(A,D\in\mathcal A\). 

\item 
We claim that either the matrices $A: H \to W$ in \(\mathcal A\) have a common non-zero kernel vector $v \in H$ or $\mathcal A=\operatorname{span}(A_0)$ for some invertible matrix \(A_0\).  
Suppose first that \(A_0\in\mathcal A\) is invertible. For \(A\in\mathcal A\), write \(A=A_0D\). Applying \cref{eqn:three-qudit-c4-AJD} to \(A_0\) and \(A\) gives $JD^T=DJ$.  Writing $D=\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{pmatrix}$ gives
\begin{equation}
\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}a&c\\b&d\end{pmatrix}
=
\begin{pmatrix}b&d\\-a&-c\end{pmatrix}
=
\begin{pmatrix}-b&a\\-d&c\end{pmatrix}
=
\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{pmatrix}.
\end{equation}
Hence, \(b=c=0\) and \(d=a\), so \(D=aI\). Therefore, \(\mathcal A=\operatorname{span}(A_0)\). Suppose instead that every matrix in \(\mathcal A\) is singular and \(\mathcal A \neq 0\). After changing bases we may choose a non-zero element of \(\mathcal A\) of the form\footnote{
Every non-zero singular \(2\times2\) matrix has rank \(1\), so it may be written as \(A_0=uv^T\) with \(u,v\neq0\), where \(u\) is a vector in \(W\) and \(v\) is a vector in \(H\). Since \(A_0:H\to W\), we may change the bases of its codomain \(W\) and domain \(H\) independently. Choose a basis change \(P\in\operatorname{GL}(W)\) such that \(P^{-1}u=e_1\), changing the basis of \(W^*\) dually so that the symplectic pairing is preserved. Independently, since \(\operatorname{SL}_2(\mathbb F_p) = \operatorname{Sp}(H)\) acts transitively on the non-zero vectors of \(H\), choose a symplectic basis change \(Q\in\operatorname{SL}_2(\mathbb F_p)\) such that \(v^TQ=e_1^T\). Under these changes of basis, the matrix of \(A_0\) becomes
$P^{-1}A_0Q=(P^{-1}u)(v^TQ)=e_1e_1^T$. 
}
\begin{equation}
A_0=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&0\end{pmatrix}.
\end{equation}
For \(A=(a_{ij})\in\mathcal A\), every matrix \(A_0+tA\) is singular. Hence, we have
\begin{equation}
0=\det(A_0+tA)=ta_{22}+t^2\det A=ta_{22}.
\end{equation}
for every $t \in \mathbb F_p$.  Hence,  \(a_{22}=0\) and 
\(a_{12}a_{21}=0\). If one element of \(\mathcal A\) has \(a_{12}\neq0\) and another has \(a_{21}\neq0\), their sum is invertible, which is a contradiction. Thus, either all matrices in \(\mathcal A\) have the common kernel line \(\mathbb F_p e_2\), or all of their images are contained in the common image line \(\mathbb F_p e_1\). Suppose we are in the latter case and that there is no common non-zero kernel vector. Then every matrix in \(\mathcal A\) has the form \(u\mu\), where \(u\) is a fixed non-zero column vector spanning the common image line and \(\mu\) is a row vector. 
We can choose independent row vectors \(\mu,\nu\) such that \(u\mu,u\nu\in\mathcal A\)\footnote{If all row vectors \(\mu\) occurring in factorizations \(u\mu\in\mathcal A\) were proportional to a fixed nonzero row vector \(\mu_0\), then every matrix \(u\mu\in\mathcal A\) would satisfy \(\ker(u\mu)=\ker\mu_0\), giving a common kernel line.}.
Applying \cref{eqn:three-qudit-c4-AJD} with $A=u \mu$ and $D=u \nu$ gives
\begin{equation}
(\mu J\nu^T)uu^T=(\nu J\mu^T)uu^T=-(\mu J\nu^T)uu^T,
\end{equation}
and hence
$2(\mu J\nu^T)uu^T=0.$
This is impossible because \(p\) is odd, \(u\neq0\), and \(\mu J\nu^T\neq0\) for independent \(\mu,\nu\). Thus the common-image case also has a common kernel, proving the claim.

\item  We now rule out the possibility that \(\mathcal A\) has a common non-zero kernel line. Let \(v\neq 0\) and suppose that \(\ell:=\operatorname{span}\{v\}\subseteq H\) satisfies \(Av=0\) for every \(A\in\mathcal A\). We have
\begin{equation}
T(I,A,Z)\begin{pmatrix}0\\v\\0\end{pmatrix}
=
\begin{pmatrix}Av\\v\\0\end{pmatrix}
=
\begin{pmatrix}0\\v\\0\end{pmatrix}.
\end{equation}
Thus, every element of \(E_U\) fixes \(\ell\) pointwise. Since \(E_U\) fixes \(W\) pointwise by construction, it follows that \(E_U\) fixes \(W\oplus\ell\) pointwise. Moreover, \(W\) is isotropic, \(\ell\subseteq H\subseteq W^\perp\), and \(\ell\) is one-dimensional, so \(W\oplus\ell\) is isotropic. Since
\begin{equation}
\dim(W\oplus\ell)=2+1=3=\frac12\dim\mathbb F_p^6,
\end{equation}
it is Lagrangian. This contradicts \cref{lem:three-qudit-large-image-obstruction}  because  \(\dim E_U=4\). 

\item By (c), we have  $\mathcal A= \operatorname{span}(A_0)$ for some invertible \(A_0\in M_2(\mathbb F_p)\). We now use this description to show that \(\beta\) has rank at most \(1\). Consider the $\mathbb F_p$-linear map
\begin{align}
\varphi:E_U&\longrightarrow\mathcal A,\\
T(I,A,Z)&\longmapsto A.
\end{align}
Its image is \(\mathcal A=\operatorname{span}(A_0)\), which has dimension \(1\). Since \(\dim E_U=4\), rank-nullity gives
$\dim_{\mathbb F_p}\ker\phi=4-1=3.$
The kernel consists of those elements of \(E_U\) whose \(A\) component is zero. Hence, 
\begin{equation}
\ker\varphi\subseteq Z_0:=\left\{T(I,0,Z):Z=Z^T\in\operatorname{Sym}_2(\mathbb F_p)\right\}.
\end{equation}
Since \(\dim \operatorname{Sym}_2(\mathbb F_p)=3\), we have $\dim Z_0 = 3$.
Thus, \(\ker\varphi\) and \(Z_0\) have the same dimension. Hence, 
$\ker\varphi=Z_0.$
Since \(A_0\in\mathcal A\), choose \(h\in\mathbb F_p^6\) such that
\begin{equation}
S_U(h)=T(I,A_0,Z_h)
\end{equation}
for some symmetric matrix \(Z_h\). Now let \(b\in\mathbb F_p^6\) satisfy \(S_U(b)\in Z_0\), so that
$S_U(b)=T(I,0,Z_b)$
for some symmetric matrix \(Z_b\).
Since \(\mathbb F_p^6\) is abelian, the affine cocycle equation applied to \(h+b=b+h\) gives
\begin{equation}
q_U(h)+S_U(h)q_U(b)=q_U(b)+S_U(b)q_U(h).
\end{equation}
Write \(q_U(a)=(\alpha(a),\gamma(a),\beta(a))\). The \(H\) component of \(T(I,A,Z)(\alpha,\gamma,\beta)\) is
$\gamma+JA^T\beta.$
Comparing the \(H\) components in the cocycle identity gives
\begin{equation}
\gamma(h)+\gamma(b)+JA_0^T\beta(b)=\gamma(b)+\gamma(h),
\end{equation}
and hence
$JA_0^T\beta(b)=0.$
Since \(J\) and \(A_0\) are invertible, we obtain \(\beta(b)=0\). It follows that \(\beta\) vanishes on \(S_U^{-1}(Z_0)\). Since \(\ker S_U=K_U\) and \(S_U\) maps \(S_U^{-1}(Z_0)\) onto \(Z_0\), we have
$S_U^{-1}(Z_0)/K_U\cong Z_0.$
Therefore,
\begin{equation}
\dim S_U^{-1}(Z_0)=\dim K_U+\dim Z_0=2+3=5.
\end{equation}
Thus \(\beta\) vanishes on a five-dimensional subspace of \(\mathbb F_p^6\), so
$\operatorname{rank}\beta\leq 6-5=1$, a contradiction.
\end{enumerate}

\item The $\dim \rho(E_U)=1$ case is proved in \cref{appendix:rank-one-codim4-three}.
\end{enumerate}
This completes the proof.
<!-- end proof-42 -->
<!-- prop-14: body_md -->
\label{lem:three-qudit-codim-five-impossible}
Let \(p\) be an odd prime and let \(U\in\mathcal C^{(3)}\) be a three-qudit gate. Set \(K_U:=\ker S_U\) and \(E_U:=\operatorname{im}S_U\). Then \(\operatorname{codim}K_U\neq5\).
<!-- end prop-14 -->
<!-- prop-15: body_md -->
\label{last}
Let \(p\) be an odd prime and let \(U\in\mathcal C^{(3)}\) be a three-qudit gate. Set \(K_U:=\ker S_U\) and \(E_U:=\operatorname{im}S_U\). Then \(\operatorname{codim}K_U\neq6\).
<!-- end prop-15 -->
<!-- proof-43: body_md -->
In this case \(K_U=0\), so \(E_U\cong\mathbb F_p^6\). In particular,
$\dim_{\mathbb F_p}E_U=6$
and \(|E_U|=p^6\).  Choose a symplectic basis
$e_1,e_2,e_3,f_1,f_2,f_3$
of \(\mathbb F_p^6\), and define $W_i:=\operatorname{span}\{e_1,\ldots,e_i\}$ for 
$0\leq i\leq 3.$
Then
\begin{equation}
0=W_0\subset W_1\subset W_2\subset W_3
\end{equation}
is a complete isotropic flag, with \(W_3\) Lagrangian. Relative to the decomposition
\begin{equation}
\mathbb F_p^6=W_3\oplus\operatorname{span}\{f_1,f_2,f_3\},
\end{equation}
the associated Sylow \(p\)-subgroup is
\begin{equation}\label{hi}
P:=\left\{\begin{pmatrix}R&RS\\0&R^{-T}\end{pmatrix}:R\in U_3(\mathbb F_p),\ S\in\operatorname{Sym}_3(\mathbb F_p)\right\},
\end{equation}
where
\begin{equation}
U_3(\mathbb F_p):=\left\{\begin{pmatrix}1&a&b\\0&1&c\\0&0&1\end{pmatrix}:a,b,c\in\mathbb F_p\right\}.
\end{equation}
If \(R \in U_3(\mathbb F_p)\), then $R$ preserves each \(W_i\) and acts trivially on every successive quotient \(W_i/W_{i-1}\). Moreover, preservation of the symplectic form by a block upper-triangular matrix
\begin{equation}
\begin{pmatrix}R&B\\0&D\end{pmatrix}
\end{equation}
forces \(D=R^{-T}\) and \(R^{-1}B\) to be symmetric. Hence, \(B=RS\) for a unique \(S\in\operatorname{Sym}_3(\mathbb F_p)\), giving \cref{hi}.
There are three free parameters in \(R\in U_3(\mathbb F_p)\) and six free parameters in \(S\in\operatorname{Sym}_3(\mathbb F_p)\). Therefore,
$|P|=p^{3+6}=p^9.$
On the other hand,
\begin{equation}
|\operatorname{Sp}_6(\mathbb F_p)|=p^9(p^2-1)(p^4-1)(p^6-1).
\end{equation}
Hence,  \(P\) is a Sylow \(p\)-subgroup of \(\operatorname{Sp}_6(\mathbb F_p)\). In fact, \(P=P(W_0,W_1,W_2,W_3)\) in the notation of \cref{wong}.
Since \(E_U\) is a \(p\)-subgroup of \(\operatorname{Sp}(\mathbb F_p^6)\), it is contained in some Sylow \(p\)-subgroup. Since all Sylow \(p\)-subgroups are conjugate, after conjugating inside \(\operatorname{Sp}(\mathbb F_p^6)\), we may assume without loss of generality that
$E_U\subseteq P.$
By \cref{wong}, \(A(W_3)\) unique abelian subgroup of largest order in \(P\). In fact, $A(W_3)$ can be identified with 
\begin{equation}
A(W_3)=\left\{\begin{pmatrix}I&S\\0&I\end{pmatrix}:S\in\operatorname{Sym}_3(\mathbb F_p)\right\},
\end{equation}
Since $|A(W_3)|=|E_U|=p^6$, we have $E_U=A(W_3)$. Therefore, \(E_U\) fixes the Lagrangian \(W_3\) pointwise.
Since \(\dim E_U=6\geq4\), this contradicts \cref{lem:three-qudit-large-image-obstruction}.
<!-- end proof-43 -->
<!-- proof-44: body_md -->
This follows from \cref{codim2-gen}, \cref{lem:three-qudit-codim-three}, \cref{lem:three-qudit-codim-four-impossible}, \cref{lem:three-qudit-codim-five-impossible} and \cref{last}.
<!-- end proof-44 -->
<!-- lem-20: body_md -->
\label{lem:single-Weyl-support}
Let \(U\in \mathcal U(\mathcal H_n)\) such that \(\partial_a U\in U(1)I\) for every \(a\in V_n\). Equivalently, suppose that there exists a phase function \(\lambda:V_n\to U(1)\) such that \(\tau_a(U)=\lambda(a)U\) for every \(a\in V_n\). Then there exist \(v\in V_n\) and \(\zeta\in U(1)\) such that
$U=\zeta w(v)$.
<!-- end lem-20 -->
<!-- proof-45: body_md -->
Expand \(U\) in the Weyl basis as \(U=\sum_{v\in V_n} c_v w(v)\). Applying \(\tau_a\) and using \cref{tau-on-Weyl}, we obtain
\begin{equation}
\sum_{v\in V_n} \lambda(a)c_v w(v)=\lambda(a)U=\tau_a(U)=\sum_{v\in V_n} c_v \tau_a(w(v))=\sum_{v\in V_n} c_v \omega^{[a,v]}w(v).
\end{equation}
Uniqueness of the Weyl expansion implies that \(c_v\omega^{[a,v]}=\lambda(a)c_v\) for all \(a,v\in V_n\). Hence, if \(c_v\neq 0\), then \(\omega^{[a,v]}=\lambda(a)\) for every \(a\in V_n\). We claim that at most one coefficient \(c_v\) can be non-zero. Indeed, if \(c_v, ,c_{v'}\neq 0\), then
\begin{equation}
\omega^{[a,v]}=\lambda(a)=\omega^{[a,v']}
\end{equation}
for every \(a\in V_n\). Therefore, \(\omega^{[a,v-v']}=1\) for every \(a\in V_n\). Since \(\omega\) is a primitive \(p\)-th root of unity, we must have \([a,v-v']=0\) for every \(a\in V_n\). The non-degeneracy of the symplectic form forces \(v-v'=0\), and hence \(v=v'\). Thus, \(U\) has support on a single Weyl basis element. Since \(U\neq 0\), there exist \(v\in V_n\) and \(\zeta\in\mathbb C\) such that \(U=\zeta w(v)\). Finally, since \(U\) and \(w(v)\) are unitary, \(|\zeta|=1\). Hence, \(\zeta\in U(1)\), as required.
<!-- end proof-45 -->
<!-- cor-10: body_md -->
\label{cor:tau-invariants-are-scalars}
Let \(U\in \mathcal U(\mathcal H_n)\). If \(\partial_a U=I\) for every \(a\in V_n\), then \(U\in U(1)I\).
<!-- end cor-10 -->
<!-- proof-46: body_md -->
Since \(\partial_a U=\tau_a(U)U^*\), the assumption \(\partial_a U=I\) implies that \(\tau_a(U)=U\) for every \(a\in V_n\). Thus, \(U\) satisfies the hypothesis of \cref{lem:single-Weyl-support} with the constant phase function \(\lambda(a)=1\). Hence, there exist \(v\in V_n\) and \(\zeta\in U(1)\) such that $U=\zeta w(v)$. Applying \(\tau_a\) and using \cref{tau-on-Weyl}, we get
\begin{equation}
\zeta w(v)=U=\tau_a(U)=\zeta \omega^{[a,v]}w(v) \quad \Longrightarrow \quad
\zeta (\omega^{[a,v]}-1)w(v) = 0.
\end{equation}
for every $a \in V_n$. It follows that $\omega^{[a,v]}=1$ for every \(a\in V_n\). As in \cref{lem:single-Weyl-support}, we conclude that \(v=0\). Therefore, \(U=\zeta w(0)=\zeta I\), and hence \(U\in U(1)I\).
<!-- end proof-46 -->
<!-- lem-21: body_md -->
\label{lem:Weyl-label-phase-uniqueness}
Let \(x,y\in V_n\) and let \(\lambda,\lambda'\in U(1)\). If $\lambda w(x)=\lambda' w(y)$, then \(x=y\) and \(\lambda=\lambda'\).
<!-- end lem-21 -->
<!-- proof-47: body_md -->
Multiplying the equality \(\lambda w(x)=\lambda' w(y)\) on the left by \(w(x)^*\), we obtain $\lambda I=\lambda' w(x)^*w(y)$.  Since \(w(x)^*w(y)\) is a scalar multiple of \(w(y-x)\), there exists \(\mu\in U(1)\) such that $\lambda I=\lambda'\mu w(y-x).$
We claim that \(x=y\). Indeed, if \(x\neq y\), then \(y-x\neq 0\), and so \(\operatorname{Tr}(w(y-x))=0\) by \cref{weyl-inner}. Taking traces in the preceding equality gives
\begin{equation}
0 \neq \lambda \operatorname{Tr}(I)=\lambda'\mu \operatorname{Tr}(w(y-x))=0.
\end{equation}
This is a contradiction. Therefore, \(x=y\). Substituting \(x=y\) into \(\lambda w(x)=\lambda' w(y)\), we obtain $\lambda w(x)=\lambda' w(x)$.  Since \(w(x)\) is unitary, it is invertible. Hence, \(\lambda=\lambda'\).
<!-- end proof-47 -->
<!-- cor-11: body_md -->
\label{lem:weyl-scalar-label}
Let \(a\in V_n\). If \(w(a)\in U(1)I\), then \(a=0\).
<!-- end cor-11 -->
<!-- proof-48: body_md -->
Since \(w(a)\in U(1)I\), there exists \(\lambda\in U(1)\) such that $w(a)=\lambda I.$ Since \(w(0)=I\), this can be rewritten as $w(a)=\lambda w(0)$. By \cref{lem:Weyl-label-phase-uniqueness}, we get \(a=0\).
<!-- end proof-48 -->
<!-- lem-22: body_md -->
\label{commutator-bicharacter-well-defined}
Let \(A\) be an abelian group, and let \(U(1)\) be equipped with the trivial \(A\)-action. If \(R\in Z^2(A,U(1))\) is a normalized \(2\)-cocycle, then the map
\begin{equation}
\operatorname{comm}_R(a,b):=\frac{R(a,b)}{R(b,a)}
\end{equation}
is an alternating bicharacter on \(A\), and hence defines an element of \(\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb Z}(\Lambda^2 A,U(1))\). Moreover, if \(R\) and \(R'\) are cohomologous normalized \(2\)-cocycles, then \(\operatorname{comm}_R=\operatorname{comm}_{R'}\).
<!-- end lem-22 -->
<!-- proof-49: body_md -->
Recall that a cohomology class \([R]\in H^2(A,U(1))\) determines an equivalence class of central extensions of \(A\) by \(U(1)\). If \(R\) is a normalized cocycle representative, then \(R(0,a)=R(a,0)=1\) for all \(a\in A\)\footnote{It can be shown that every \(2\)-cocycle is cohomologous to a normalized \(2\)-cocycle.}. In this case, an explicit central extension is given by
\begin{equation} 
1\longrightarrow U(1)\longrightarrow E_R\longrightarrow A\longrightarrow 1.
\end{equation}
Here \(E_R=U(1)\times A\) as a set, the map $U(1) \to E_R$ is the inclusion map and $E_R \to A$ is the projection map. The multiplication law on $E_R$ is
\begin{equation} 
(z,a)(w,b)=(zwR(a,b),a+b).
\end{equation}
The cocycle identity gives associativity, and the normalization of \(R\) implies that \((1,0)\) is the identity element and that \(U(1) \times \{0\}\) is contained in the center of $E_R$. Thus, this defines a central extension of \(A\) by \(U(1)\). Since \(A\) is abelian, every commutator in \(E_R\) maps trivially to \(A\). Therefore, every commutator in \(E_R\) is in the kernel of the map $E_R \to A$, which is precisely \(U(1)\times\{0\}\). Therefore, for \(a,b\in A\), choose lifts \(\widetilde a,\widetilde b\in E_R\) and define
\begin{equation}
[\widetilde a,\widetilde b]\in U(1)\times\{0\}\cong U(1).
\end{equation}
This is independent of the chosen lifts. Indeed, if \(\widetilde a'\) and \(\widetilde b'\) are other lifts, then \(\widetilde a'=u\widetilde a\) and \(\widetilde b'=v\widetilde b\) for some \(u,v\in U(1)\times\{0\}\). Since \(U(1)\times\{0\}\) is contained in the center of \(E_R\), the elements \(u\) and \(v\) commute with all elements of \(E_R\). Indeed, we have 
\begin{align}
[u\widetilde a,v\widetilde b]
&= u\widetilde a v\widetilde b \widetilde a^{-1}u^{-1}\widetilde b^{-1}v^{-1} \\
&= \widetilde a\widetilde b\widetilde a^{-1}\widetilde b^{-1} \\
&= [\widetilde a,\widetilde b].
\end{align}
Thus, the commutator is independent of the chosen lifts and the central extension \(E_R\) defines a well-defined commutator pairing. 
\begin{comment}
             
                                                                                  
           
\end{comment}
We now compute this commutator pairing explicitly using the standard lift \((1,a)\) of each element \(a\in A\). For $a,b \in A$, we have
\begin{align}
(1,a)(1,b) &= (R(a,b),a+b), \\
(1,b)(1,a) &= (R(b,a),a+b).
\end{align}
We compute the commutator directly. Since $(1,x)^{-1}=(R(x,-x)^{-1},-x)$\footnote{
This follows from the cocycle identity and normalization applied to the triple \((x,-x,x)\).} for all $x \in A$, we have
\begin{align}
[(1,a),(1,b)]
&=(1,a)(1,b)(1,a)^{-1}(1,b)^{-1}\\
&=(1,a)(1,b)(R(a,-a)^{-1},-a)(R(b,-b)^{-1},-b)\\
&=(R(a,b),a+b)(R(a,-a)^{-1},-a)(R(b,-b)^{-1},-b)\\
&=(R(a,b)R(a,-a)^{-1}R(a+b,-a),b)(R(b,-b)^{-1},-b)\\
&=(R(a,b)R(a,-a)^{-1}R(a+b,-a),0).
\end{align}
Noting that $R(a,-a)^{-1}R(a+b,-a)=R(b,a)^{-1}$\footnote{This follows from the cocycle identity and normalization applied to the triple \((b,a,-a)\).}, we have
\begin{equation}
[(1,a),(1,b)]=\left(\frac{R(a,b)}{R(b,a)},0\right).
\end{equation}
for all $a,b \in A$. Hence, the commutator pairing is given by the map
\begin{align}
A\times A &\longrightarrow U(1) \\
(a,b) &\longmapsto \frac{R(a,b)}{R(b,a)}.
\end{align}
This is exactly the map \(\operatorname{comm}_R\). It remains to check that the commutator pairing is an alternating map. For any \(x,x',y\in E_R\), we have 
\begin{align}
[xx',y]
&=xx'y(xx')^{-1}y^{-1}  \\
&=xx'yx'^{-1}x^{-1}y^{-1} \\
&=x[x',y]yx'x'^{-1}x^{-1}y^{-1} \\
&=x[x',y]yx^{-1}y^{-1} \\
&=[x',y]xyx^{-1}y^{-1}=[x',y][x,y]=[x,y][x',y].
\end{align}
Similarly, one has \( [x,yy']=[x,y][x,y'] \). Together with $\operatorname{comm}_R(a,a)=R(a,a)/R(a,a)=1$, these identities show that the commutator pairing is an alternating bicharacter. By the universal property of alternating maps, every alternating bicharacter $A\times A\longrightarrow U(1)$ determines a unique homomorphism $\Lambda^2 A\longrightarrow U(1).$
Therefore \(\operatorname{comm}_R\) defines an element of $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb Z}(\Lambda^2 A,U(1)).$ Suppose that \([R]=[R']\). Then $R'=R\,\delta\alpha$ for some \(1\)-cochain \(\alpha:A\to U(1)\), where
\begin{equation}
(\delta\alpha)(a,b)
=\frac{\alpha(a)\alpha(b)}{\alpha(a+b)}
=\frac{\alpha(b)\alpha(a)}{\alpha(b+a)}=(\delta\alpha)(b,a).
\end{equation}
Therefore, we have
\begin{equation}
\operatorname{comm}_{R'}(a,b)=\frac{R'(a,b)}{R'(b,a)}=\frac{R(a,b)(\delta\alpha)(a,b)}{R(b,a)(\delta\alpha)(b,a)}=\frac{R(a,b)}{R(b,a)}=\operatorname{comm}_R(a,b).
\end{equation}
This completes the proof.
<!-- end proof-49 -->
<!-- lem-23: body_md -->
\label{h2-finite-abelian-alt2}
Let \(A\) be a finite abelian group. Then \(H^2(A,U(1)) \cong \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb Z}(\Lambda^2 A,U(1))\), and both groups are finite.
<!-- end lem-23 -->
<!-- proof-50: body_md -->
We compute group cohomology using the classifying space \(BA\). Since \(A\) is discrete and the \(A\)-action on \(U(1)\) is trivial, group cohomology agrees with the singular cohomology of \(BA\) with $U(1)$ coefficients. That is, 
\begin{equation}
H^m(A,U(1))\cong H^m(BA;U(1)).
\end{equation}
By abuse of notation, we continue to denote the singular cohomology groups \(H^m(BA;U(1))\) by \(H^m(A,U(1))\). Recall that \(BA\) is an Eilenberg--Mac Lane space \(K(A,1)\). The universal coefficient theorem for singular cohomology gives a short exact sequence of abelian groups
\begin{equation}\label{uct}
0 \longrightarrow \operatorname{Ext}^1_{\mathbb Z}(H_1(BA;\mathbb Z),U(1)) \longrightarrow H^2(BA;U(1)) \longrightarrow \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb Z}(H_2(BA;\mathbb Z),U(1)) \longrightarrow 0.
\end{equation}
Since \(U(1)\) is a divisible group and divisible abelian groups are injective objects in the category of abelian groups, we have $\operatorname{Ext}^1_{\mathbb Z}(H_1(BA;\mathbb Z),U(1)) = 0$. By \cref{uct}, we have
\begin{equation}\label{uct-cons}
H^2(A,U(1)) \cong \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb Z}(H_2(BA;\mathbb Z),U(1)).
\end{equation}
It remains to identify \(H_2(BA;\mathbb Z)\). Since \(A\) is a finite abelian group, we have $A\cong \bigoplus_{i=1}^r \mathbb{Z}_{m_i}$. Since both \(BA\) and \(\prod_{i=1}^r B\mathbb Z_{m_i}\) are \(K(A,1)\)-spaces, uniqueness of Eilenberg--Mac Lane spaces up to homotopy equivalence implies that we have
\begin{equation}\label{eq:BA-product-decomposition}
BA\simeq \prod_{i=1}^r B\mathbb Z_{m_i}.
\end{equation}
We use the standard topological model $B\mathbb Z_m \simeq \mathbb S^\infty/\mathbb Z_m$,  where \(\mathbb Z_m\) acts freely on \(\mathbb S^\infty \subseteq \mathbb C^\infty\) by scalar multiplication by \(m\)-th roots of unity. The quotient \(\mathbb S^\infty/\mathbb Z_m\) is the infinite lens space \(L(\infty,m)\), and it is a \(K(\mathbb Z_m,1)\) space. It is well known that
\begin{equation}\label{eq:homology-infinite-lens-space}
H_k(L(\infty,m);\mathbb Z)\cong
\begin{cases}
\mathbb Z, & k=0,\\
\mathbb Z_m, & k>0 \text{ odd},\\
0, & k>0 \text{ even}.
\end{cases}
\end{equation}
We now apply the Künneth theorem. Note that the possible \(\operatorname{Tor}\)-terms in degree \(2\) vanish, since they involve \(H_0(B\mathbb Z_{m_i};\mathbb Z)\cong \mathbb Z\), and \(\operatorname{Tor}_1^{\mathbb Z}(\mathbb Z,M)=\operatorname{Tor}_1^{\mathbb Z}(M,\mathbb Z)=0\) for every abelian group \(M\). Thus the degree-two homology receives contributions only from tensor products of degree-one homology groups from distinct factors. Hence, we have
\begin{equation}\label{eq:H2-BA-kunneth}
H_2(BA;\mathbb Z) \cong \bigoplus_{1\leq i<j\leq r} H_1(B\mathbb Z_{m_i};\mathbb Z)\otimes_{\mathbb Z} H_1(B\mathbb Z_{m_j};\mathbb Z) \cong \bigoplus_{1\leq i<j\leq r} \mathbb Z_{m_i}\otimes_{\mathbb Z} \mathbb Z_{m_j}.
\end{equation}
On the other hand, $\Lambda^2 A$ decomposes as
\begin{equation}
\Lambda^2\left(\bigoplus_{i=1}^r \mathbb Z_{m_i}\right) \cong \left(\bigoplus_{i=1}^r \Lambda^2 \mathbb Z_{m_i}\right) \oplus \left(\bigoplus_{1\leq i<j\leq r} \mathbb Z_{m_i}\otimes_{\mathbb Z}\mathbb Z_{m_j}\right).
\end{equation}
Since each \(\mathbb Z_{m_i}\) is cyclic,  we have \(\Lambda^2 \mathbb Z_{m_i}=0\). Therefore, we have
\begin{equation}\label{h2-ba}
H_2(BA;\mathbb Z) \cong \bigoplus_{1\leq i<j\leq r} \mathbb Z_{m_i}\otimes_{\mathbb Z} \mathbb Z_{m_j} \cong \Lambda^2 A,
\end{equation}
\cref{uct-cons} and \cref{h2-ba} imply \(H^2(A,U(1))\cong \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb Z}(\Lambda^2 A,U(1))\).
<!-- end proof-50 -->
<!-- cor-12: body_md -->
\label{comm-map-iso}
Let \(A\) be a finite abelian group. Then the commutator pairing
\begin{align}
H^2(A,U(1)) &\longrightarrow \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb{Z}}(\Lambda^2A,U(1)), \\
[R] &\longmapsto \operatorname{comm}_R
\end{align}
is an isomorphism of finite groups.
<!-- end cor-12 -->
<!-- proof-51: body_md -->
By \cref{h2-finite-abelian-alt2}, we have an abstract isomorphism \(H^2(A,U(1)) \cong \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb Z}(\Lambda^2 A,U(1))\) of finite groups. Hence, it suffices to show that the commutator pairing from \cref{commutator-bicharacter-well-defined} is injective. Let $[R] \in H^2(A,U(1)) $ such that \(\operatorname{comm}_R(a,b)=1\) for all \(a,b\in A\). Equivalently, in the corresponding central extension \(E_R\), the commutator of any two lifts of elements of \(A\) is trivial. Let \(x,y\in E_R\). If \(a,b\in A\) are their images, then \(x=u\widetilde a\) and \(y=v\widetilde b\) for some lifts \(\widetilde a,\widetilde b\) of \(a,b\) and \(u,v\in U(1)\). Since \(U(1)\) lies in the center of \(E_R\), we have \([x,y]=[\widetilde a,\widetilde b]\). By assumption this commutator is trivial, so \([x,y]=1\) for all $x,y \in E_R$. Thus, \(E_R\) is an abelian group. Hence, we obtain a short exact sequence of abelian groups
\begin{equation}\label{ses-ab}
0 \longrightarrow U(1) \longrightarrow E_R \longrightarrow A \longrightarrow 0.
\end{equation}
Since \(U(1)\) is a divisible group, it is injective in the category of abelian groups. Therefore, the short exact sequence in \cref{ses-ab} splits in the category of abelian groups. Choose a splitting \(s:A\to E_R\) such that \(s(a)=(\alpha(a),a)\), where $\alpha : A \to U(1)$ is a map. The condition that \(s\) is a homomorphism gives
\begin{equation}
(\alpha(a+b),a+b)=s(a+b)=s(a)s(b)=(\alpha(a)\alpha(b)R(a,b),a+b).
\end{equation}
Therefore, we have
\begin{equation}\label{preceding}
R(a,b)=\frac{\alpha(a+b)}{\alpha(a)\alpha(b)}.
\end{equation}
With the convention that, for a \(1\)-cochain \(\beta\),
$(\delta\beta)(a,b)=\frac{\beta(a)\beta(b)}{\beta(a+b)},$
\cref{preceding} gives \(R=\delta(\alpha^{-1})\). Hence, \(R\) is a $2$-coboundary, so \([R]=0\). Thus \(\ker \Phi=0\), and therefore \(\Phi\) is injective. This completes the proof.
<!-- end proof-51 -->
<!-- cor-13: body_md -->
\label{cor:coboundary-iff-trivial-commutator}
Let \(A\) be a finite abelian group, and let \(R\in Z^2(A,U(1))\) be a normalized \(2\)-cocycle. Then $[R]=0\in H^2(A,U(1))$ if and only if $\frac{R(a,b)}{R(b,a)}=1$ for all \(a,b\in A\). In particular, if \(V\) is a finite-dimensional vector space over \(\mathbb F_p\) with basis \(e_1,\ldots,e_m\), then for any normalized \(2\)-cocycle \(R\in Z^2(V,U(1))\), one has $[R]=0\in H^2(V,U(1))$ if and only if
\begin{equation}\label{basis-comm}
\frac{R(e_i,e_j)}{R(e_j,e_i)}=1
\end{equation}
for all \(1\leq i,j\leq m\).
<!-- end cor-13 -->
<!-- proof-52: body_md -->
By \cref{comm-map-iso}, the class \([R]\) vanishes if and only if its image under the commutator pairing in \(\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb Z}(\Lambda^2 A,U(1))\) vanishes. Since this image is the alternating bicharacter \(\operatorname{comm}_R\), it follows that \([R]=0\) if and only if $\frac{R(a,b)}{R(b,a)}=1$ for all \(a,b\in A\). Take \(A=V\). Since \(\operatorname{comm}_R\) is biadditive, it is determined by its values on pairs of basis vectors. Indeed, if \(v=\sum_i \lambda_i e_i\) and \(w=\sum_j \mu_j e_j\), then biadditivity gives
\begin{equation}
\operatorname{comm}_R(v,w)
=
\prod_{i,j}\operatorname{comm}_R(e_i,e_j)^{\lambda_i\mu_j}.
\end{equation}
Thus \(\operatorname{comm}_R\) is determined by its values on pairs of basis vectors. Therefore, \(\operatorname{comm}_R\) is trivial on \(V\times V\) if and only if \(\operatorname{comm}_R(e_i,e_j)=1\) for all \(1\leq i,j\leq m\). This is exactly \cref{basis-comm}.
<!-- end proof-52 -->
<!-- lem-24: body_md -->
\label{lem:qubit-clifford-extension-cocycle}
The map
\begin{equation}
c:
\operatorname{Sp}(V_n)\times\operatorname{Sp}(V_n)
\longrightarrow
V_n
\end{equation}
is a normalized \(2\)-cocycle for the natural action of \(\operatorname{Sp}(V_n)\) on \(V_n\), given by
\(S\cdot v:=Sv\). Explicitly,
\begin{equation}
\label{eqn:qubit-c-cocycle}
c(S,T)+c(ST,R) = Sc(T,R)+c(S,TR)
\end{equation}
for all \(S,T,R\in\operatorname{Sp}(V_n)\).
<!-- end lem-24 -->
<!-- proof-53: body_md -->
