By associativity, $(M_SM_T)M_R=M_S(M_TM_R).$ Using \cref{eqn:qubit-clifford-section-product} on the left-hand side, and collecting scalar factors into a phase \(\lambda\in U(1)\), we obtain
\begin{equation}
(M_SM_T)M_R = \lambda\, w(c(S,T)+c(ST,R))M_{STR}.
\end{equation}
On the other hand, using \cref{eqn:qubit-clifford-representative-action} and \cref{eqn:qubit-clifford-section-product} on the right-hand side gives, for some \(\lambda'\in U(1)\),
\begin{equation}
M_S(M_TM_R) = \lambda'\,
w(Sc(T,R)+c(S,TR))M_{STR}.
\end{equation}
\cref{lem:Weyl-label-phase-uniqueness} implies \cref{eqn:qubit-c-cocycle}. The normalization follows from \cref{eqn:qubit-c-normalization}.
<!-- end proof-53 -->
<!-- prop-16: body_md -->
\label{prop:qubit-third-level-classification}
For each \(a\in V_n\), write
\begin{equation}\label{eqn:qubit-third-level-B-normal-form} B(a)=\alpha_B(a)w(q_B(a))M_{S_B(a)}, \end{equation}
where \(\alpha_B(a)\in U(1)\), \(q_B(a)\in V_n\), and \(S_B(a)\in\operatorname{Sp}(V_n)\). Then \(B\in Y^3_2(V_n)\) if and only if
\begin{align}
S_B(a+b) &= S_B(a)S_B(b), \label{eqn:qubit-third-level-S-equation}\\
q_B(a+b) &= q_B(a)+S_B(a)q_B(b)+c(S_B(a),S_B(b)), \label{eqn:qubit-third-level-q-equation}\\
\alpha_B(a+b) &= \alpha_B(a)\alpha_B(b)\gamma_{S_B(a)}(q_B(b))\kappa(S_B(a),S_B(b)) \notag\\
&\qquad\times i^{\mu(q_B(a),S_B(a)q_B(b))+\mu(q_B(a)+S_B(a)q_B(b),c(S_B(a),S_B(b)))-\mu(a,b)}. \label{eqn:qubit-third-level-alpha-equation}
\end{align}
for all \(a,b\in V_n\).
<!-- end prop-16 -->
<!-- proof-54: body_md -->
By \cref{rem:equiv-abstract-qubit}, we have \(B\in Y^3_2(V_n)\) if and only if
$B(a)B(b)=i^{\mu(a,b)}B(a+b)$ for all \(a,b\in V_n\). Using \cref{eqn:qubit-clifford-representative-action}, we obtain
\begin{align}
B(a)B(b) &= \alpha_B(a)\alpha_B(b)w(q_B(a))M_{S_B(a)}w(q_B(b))M_{S_B(b)}\\
&= \alpha_B(a)\alpha_B(b)\gamma_{S_B(a)}(q_B(b))w(q_B(a))w(S_B(a)q_B(b))M_{S_B(a)}M_{S_B(b)}.
\end{align}
Applying \cref{qubit-mult-comm} and \cref{eqn:qubit-clifford-section-product}, we get
\begin{align}
B(a)B(b) &= \alpha_B(a)\alpha_B(b)\gamma_{S_B(a)}(q_B(b))\kappa(S_B(a),S_B(b)) \notag\\
& \times i^{\mu(q_B(a),S_B(a)q_B(b))}w(q_B(a)+S_B(a)q_B(b))w(c(S_B(a),S_B(b)))M_{S_B(a)S_B(b)}\\
&= \alpha_B(a)\alpha_B(b)\gamma_{S_B(a)}(q_B(b))\kappa(S_B(a),S_B(b)) \notag\\
& \times i^{\mu(q_B(a),S_B(a)q_B(b))+\mu(q_B(a)+S_B(a)q_B(b),c(S_B(a),S_B(b)))} \notag\\
& \times w(q_B(a)+S_B(a)q_B(b)+c(S_B(a),S_B(b)))M_{S_B(a)S_B(b)}.
\end{align}
On the other hand,
\begin{equation}
i^{\mu(a,b)}B(a+b)=i^{\mu(a,b)}\alpha_B(a+b)w(q_B(a+b))M_{S_B(a+b)}.
\end{equation}
Comparing the two expressions and using the uniqueness of the normal form as in \cref{clifford-normal-form} gives \cref{eqn:qubit-third-level-S-equation,eqn:qubit-third-level-q-equation,eqn:qubit-third-level-alpha-equation}.
<!-- end proof-54 -->
<!-- lem-25: body_md -->
\label{lem:qubit-twisted-affine-extension}
The multiplication in \cref{eqn:qubit-twisted-affine-product} defines a group structure on \(\operatorname{ASp}_c(V_n)\), and there is a short exact sequence
\begin{equation}\label{eqn:qubit-twisted-affine-extension}
1\longrightarrow V_n\longrightarrow \operatorname{ASp}_c(V_n)\longrightarrow \operatorname{Sp}(V_n)\longrightarrow 1.
\end{equation}
Moreover, the normal form in \cref{clifford-normal-form} induces an isomorphism
\begin{equation}\label{eqn:qubit-clifford-quotient-twisted-affine}
\overline{\mathcal C}^{(2)}\cong \operatorname{ASp}_c(V_n).
\end{equation}
<!-- end lem-25 -->
<!-- proof-55: body_md -->
Associativity of the multiplication in \cref{eqn:qubit-twisted-affine-product} follows from the cocycle identity in \cref{eqn:qubit-c-cocycle}, while \cref{eqn:qubit-c-normalization} implies that \((0,\operatorname{Id}_{V_n})\) is the identity element. For \((q,S)\in\operatorname{ASp}_c(V_n)\), an inverse is given by
\begin{equation}
(q,S)^{-1}= (-S^{-1}\bigl(q+c(S,S^{-1})\bigr),S^{-1} ).
\end{equation}
Indeed, the product of \((q,S)\) with this element on the right is \((0,\operatorname{Id}_{V_n})\), and the cocycle identity implies that the same element is also a left inverse. Hence, \cref{eqn:qubit-twisted-affine-product} defines a group structure on \(\operatorname{ASp}_c(V_n)\). The inclusion \(V_n\to\operatorname{ASp}_c(V_n)\) is given by \(q\mapsto(q,\operatorname{Id}_{V_n})\), while the projection \(\operatorname{ASp}_c(V_n)\to\operatorname{Sp}(V_n)\) is given by \((q,S)\mapsto S\). The projection is surjective and its kernel is precisely the image of \(V_n\), which gives \cref{eqn:qubit-twisted-affine-extension}. For the second statement, define
\begin{align}
\Xi:\operatorname{ASp}_c(V_n) &\longrightarrow \overline{\mathcal C}^{(2)},\\
(q,S) &\longmapsto [w(q)M_S].
\end{align}
Since the analog of the normal form in \cref{clifford-normal-form} continues to hold when \(p=2\), it follows that \(\Xi\) is a bijection. Using \cref{eqn:qubit-clifford-representative-action,eqn:qubit-clifford-section-product} and discarding scalar phases in \(\overline{\mathcal C}^{(2)}\), we obtain
\begin{align}
[w(q)M_S][w(r)M_T] &= [w(q)w(Sr)w(c(S,T))M_{ST}]= [w(q+Sr+c(S,T))M_{ST}].
\end{align}
Thus, \(\Xi\) is a group homomorphism and hence an isomorphism.
<!-- end proof-55 -->
<!-- cor-14: body_md -->
\label{cor:qubit-affine-cohomological-obstruction}
Let \(S:V_n\to\operatorname{Sp}(V_n)\) be a homomorphism. A map \(q:V_n\to V_n\) satisfying \cref{eqn:qubit-third-level-q-equation} exists if and only if
\begin{equation}\label{eqn:qubit-affine-obstruction-class}
[c_S]=0\in H^2(V_n,V_{n,S}).
\end{equation}
If this obstruction vanishes and \(q_0\) is one solution, then every solution is of the form \(q=q_0+z\) for some \(z\in Z^1(V_n,V_{n,S})\). Replacing \(q\) by \(q+q_v\), where
\begin{equation}
q_v(a):=S(a)v-v,
\end{equation}
corresponds to conjugating the twisted affine homomorphism \(\Phi_{q,S}:V_n\to\operatorname{ASp}_c(V_n)\) by the translation \((-v,\operatorname{Id}_{V_n})\in\operatorname{ASp}_c(V_n)\). Consequently, when \([c_S]=0\), twisted affine homomorphisms with fixed symplectic part \(S\), modulo conjugation by translations, form a torsor over \(H^1(V_n,V_{n,S})\).
<!-- end cor-14 -->
<!-- proof-56: body_md -->
A solution \(q\) exists if and only if \(c_S\) is a \(2\)-coboundary, which is equivalent to \([c_S]=0\in H^2(V_n,V_{n,S})\). Suppose that \(q_0\) is one solution. If \(q\) is any other solution, then \(\delta(q-q_0)=0\), so \(q-q_0\in Z^1(V_n,V_{n,S})\). Conversely, if \(z\in Z^1(V_n,V_{n,S})\), then
\begin{equation}
\delta(q_0+z)=\delta q_0+\delta z=-c_S,
\end{equation}
so \(q_0+z\) is again a solution. Thus, the set of solutions is a torsor over \(Z^1(V_n,V_{n,S})\).

For the second statement, let \(v\in V_n\). Using the multiplication law in \(\operatorname{ASp}_c(V_n)\) and the normalization \(c(\operatorname{Id}_{V_n},S)=c(S,\operatorname{Id}_{V_n})=0\), we have
\begin{align}
(-v,\operatorname{Id}_{V_n})(q(a),S(a))(v,\operatorname{Id}_{V_n}) &= (-v+q(a),S(a))(v,\operatorname{Id}_{V_n})\\
&= (q(a)+S(a)v-v,S(a))\\
&= (q(a)+q_v(a),S(a)).
\end{align}
Thus, conjugation by the translation \((-v,\operatorname{Id}_{V_n})\) replaces \(q\) by \(q+q_v\). The maps \(q_v\) are precisely the \(1\)-coboundaries in \(B^1(V_n,V_{n,S})\). Hence, after quotienting by translation conjugacy, the torsor over \(Z^1(V_n,V_{n,S})\) descends to a torsor over \(H^1(V_n,V_{n,S})\).
<!-- end proof-56 -->
<!-- lem-26: body_md -->
\label{lem:qubit-phase-obstruction-cocycle}
Define \(F_{q,S}:V_n\times V_n\to U(1)\) by
\begin{align}
F_{q,S}(a,b) &:= i^{\mu(q(a),S(a)q(b))+\mu(q(a)+S(a)q(b),c_S(a,b))} \gamma_{S(a)}(q(b))\kappa(S(a),S(b)). 
\label{eqn:qubit-Fqs}
\end{align}
Then
\begin{equation}
T_{q,S}(a)T_{q,S}(b)=F_{q,S}(a,b)T_{q,S}(a+b),
\end{equation}
and hence \(F_{q,S}\) is a normalized \(U(1)\)-valued \(2\)-cocycle on \(V_n\). Consequently,
\begin{equation}\label{eqn:qubit-Rqs}
R_{q,S}(a,b):=F_{q,S}(a,b)i^{-\mu(a,b)}
\end{equation}
is also a normalized \(U(1)\)-valued \(2\)-cocycle.
<!-- end lem-26 -->
<!-- proof-57: body_md -->
The calculation in \cref{prop:qubit-third-level-classification}, together with \cref{eqn:qubit-third-level-q-equation}, gives
\begin{equation}
T_{q,S}(a)T_{q,S}(b)=F_{q,S}(a,b)T_{q,S}(a+b).
\end{equation}
Associativity of multiplication implies that \(F_{q,S}\) satisfies the \(2\)-cocycle identity. Moreover, \(q(0)=0\), \(S(0)=\operatorname{Id}_{V_n}\), and \(M_{\operatorname{Id}_{V_n}}=I\), so $T_{q,S}(0)=I$. Setting either argument equal to \(0\) in the preceding multiplication law therefore gives $F_{q,S}(a,0)=F_{q,S}(0,a)=1.$
Hence, \(F_{q,S}\) is a normalized \(U(1)\)-valued \(2\)-cocycle. The multiplication law
\begin{equation}
w(a)w(b)=i^{\mu(a,b)}w(a+b)
\end{equation}
implies, by associativity of the Weyl operators, that \(i^{\mu(a,b)}\) satisfies the \(2\)-cocycle identity. Since \(w(0)=I\), setting either argument equal to \(0\) gives $i^{\mu(a,0)}=i^{\mu(0,a)}=1.$ Thus, \((a,b)\mapsto i^{\mu(a,b)}\) is also a normalized \(U(1)\)-valued \(2\)-cocycle. Therefore, the ratio in \cref{eqn:qubit-Rqs} is a normalized \(U(1)\)-valued \(2\)-cocycle.
<!-- end proof-57 -->
<!-- cor-15: body_md -->
\label{cor:qubit-phase-cohomological-obstruction}
Let \(S:V_n\to\operatorname{Sp}(V_n)\) be a homomorphism and let \(q:V_n\to V_n\) satisfy \cref{eqn:qubit-third-level-q-equation}. There exists a phase function \(\alpha:V_n\to U(1)\) such that
\begin{equation}
B(a):=\alpha(a)w(q(a))M_{S(a)}
\end{equation}
belongs to \(Y^3_2(V_n)\) if and only if
\begin{equation}\label{eqn:qubit-phase-obstruction-class}
[R_{q,S}]=0\in H^2(V_n,U(1)).
\end{equation}
<!-- end cor-15 -->
<!-- proof-58: body_md -->
By \cref{prop:qubit-third-level-classification}, the phase equation is equivalent to
\begin{equation}
\frac{\alpha(a+b)}{\alpha(a)\alpha(b)}=R_{q,S}(a,b)
\end{equation}
for all \(a,b\in V_n\). Recall that for a \(1\)-cochain \(\phi:V_n\to U(1)\), its \(2\)-coboundary is given by \((\delta\phi)(a,b)=\frac{\phi(a)\phi(b)}{\phi(a+b)}\). Hence, the preceding equation is equivalent to $R_{q,S}=\delta(\alpha^{-1})$. Therefore, such an \(\alpha\) exists if and only if \(R_{q,S}\) is a \(2\)-coboundary, which is equivalent to \cref{eqn:qubit-phase-obstruction-class}.
<!-- end proof-58 -->
<!-- prop-17: body_md -->
\label{prop:qubit-section-independence}
Let \(S\mapsto M_S\) and \(S\mapsto M'_S\) be two normalized choices of representatives in \(\mathcal C^{(2)}\). Then there exist functions
\begin{align}
\eta:\operatorname{Sp}(V_n)  \longrightarrow U(1), \qquad
d:\operatorname{Sp}(V_n)  \longrightarrow V_n
\end{align}
such that
\begin{equation}\label{eqn:qubit-change-section}
M'_S=\eta(S)w(d(S))M_S.
\end{equation}
If \(c\) and \(c'\) are the corresponding \(V_n\)-valued cocycles, then
\begin{equation}\label{eqn:qubit-c-section-change}
c'(S,T)=c(S,T)+d(S)+Sd(T)-d(ST).
\end{equation}
Consequently, $[c']=[c]\in H^2(\operatorname{Sp}(V_n),V_n)$.  For a fixed homomorphism \(S:V_n\to\operatorname{Sp}(V_n)\), the corresponding pulled-back classes satisfy $[c'_S]=[c_S]\in H^2(V_n,V_{n,S})$. Moreover, if \(q\) is compatible with \(c_S\), define
\begin{equation}\label{eqn:qubit-q-section-change}
q'(a):=q(a)-d(S(a)).
\end{equation}
Then \(q'\) is compatible with \(c'_S\), and the corresponding phase-obstruction classes satisfy $[R^{\prime}_{q',S}]=[R_{q,S}]\in H^2(V_n,U(1))$.
<!-- end prop-17 -->
<!-- proof-59: body_md -->
Since \(M'_S\) and \(M_S\) have the same image under \(\Psi\), the operator \(M'_SM_S^*\) lies in \(\ker\Psi=\mathcal C^{(1)}\). Thus, \cref{eqn:qubit-change-section} follows from the analog of \cref{clifford-normal-form}. Comparing the labels in the products \(M'_SM'_T\) and \(M'_{ST}\) and using \cref{eqn:qubit-clifford-representative-action} gives
\begin{equation}
c'(S,T)+d(ST)=d(S)+Sd(T)+c(S,T).
\end{equation}
This is precisely \cref{eqn:qubit-c-section-change}. Hence, \(c'\) and \(c\) differ by the \(2\)-coboundary of the \(1\)-cochain \(d\), and therefore determine the same class in \(H^2(\operatorname{Sp}(V_n),V_n)\). Pulling back along \(S\) gives \([c'_S]=[c_S]\). Define $d_S(a):=d(S(a)).$ By \cref{eqn:qubit-c-section-change}, we have
\begin{equation}
c'_S=c_S+\delta d_S.
\end{equation}
If \(\delta q=-c_S\), then \cref{eqn:qubit-q-section-change} gives
\begin{equation}
\delta q'=\delta q-\delta d_S=-c_S-\delta d_S=-c'_S.
\end{equation}
Thus, \(q'\) is compatible with the new section. Finally, define
\begin{align}
T(a) :=w(q(a))M_{S(a)}, \qquad
T'(a):=w(q'(a))M'_{S(a)}.
\end{align}
Using \cref{eqn:qubit-change-section}, \cref{eqn:qubit-q-section-change} and the characteristic-two multiplication law, we obtain $T'(a)=\lambda(a)T(a),$ where $\lambda(a):=\eta(S(a))i^{\mu(q'(a),d(S(a)))}.$ Therefore, if \(F_{q,S}\) and \(F'_{q',S}\) denote the corresponding projective multipliers, then $F'_{q',S}=F_{q,S}\cdot\delta\lambda.$ Since \(i^{\mu(a,b)}\) is unchanged, it follows that $R'_{q',S}=R_{q,S}\cdot\delta\lambda.$
Hence, \(R'_{q',S}\) and \(R_{q,S}\) determine the same class in \(H^2(V_n,U(1))\).
<!-- end proof-59 -->
<!-- cor-16: body_md -->
\label{cor:qubit-third-level-generator-equations}
A pair of maps \(S:V_n\to\operatorname{Sp}(V_n)\) and \(q:V_n\to V_n\) satisfies \cref{eqn:qubit-third-level-S-equation,eqn:qubit-third-level-q-equation} if and only if
\begin{align}
S_iS_j &= S_jS_i, \label{eqn:qubit-generator-S-commute}\\
S_i^2 &= \operatorname{Id}_{V_n}, \label{eqn:qubit-generator-S-order}\\
q_i+S_iq_j+c(S_i,S_j) &= q_j+S_jq_i+c(S_j,S_i), \label{eqn:qubit-generator-q-commute}\\
q_i+S_iq_i+c(S_i,S_i) &= 0. \label{eqn:qubit-generator-q-order}
\end{align}
for all \(1\leq i,j\leq 2n\).
<!-- end cor-16 -->
<!-- proof-60: body_md -->
By \cref{eqn:qubit-twisted-affine-homomorphism}, specifying \((q,S)\) is equivalent to specifying a group homomorphism
\begin{align}
\Phi_{q,S}:V_n &\longrightarrow \operatorname{ASp}_c(V_n),\\
a &\longmapsto (q(a),S(a)).
\end{align}
The additive group \(V_n\) is generated by \(e_1,\ldots,e_{2n}\), subject to the relations
\begin{equation}
e_i+e_j=e_j+e_i,\qquad 2e_i=0.
\end{equation}
Hence, \(\Phi_{q,S}\) is a homomorphism if and only if the elements \((q_i,S_i)\) commute pairwise and have order dividing \(2\). Using \cref{eqn:qubit-twisted-affine-product}, pairwise commutativity is equivalent to \cref{eqn:qubit-generator-S-commute,eqn:qubit-generator-q-commute}. Moreover,
\begin{equation}
(q_i,S_i)^2=(q_i+S_iq_i+c(S_i,S_i),S_i^2).
\end{equation}
Thus, \((q_i,S_i)^2=(0,\operatorname{Id}_{V_n})\) is equivalent to \cref{eqn:qubit-generator-S-order,eqn:qubit-generator-q-order}.
<!-- end proof-60 -->
<!-- cor-17: body_md -->
\label{cor:qubit-phase-generator-obstruction}
Let \(q\) and \(S\) satisfy \cref{eqn:qubit-third-level-S-equation,eqn:qubit-third-level-q-equation}. Then $[R_{q,S}]=0\in H^2(V_n,U(1))$ if and only if
\begin{equation}\label{eqn:qubit-phase-generator-test}
\frac{R_{q,S}(e_i,e_j)}{R_{q,S}(e_j,e_i)}=1
\end{equation}
for all \(1\leq i,j\leq 2n\). Equivalently,
\begin{equation}\label{eqn:qubit-phase-generator-test-expanded}
\frac{\gamma_{S_i}(q_j)\kappa(S_i,S_j)}{\gamma_{S_j}(q_i)\kappa(S_j,S_i)}i^{\Delta_{ij}}=1,
\end{equation}
where
\begin{align}
\Delta_{ij} &:= \mu(q_i,S_iq_j)-\mu(q_j,S_jq_i) \notag\\
&\quad+\mu(q_i+S_iq_j,c(S_i,S_j))-\mu(q_j+S_jq_i,c(S_j,S_i)) \notag\\
&\quad-\mu(e_i,e_j)+\mu(e_j,e_i)
\end{align}
in $\mathbb Z_4$
<!-- end cor-17 -->
<!-- proof-61: body_md -->
By \cref{lem:qubit-phase-obstruction-cocycle}, \(R_{q,S}\) is a normalized \(U(1)\)-valued \(2\)-cocycle on the finite abelian group \(V_n\). Therefore, \cref{cor:coboundary-iff-trivial-commutator} implies that its cohomology class vanishes if and only if its commutator bicharacter is trivial on pairs of basis vectors. This gives \cref{eqn:qubit-phase-generator-test}. Substituting \cref{eqn:qubit-Fqs,eqn:qubit-Rqs} gives \cref{eqn:qubit-phase-generator-test-expanded}.
<!-- end proof-61 -->
<!-- lem-27: body_md -->
\label{lem:upper-unipotent-commuting-lifts}
Let \(p\) be an odd prime and let \(m\geq 1\). Write $V_m=\mathbb F_p^m\oplus \mathbb F_p^m$
with its standard symplectic form. For each symmetric matrix \(C\in\operatorname{Sym}_m(\mathbb F_p)\), define
\begin{equation}
u_C:=\begin{pmatrix}I&C\\0&I\end{pmatrix}\in\operatorname{Sp}(V_m).
\end{equation}
Then there exist Clifford unitaries \(N_C\) such that
\begin{equation}
N_Cw(s,t)N_C^*=w(s+Ct,t)
\end{equation}
for all \((s,t)\in V_m\), and $N_CN_D=N_{C+D}$
for all \(C,D\in\operatorname{Sym}_m(\mathbb F_p)\). Moreover, if \(M_{u_C}\) denotes any fixed choice of Clifford representative implementing \(u_C\), then the operators \(M_{u_C}\) commute pairwise.
<!-- end lem-27 -->
<!-- proof-62: body_md -->
The assignment \(C\mapsto u_C\) is a homomorphism from the additive group \(\operatorname{Sym}_m(\mathbb F_p)\) to \(\operatorname{Sp}(V_m)\). We now choose explicit Clifford lifts of these symplectic matrices using diagonal quadratic phase gates and the \(m\)-qudit Fourier transform. For \(C\in\operatorname{Sym}_m(\mathbb F_p)\), define the diagonal quadratic phase gate
\begin{equation}
D_C\ket{x}:=\omega^{\frac12 x^TCx}\ket{x}.
\end{equation}
We first compute the conjugation action of \(D_C\) on Weyl operators. For \(s,t,x\in\mathbb F_p^m\), we have
\begin{align}
D_Cw(s,t)D_C^*\ket{x}&=D_C (\omega^{-\frac12 s\cdot t}Z^tX^s\omega^{-\frac12 x^TCx}\ket{x} )\\
&=D_C (\omega^{-\frac12 s\cdot t-\frac12 x^TCx+t\cdot(x+s)}\ket{x+s} )\\
&=\omega^{-\frac12 s\cdot t-\frac12 x^TCx+t\cdot(x+s)+\frac12(x+s)^TC(x+s)}\ket{x+s}.
\end{align}
Since \(C=C^T\), we have
\begin{equation}
(x+s)^TC(x+s)-x^TCx=2x^TCs+s^TCs.
\end{equation}
Therefore, we have
\begin{align}
D_Cw(s,t)D_C^*\ket{x}&=\omega^{-\frac12 s\cdot t+t\cdot(x+s)+x^TCs+\frac12 s^TCs}\ket{x+s}\\
&=\omega^{-\frac12 s\cdot(t+Cs)+(t+Cs)\cdot(x+s)}\ket{x+s}\\
&=\omega^{-\frac12 s\cdot(t+Cs)}Z^{t+Cs}X^s\ket{x}=w(s,t+Cs)\ket{x}.
\end{align}
Since this holds for every computational basis vector \(\ket{x}\), we obtain
\begin{equation}\label{eqn:DC-conjugation-general-m}
D_Cw(s,t)D_C^*=w(s,t+Cs).
\end{equation}
Let \(\mathcal F\) denote the \(m\)-qudit Fourier transform
\begin{equation}
\mathcal F\ket{x}:=\frac{1}{p^{m/2}}\sum_{y\in\mathbb F_p^m}\omega^{x\cdot y}\ket{y}.
\end{equation}
We have, 
\begin{align}
\mathcal F X^s\mathcal F^*\ket{x}
&=\frac{1}{p^{m/2}}\sum_{y\in\mathbb F_p^m}\omega^{-x\cdot y}\mathcal F\ket{y+s}\\
&=\frac{1}{p^m}\sum_{y,z\in\mathbb F_p^m}\omega^{-x\cdot y+(y+s)\cdot z}\ket{z}\\
&=\frac{1}{p^m}\sum_{z\in\mathbb F_p^m}\omega^{s\cdot z}\left(\sum_{y\in\mathbb F_p^m}\omega^{y\cdot(z-x)}\right)\ket{z}=\omega^{s\cdot x}\ket{x}=Z^s\ket{x}.
\end{align}
Thus, $\mathcal F X^s\mathcal F^*=Z^s$. Similarly, we have
\begin{align}
\mathcal F Z^t\mathcal F^*\ket{x}
&=\frac{1}{p^{m/2}}\sum_{y\in\mathbb F_p^m}\omega^{-x\cdot y}\mathcal F Z^t\ket{y}\\
&=\frac{1}{p^{m/2}}\sum_{y\in\mathbb F_p^m}\omega^{-x\cdot y+t\cdot y}\mathcal F\ket{y}\\
&=\frac{1}{p^m}\sum_{y,z\in\mathbb F_p^m}\omega^{(t-x)\cdot y+y\cdot z}\ket{z}=\ket{x-t}=X^{-t}\ket{x}.
\end{align}
Thus, $\mathcal F Z^t\mathcal F^*=X^{-t}$. 
Therefore, we have
\begin{align}
\mathcal Fw(s,t)\mathcal F^*
&=\omega^{-\frac12 s\cdot t}\mathcal F Z^tX^s\mathcal F^*\\
&=\omega^{-\frac12 s\cdot t}X^{-t}Z^s\\
&=\omega^{-\frac12 s\cdot t}\omega^{s\cdot t}Z^sX^{-t}=\omega^{\frac12 s\cdot t}Z^sX^{-t}=w(-t,s).
\end{align}
Define $N_C:=\mathcal F^*D_{-C}\mathcal F$. Then \(N_C\) implements the upper unipotent symplectic transformation \(u_C\). Indeed, we have
\begin{align}
N_Cw(s,t)N_C^*
&=\mathcal F^*D_{-C}\mathcal Fw(s,t)\mathcal F^*D_{-C}^*\mathcal F\\
&=\mathcal F^*D_{-C}w(-t,s)D_{-C}^*\mathcal F\\
&=\mathcal F^*w(-t,s+Ct)\mathcal F=w(s+Ct,t)=w(u_C(s,t)).
\end{align}
Thus, \(N_C\) is a Clifford lift of \(u_C\). Moreover, these lifts commute because
\begin{align}
N_CN_D
&=\mathcal F^*D_{-C}\mathcal F\mathcal F^*D_{-D}\mathcal F\\
&=\mathcal F^*D_{-C}D_{-D}\mathcal F\\
&=\mathcal F^*D_{-(C+D)}\mathcal F=N_{C+D}=N_{D+C}=N_DN_C.
\end{align}
Finally, let \(M_{u_C}\) denote the fixed Clifford representative implementing \(u_C\). Both \(M_{u_C}\) and \(N_C\) implement the same conjugation action on Weyl operator and \(N_C^*M_{u_C}\) commutes with every Weyl operator. Hence, there exists \(\eta(C)\in U(1)\) such that $M_{u_C}=\eta(C)N_C.$
Consequently, the fixed lifts \(M_{u_C}\) also commute pairwise. Indeed, we have
\begin{align}
M_{u_C}M_{u_D}
&=\eta(C)\eta(D)N_CN_D\\
&=\eta(C)\eta(D)N_DN_C\\
&=M_{u_D}M_{u_C}.
\end{align}
This completes the proof.
<!-- end proof-62 -->
<!-- proof-63: body_md -->
Let \(A_Z\subseteq\mathcal C^{(1)}\) denote the maximal abelian subgroup generated by the \(Z\)-type Weyl operators. Explicitly,
\begin{equation}
A_Z:=\{\lambda Z^t:\lambda\in U(1),\ t\in\mathbb F_p^n\}.
\end{equation}
Suppose that \(U\) is semi-Clifford. By definition, there exist \(C_1,C_2\in\mathcal C^{(2)}\) and a diagonal unitary operator \(D\) such that $U=C_1DC_2$. Since \(D\) is diagonal, it commutes with \(A_Z\). Hence, $DA_ZD^*=A_Z$. Set
\begin{equation}
A:=C_2^*A_ZC_2,\qquad A':=C_1A_ZC_1^*.
\end{equation}
Since \(C_1\) and \(C_2\) act on \(\mathcal C^{(1)}\) by automorphisms, both \(A\) and \(A'\) are maximal abelian subgroups of \(\mathcal C^{(1)}\). Moreover, we have
\begin{equation}
UAU^*=C_1DC_2(C_2^*A_ZC_2)C_2^*D^*C_1^*=C_1DA_ZD^*C_1^*=C_1A_ZC_1^*=A'.
\end{equation}
Thus, \(U\) maps a maximal abelian subgroup of \(\mathcal C^{(1)}\) to another maximal abelian subgroup of \(\mathcal C^{(1)}\). Conversely, suppose that there exist maximal abelian subgroups \(A,A'\subseteq\mathcal C^{(1)}\) such that $UAU^*=A'$.  It is known that \(\mathcal C^{(2)}\) acts transitively on maximal abelian subgroups of \(\mathcal C^{(1)}\). Hence, there exist \(C_R,C_L\in\mathcal C^{(2)}\) such that $C_RA_ZC_R^*=A$ and $ C_LA'C_L^*=A_Z$. 
Define $V:=C_LUC_R$. We have
\begin{align}
V A_Z V^*
&= C_L U C_R A_Z C_R^* U^* C_L^* = C_L U A U^* C_L^*= C_L A' C_L^*= A_Z.
\end{align}
Hence, \(V\) determines an automorphism of \(A_Z\) via conjugation that fixes scalar phases. This automorphism is implemented by a \(K\in\mathcal C^{(2)}\). This is because any automorphism of \(A_Z\) fixing scalar phases has the form $Z^t\mapsto \chi(t)Z^{Mt}$, where \(M\in \operatorname{GL}(\mathbb F^n_p)\) and \(\chi:\mathbb F_p^n\to U(1)\) is a character.\footnote{Since \(A_Z/U(1) \cong \mathbb F_p^n\), any automorphism of \(A_Z\) fixing scalar phases descends to an automorphism of \(\mathbb F_p^n\). Hence it is given by some \(M\in \operatorname{GL}(\mathbb F^n_p)\). Therefore, the image of \(Z^t\) must lie in the coset corresponding to \(Mt\), so it has the form $Z^t\longmapsto \chi(t)Z^{Mt}$
for some phase \(\chi(t)\in U(1)\). Since the automorphism is a group homomorphism and \(Z^{t+s}=Z^tZ^s\), we get
\[
\chi(t+s)Z^{(Mt+Ms)}
=
\chi(t+s)Z^{M(t+s)}
=
\chi(t)\chi(s)Z^{Mt+Ms}.
\]
Thus \(\chi(t+s)=\chi(t)\chi(s)\), so \(\chi:\mathbb F_p^n\to U(1)\) is a character. Therefore, the automorphism of \(A_Z\) is implemented by some Clifford operator \(K\in\mathcal C^{(2)}\) normalizing \(A_Z\).
}
The linear part \(t\mapsto Mt\) is implemented by a permutation of the computational basis, hence by an element of \(\mathcal C^{(2)}\). The character factor \(\chi(t)\) is implemented by conjugation with an \(X\)-type Weyl operator\footnote{
For \(L\in\operatorname{GL}(\mathbb F^n_p)\), define the permutation \(P_L\) by $P_L\ket{x}=\ket{Lx}$. 
Then
\[
P_L Z^t P_L^*\ket{x}=\omega^{t\cdot L^{-1}x}\ket{x}=\omega^{((L^{-1})^{T}t)\cdot x}\ket{x}=Z^{(L^{-1})^{T}t}\ket{x}.
\]
Thus, choosing \(L\) such that \((L^{-1})^{T}=M\), the unitary \(P_L\) implements \(Z^t\mapsto Z^{Mt}\). \(P_L \in \mathcal{C}^{(2)}\) since it maps Weyl operators to Weyl operators. Moreover, every character \(\chi:\mathbb F_p^n\to U(1)\) has the form \(\chi(t)=\omega^{s\cdot t}\) for some \(s\in\mathbb F_p^n\). Conjugation by \(X^s\) gives
$X^s Z^t (X^s)^*=\omega^{-s\cdot t}Z^t.$
Choosing \(s\) with the appropriate sign therefore implements the factor \(Z^t\mapsto \chi(t)Z^t\).}. Hence, we have $VK^*aKV^*=a$ for every \(a\in A_Z\). Hence, \(VK^*\) commutes with \(A_Z\). Since the algebra generated by \(A_Z\) is the diagonal maximal abelian algebra, its commutant is itself. Therefore \(VK^*\) is diagonal. Write $D:=VK^*$. Then \(D\) is diagonal and $V=DK$. Consequently, we have
$U=C_L^*DKC_R^*.$
Since \(C_L^*, KC_R^* \in \mathcal{C}^{(2)}\), \(U\) is semi-Clifford in the sense of \cref{def:semi-clifford}.
<!-- end proof-63 -->
<!-- proof-64: body_md -->
Suppose, for contradiction, that \(\operatorname{codim}K_U=5\).  Then \(\dim K_U=1\) and
$\dim E_U=5.$
The symplectic form on $K_U$ is identically zero.  Set \(W:=q_U(K_U)\). 
By \cref{lem:kernel-cocycle-consequences}, \(W\) fixed pointwise by \(E_U\) and symplectic form on $W$ vanishes. As in \cref{lem:three-qudit-codim-four-impossible}, we choose a symplectic decomposition adapted to \(W\) by choosing a four-dimensional non-degenerate symplectic subspace \(H\subseteq W^\perp\), and choosing an isotropic line \(W^*\subseteq H^\perp\) dual to \(W\). Thus,
\begin{equation}\label{eqn:three-qudit-c5-witt}
\mathbb F_p^6=W\oplus H\oplus W^*.
\end{equation}
Choose dual bases of \(W\) and \(W^*\), choose a symplectic basis of \(H\), and let \(J\) denote the matrix of the symplectic form on \(H\). With the same ordering of the basis as in \cref{lem:three-qudit-codim-four-impossible}, the symplectic form on $\mathbb F_p^6$ is represented by the matrix in \cref{eqn:three-qudit-c4-symplectic-matrix} with block sizes \(1,4,1\) in place of \(2,2,2\). As in \cref{lem:three-qudit-codim-four-impossible}, 
every symplectic transformation fixing \(W\) pointwise therefore has a unique expression
\begin{equation}\label{eqn:three-qudit-c5-stabilizer}
T(g,A,z):=\begin{pmatrix}1&A&z\\0&g&gJA^T\\0&0&1\end{pmatrix},
\end{equation}
where \(g\in\operatorname{Sp}(H)\), \(A\in M_{1\times4}(\mathbb F_p)\), and \(z\in\mathbb F_p\). 
A direct block multiplication gives
\begin{equation}\label{eqn:three-qudit-c5-product}
T(g_1,A_1,z_1)T(g_2,A_2,z_2)=T\left(g_1g_2,A_2+A_1g_2,z_1+z_2+A_1g_2JA_2^T\right).
\end{equation}
As in \cref{lem:three-qudit-codim-four-impossible}, we record the induced action on the non-degenerate symplectic component \(H \cong \mathbb F_p^4\). Taking the middle diagonal block defines a homomorphism
\begin{align}
\rho:E_U&\longrightarrow \operatorname{Sp}(\mathbb F_p^4),\\
T(g,A,z)&\longmapsto g.
\end{align}
Set \(r:=\dim \rho(E_U) \) and \(E_0:=\ker\rho\). Hence, 
$\dim E_0=5-r$. Moreover, \(\rho(E_U)\) is an abelian \(p\)-subgroup of \(\operatorname{Sp}(\mathbb F_p^4)\). Since such a  subgroup has order at most \(p^3\), we have \(r\leq3\).
We next analyze the \(A\) components of the elements of \(E_0\), analogous  to the analysis in \cref{lem:three-qudit-codim-four-impossible}. Define
\begin{equation}
\mathcal A:=\{A\in M_{1\times4}(\mathbb F_p):T(I,A,z)\in E_0\text{ for some }z\}.
\end{equation}
As in \cref{lem:three-qudit-codim-four-impossible},  \(\mathcal A\) is a linear subspace. As in \cref{lem:three-qudit-codim-four-impossible}, we 
get $AJD^T=DJA^T$
for all \(A,D\in\mathcal A\). On the other hand, \(AJD^T\) is a scalar and since \(J^T=-J\), we have
\begin{equation}
AJD^T=(AJD^T)^T=DJ^TA^T=-DJA^T.
\end{equation}
Hence, \(2AJD^T=0\). Since \(p\) is odd, we have
$AJD^T=0$
for all \(A,D\in\mathcal A\).
Thus, \(M_{1\times4}(\mathbb F_p)\) becomes a four-dimensional symplectic vector space with alternating form
\begin{equation}
\omega(A,D):=AJD^T.
\end{equation}
Indeed, \(\omega(A,A)=AJA^T=0\) because \(J\) is skew-symmetric, and the form is non-degenerate since \(AJD^T=0\) for every \(D\) implies \(AJ=0\)\footnote{
If we choose \(D=e_i\), where \(e_i\) is the \(i\)-th standard basis row vector of \(\mathbb F_p^4\), then \(AJD^T\) is the \(i\)-th entry of \(AJ\). Since \(AJD^T=0\) for every \(D\), each entry of \(AJ\) vanishes. Hence, \(AJ=0\).
}, hence \(A=0\) because \(J\) is invertible. By the condition $AJD^T=0$, the restriction of \(\omega\) to \(\mathcal A\) vanishes identically, so \(\mathcal A\) is isotropic. Since an isotropic subspace of a four-dimensional symplectic vector space has dimension at most \(2\), we conclude that
$\dim\mathcal A\leq2.$ 
The homomorphism
\begin{align}
\phi : E_0 &\longrightarrow \mathcal A,\\
T(I,A,z) &\longmapsto A.
\end{align}
has kernel of dimension at most \(1\), since $\ker \phi$ is contained in \(\{T(I,0,z):z\in\mathbb F_p\}\). Since the homomorphism \(E_0\to\mathcal A\), \(T(I,A,z)\mapsto A\), has image of dimension at most \(2\) and kernel of dimension at most \(1\), the rank-nullity theorem gives
$\dim E_0\leq2+1=3.$
Since \(\dim E_0=5-r\), we obtain \(r\geq2\). Hence,
$r=2,3.$
As in \cref{lem:three-qudit-codim-four-impossible}, we rule out the possible ranks of the induced action separately.

\begin{enumerate}

\item Suppose first that \(r=2\). Since \(\dim E_0=3\), 
rank-nullity gives
$\dim\operatorname{im}\phi\geq2.$
Since \(\operatorname{im}\phi=\mathcal A\) and we already know that \(\dim\mathcal A\leq2\), it follows that \(\dim\mathcal A=2\). After choosing a symplectic basis of \(H\), we identify \(H\) with \(\mathbb F_p^4\), so that each \(A\in M_{1\times 4}(\mathbb F_p)\) defines a linear functional on \(H\), while \(JA^T\) defines a vector in \(H\). Set
\begin{equation}
L_0:=\{h\in H:Ah=0\text{ for every }A\in\mathcal A\}.
\end{equation}
For \(A,D\in\mathcal A\), we have
\begin{equation}
D(JA^T)=DJA^T=-AJD^T=0.
\end{equation}
Hence \(JA^T\in L_0\) for every \(A\in\mathcal A\), and therefore
\begin{equation}
\{JA^T:A\in\mathcal A\}\subseteq L_0.
\end{equation}
Since \(J\) is invertible, the map \(A\mapsto JA^T\) is injective, and hence its image has dimension \(2\). On the other hand, since \(\dim\mathcal A=2\), the space \(L_0\) is the common kernel of two linearly independent linear functionals on the four-dimensional space \(H\), so \(\dim L_0=2\). It follows that
\begin{equation}
L_0=\{JA^T:A\in\mathcal A\}.
\end{equation}
Finally, for \(A,D\in\mathcal A\), the symplectic pairing of the corresponding vectors in \(L_0\) is
\begin{equation}
(JA^T)^T J(JD^T)=AJD^T=0.
\end{equation}
Thus, \(L_0\) is isotropic. Since \(\dim L_0=2\) and \(H\) is four-dimensional and symplectic, \(L_0\) is Lagrangian.
Let \(T(g,B,z)\in E_U\) and \(T(I,A,y)\in E_0\). Since \(E_U\) is abelian, comparison of the \(A\) components in \cref{eqn:three-qudit-c5-product} gives
$Ag=A.$
Hence, for every \(A\in\mathcal A\),
\begin{equation}
gJA^T=Jg^{-T}A^T=JA^T,
\end{equation}
so \(g\) fixes \(L_0\) pointwise. Comparing the last components in the same two products gives
\begin{equation}
BJA^T=AgJB^T=AJB^T=-BJA^T.
\end{equation}
Since \(p\) is odd, \(BJA^T=0\). Thus \(B\) vanishes on \(L_0\). By \cref{eqn:three-qudit-c5-stabilizer}, every element of \(E_U\) therefore fixes \(L_0\) pointwise. Since \(E_U\) also fixes \(W\) pointwise, it fixes \(W\oplus L_0\) pointwise. The subspace \(W\oplus L_0\) is three-dimensional and isotropic, and hence is Lagrangian. This contradicts \cref{lem:three-qudit-large-image-obstruction}.



\item Suppose now that \(r=3\). Then \(\rho(E_U)\) is an abelian \(p\)-subgroup of \(\operatorname{Sp}(H)\cong\operatorname{Sp}(\mathbb F_p^4)\) of order \(p^3\). By \cref{wong}, exactly as in the proof of \cref{lem:three-qudit-codim-three}, after changing the symplectic basis of \(H\) we may write $H=L_0\oplus L_0^*$ and 
\begin{equation}\label{eqn:three-qudit-c5-rank-three-image}
\rho(E_U)=\left\{g_C:=\begin{pmatrix}I&C\\0&I\end{pmatrix}:C=C^T\in\operatorname{Sym}_2(\mathbb F_p)\right\},
\end{equation}
where \(L_0\) is Lagrangian in \(H\) and is fixed pointwise by \(\rho(E_U)\).
We show that the \(A\) component of every element of \(E_U\) vanishes on \(L_0\). First let \(T(I,A,z)\in E_0\), and write \(A=(a\;\;b)\) relative to \(H=L_0\oplus L_0^*\), with \(a,b\in M_{1\times2}(\mathbb F_p)\). As in the one-dimensional image case of \cref{lem:three-qudit-codim-four-impossible}, commuting this element with an element of \(E_U\) whose image under \(\rho\) is \(g_C\) gives \(Ag_C=A\). Hence
\begin{equation}
(a\;\;aC+b)=(a\;\;b)
\end{equation}
for every \(C\in\operatorname{Sym}_2(\mathbb F_p)\). Taking \(C=I\) gives \(a=0\). Thus, every element of \(E_0\) has an \(A\) component that vanishes on \(L_0\).
For each \(C\in\operatorname{Sym}_2(\mathbb F_p)\), choose an element \(T(g_C,A_C,z_C)\in E_U\) and write \(A_C=(a_C\;\;b_C)\). Since changing the choice changes \(A_C\) by the \(A\) component of an element of \(E_0\), the row vector \(a_C\) is independent of the choice. Since \(E_U\) is abelian, comparison of the \(A\) components of the products corresponding to \(C\) and \(D\) gives
\begin{equation}\label{eqn:three-qudit-c5-aC-relation}
a_CD=a_DC
\end{equation}
for all  \(C,D \in\operatorname{Sym}_2(\mathbb F_p)\). This is the same relation that appears in the codimension \(4\) argument in \cref{lem:three-qudit-codim-four-impossible}. Taking \(D=I\) and setting \(t:=a_I^T\), we obtain
$a_C^T=Ct.$
Substituting this into \cref{eqn:three-qudit-c5-aC-relation} gives
\begin{equation}
(DC-CD)t=0
\end{equation}
for all \(C,D \in\operatorname{Sym}_2(\mathbb F_p)\). As in \cref{lem:three-qudit-codim-four-impossible}, taking
\begin{equation}
C=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad D=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}
\end{equation}
gives an invertible commutator, so \(t=0\). Hence \(a_C=0\) for every \(C\). Therefore, the \(A\) component of every element of \(E_U\) vanishes on \(L_0\).
By \cref{eqn:three-qudit-c5-rank-three-image}, the \(g\) component of every element of \(E_U\) fixes \(L_0\) pointwise. Together with \cref{eqn:three-qudit-c5-stabilizer}, this shows that \(E_U\) fixes \(L_0\) pointwise. As in \cref{lem:three-qudit-codim-four-impossible}, adjoining the already fixed isotropic line \(W\) gives the Lagrangian subspace \(W\oplus L_0\), which is fixed pointwise by \(E_U\). This again contradicts \cref{lem:three-qudit-large-image-obstruction}.
\end{enumerate}
This completes the proof.
<!-- end proof-64 -->
